Title: The Weight Of The Avatar
Summary: Why 2026 isn't about running, but accepting.
Meta Title: The Weight of the Avatar: Aang's Lesson for 2026
Meta Description: Aang ran from being the Avatar because it was heavy. See what his story teaches about facing 2026 and accepting who you already are.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
2026 is a big year for a lot of us. A year filled with expectations, hopes, and dreams. But on the flip side of that, there is also anxiety, fear, and dreams left unfulfilled.

With the New Year already here, we have to make sure our minds are clear so that we are ready to receive all that is in store. The best way to do that is by looking at the life of Aang from Avatar: The Last Airbender.

Now before the anime police kick down the door, yes, we know Avatar isn’t officially anime. It’s more anime-adjacent, but it still holds the same values, principles, and lessons that traditional anime does, which we believe earns it a seat at the table. Now that that’s out of the way, let’s get back to the lesson at hand.

⚔️ The Fight That Tested His Soul

Aang did not reject being the Avatar because he was weak.
He rejected it because it was heavy.

The moment he learned who he was, the weight of the world landed on him. Saving everyone meant responsibility, sacrifice, and pressure… things he was not ready to carry. So, he ran from his destiny, not because he did not care, but because he cared too much.

💭 The Message Behind the Madness

At the start of a new year, we feel the pull to become more… more for our families, our future and our purpose. But we hesitate because stepping into that role means pressure. It means choosing growth over comfort. It means realizing that, like the Avatar, we cannot move forward until we are willing to master every element of our life, not just the ones that come easy.

Aang didn’t become the Avatar by suddenly wanting the responsibility.
He became the Avatar by accepting that running from who he was caused more damage than facing it ever could.

🔑 The Takeaway

2026 doesn’t need you to be perfect.
It just needs you to stop running.

Sometimes the new year is not about becoming someone new.
It is about finally accepting who you already are.

Title: 🧠 Think Like Shikamaru
Summary: Win With What You've Got
Meta Title: Think Like Shikamaru: Win With What You've Got
Meta Description: Shikamaru wins with what he already has, not more power. See what Naruto's sharpest mind teaches about strategy, patience, and your edge.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Most people think growth looks like becoming stronger, faster or even being more assertive. In the world of Naruto, where power often means brute strength, explosive jutsu, or endless energy, Shikamaru Nara never moved that way.

He didn’t rely on force. He relied on his mind.

♟️ The Mind That Changed the Game

Shikamaru wasn’t the fastest, strongest, or most motivated ninja around. In fact, he was famously lazy.

But when things got serious, he was always the one you wanted in your corner.

Why?

Because he could outthink nearly anyone.

He wasn’t trying to be everything. He simply mastered what he was naturally good at: strategy, awareness, and adaptability.

🔥 The Moment That Proved It

Take his Chunin Exams match against Temari.

On the surface, he lost the fight. He forfeited. But look deeper, and you’ll see a perfect execution of his strengths. He predicted her moves, manipulated the battlefield, and placed her in a no-win situation.

The “loss” was strategic.

The end goal of the Chunin exams is to be promoted. Shikamaru knew this, so he knew he just had to exemplify he was competent, and not exactly “win.”

And that’s how he earned a promotion. He showed his value not by overpowering, but by outmaneuvering.

And that’s the point.

💭 The Lesson Behind the Laziness

Too often, we get stuck focusing on our weaknesses.

We stress over what we’re lacking, such as resources, experience, talent, time. But Shikamaru teaches us something different.

Your edge doesn’t come from checking every box. It comes from identifying your unique strength and doubling down on it.

Maybe you’re not the loudest in the room, the most outgoing, or the one with the most connections. But maybe you’re a quiet observer who sees what others miss. Maybe you can read people. Maybe you stay calm under pressure.

That’s your shadow possession jutsu.

🔑 The Takeaway

Your advantage doesn’t have to look like everyone else’s.

In fact, it’s better if it doesn’t.

So stop obsessing over what you don’t have and start maximizing what you do have.

Think like Shikamaru. Play your game.

And remember, strategy will always outlast brute strength.

— Your Weekly Anime Plug ⚡

Title: 🏴‍☠️ Take the Jump
Summary: "If you don't take risks, you can't create a future.” – Monkey D. Luffy.
Meta Title: Take the Jump: A One Piece Lesson on Facing Fear
Meta Description: Luffy never waited to feel ready. See how One Piece teaches you to welcome fear, win the small daily battles, and become your Pirate King.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
🚨Warning: The gifs in this post contain One Piece spoilers

Yeah, that’s right… I said it. Jump.

Okay, what I mean is, take that risk on yourself

😤 Welcome the fear

With anything meaningful in life, you will be faced with uncertainty

With uncertainty comes fear… and it doesn’t go away

Will you welcome the fear and continue to move forward?

Every shonen anime character you ever respected has… so why not you?

It’s easier said than done, but… YOU JUST NEED TO BELIEVE

⚔️ Win the small battles

Now, it doesn’t have to be all at once

It’s not like Luffy just woke up and started beating up Big Mom

Take your big dreams, and break them down into small habits

So small to the point that even on your worst days, you can still do them

From there, just focus on winning those little battles each day

For example, these big goals:

  • Run 3 marathons this year
  • Bench 225 lbs
  • Finish 10 books a month
  • Hit 100,000 subs on youtube
  • Build a $1 million business
  • Catch up to One Piece

Turn into these small habits:

  • Walk for 10 min
  • Open the gym door today
  • Read 1 page of my new book
  • Write the hook of my next youtube video
  • Spend 10 min on that business idea
  • Watch 1 One Piece episode

Of course, you can always level up these habits as you build consistency

Though at the end of the day

Stacking these little wins will ultimately lead you to the outcomes you want

👂 Listen to your gut

Whatever you choose to do, follow your gut

When met with fear, really just sit with it inside your body and listen

Listen for what feels alive behind the fear

Listen for what excites you

Even in the midst of uncertainty, that excitement will lead you to the life you so desire

🧠 Don’t need a high IQ

Remember, you don’t need to be the smartest to get started

This dude Luffy is def not the smartest by a long shot

You don’t need to know everything to get started

Luffy just knows one thing, to become pirate king

🔑 The takeaway

The only thing standing between you and the future you want is a simple skill

When faced with fear, take a step forward

No matter how small it may be

It might seem daunting, but just know, it’s a skill at the end of the day

And skills take time

Just keep showing up and win these small daily battles, and one day…

🏴‍☠️ You’ll be Pirate King 👑

A.K.A That version of yourself you always wanted to be

If you want to get started, leave a comment of your Big Goal and Small Habit that’s gonna lead you there

The Kam Fam will hold you accountable 😤

Remember to finish out the week strong homies!

- Kaminari ⚡️

Title: Stop Being Hollow and Find the Courage to Feel
Summary: Learn from Hell’s Paradise: Gabimaru the Hollow
Meta Title: Hell's Paradise: Gabimaru and the Courage to Feel
Meta Description: Gabimaru the Hollow learned that real strength is feeling, not shutting down. See what Hell's Paradise teaches about courage and balance.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
What’s up Kam Fam. Happy Wednesday ⚡
We hope your week is off to an electric start.

This week’s anime breakdown comes from Hell’s Paradise, and we’re pulling a powerful lesson from the main character, Gabimaru the Hollow.

We’ll keep spoilers light because this series is incredible, and season two recently dropped on Crunchyroll.

Before we dive in, if this is your first time here, subscribe to stay tapped in. If you’re already subbed, share this with a homie who’d love this!

Share

🥷 Born Hollow

Gabimaru comes from the Iwagakure clan, a group of ninjas known as the most dangerous and violent to ever exist.

From birth, they are mentally conditioned to do one thing and one thing only. Kill with no remorse.

Emotion is treated as a liability. Compassion is weakness. Any sign of feeling is something to be erased.

That is why Gabimaru is called “the Hollow.”

Stoic. Detached. Empty.

A man who completes the mission no matter the cost.

🔥 Hell and Paradise 🏝️

One of the reasons we love the name Hell’s Paradise is because that is what life often feels like.

So much of life is moving through hell in the hope of finding paradise, only to realize they are deeply connected.

You cannot truly appreciate one without the other.

  • What is joy if you have never felt sadness?
  • What is confidence if you have never felt doubt?

That is where this story hits deeper.

In season one, episode three, Yamada Asaemon Sagiri tells Gabimaru something that changes everything.

True courage is not the absence of emotion. True courage is being honest with it.

That lesson mirrors a belief many of us carry in the real world. That respect, love, and success come from being hardened.

From staying emotionally distant.

From pushing our true feelings aside and powering through life hollowed out.

From believing that as long as the mission gets accomplished, it does not matter who we have to step on to get there.

But just like Gabimaru learns, real strength is not found in shutting down.

It is found in how you treat others with care, and just as importantly, how you treat yourself.

📡 Emotions Are Signals

Sagiri teaches Gabimaru that strength comes from not fleeing your emotions. From staying present with them instead of running.

Emotions are not weaknesses. They are signals.

If you feel intense happiness, ask yourself why. What created that feeling, and how can you invite more of it into your life?

If you are feeling sadness, heaviness, or frustration, those feelings exist for a reason too. Sit with them. Dig deep. Learn what they are trying to teach you.

  • Happiness shows you what aligns with you.
  • Sadness shows you what needs care.
  • Frustration shows you where something is out of balance.

When you suppress emotion, you lose the message.

When you drown in it, you lose yourself.

Listen with compassion and allow the feeling to be there.

Everyone walks a different path. Your strength is finding your balance.

That’s where Tao comes in.

️ Find Your Tao

In Hell’s Paradise, there is a power called Tao. Its entire premise is finding the middle way.

Not being overly rigid. Not being overwhelmed by emotion. But balancing strength and vulnerability together.

You do not have to be unbreakable.
You do not have to be fragile.

True power lives in balance.

Find your Tao.
Your yin and yang.
The place where strength and vulnerability meet.

That is where real courage lives.

And just like Gabimaru, that is where you stop being hollow and start becoming whole. ⚡

What’s good, Kam Fam ⚡ Happy Wednesday.

🥤 What If Life Worked Like a Vending Machine?

Have you ever thought to yourself, wouldn’t life be better if it worked like a vending machine?

Now before you start to think we’re crazy, hear us out.

Imagine this: you walk up, make a deposit, press the exact buttons necessary, and out comes exactly what you ordered.

No guessing. No waiting. No confusion. Just reward on demand. Sounds beautiful, doesn’t it?

But is that how life works? Of course not.

Things don’t even turn out that picture-perfect in an anime.

So let’s talk about what life actually requires, using that same vending machine analogy.

🔁 The Reality of the Deposit

You walk up to the machine.

You do everything right.

You take the proper steps.

You make the sacrifice.

And instead of hearing “transaction complete,” the machine lights up and flashes one message:

“Deposit again.”

At first, it’s annoying. You try again anyway.

Same effort. Same belief. Same hope.

And still nothing. Just another blinking light asking for more.

That’s exactly what life demands from us.

Sometimes the deposit required is money. But more often than not, it’s things that indirectly cost just as much:

  • Time
  • Sleep
  • Comfort
  • Missed social plans

All because there’s something you’re building that matters more.

The quiet grind.

The nights spent alone working when you’d rather be anywhere else.

You keep depositing because… the mission is worth it, even when the reward refuses to show itself.

That feeling right there is willpower.

🥊 Ippo’s Willpower

The anime Hajime no Ippo explains this better than most stories ever will.

Ippo is the main character, and his life is one long series of deposits with no guarantee of return.

He starts boxing shy, unsure, and underestimated. He trains harder than everyone around him.

He loses.

He gets hurt.

He doubts himself.

And still, he shows up the next day and deposits again.

Not because he thinks he’s special, but because quitting never feels like a real option.

⚖️ The Tipping Point

That truth comes into sharp focus during Ippo’s fight with Sawamura.

Sawamura isn’t just dangerous. He’s designed to break fighters.

He disrupts rhythm.

Shatters confidence.

Drags his opponents into chaos.

And by the later rounds, Ippo is finished by any logical measure.

His body is battered.

His vision is fading.

His legs barely respond.

This is where most people stop. But something strange happens. Even when Ippo’s conscious mind can no longer keep up, his body keeps moving.

He dodges.

Counters.

Presses forward on instinct alone.

Not because he has energy left, but because his will refuses to let him fall.

That isn’t muscle memory.

That’s willpower fighting for him.

Ippo doesn’t win because he’s faster or stronger.

He wins because every hit he takes becomes another deposit.

Another quiet decision to keep going when stopping would make sense.

He isn’t fighting to prove he can box.

He’s fighting because losing is not something his heart accepts.

That is what real willpower looks like.

🔑 The Lesson for Real Life

Life will ask you to deposit again long before it ever gives you a reward.

You will do the right things and see nothing happen.

You will feel tired, frustrated, and invisible.

And that is exactly when willpower matters most.

Because sometimes it isn’t skill or strategy that carries you forward.

It’s a belief so deep that even your instincts refuse to quit.

🏋️‍♀️ This Week’s Challenge

Push past the point where most people stop.

When your body feels done, let your spirit take another step.

When doubt creeps in, remind yourself who’s really in charge.

Because when your heart keeps fighting, you don’t just survive.

You win.

Title: One Piece Filler List: Every Episode to Skip
Summary: Skip smart with our complete One Piece filler list. Only 8% is filler, and some of it is secretly worth your time. ⚓🏴‍☠️
Meta Title: One Piece Filler List: Every Episode to Skip
Meta Description: One Piece filler list, sorted by arc. Only about 8% is filler, and picks like G-8 are secretly worth it. See exactly what to skip and keep.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
With over 1,160 episodes, catching up on One Piece can feel like a boss fight you're not sure you can win. The good news: only about 8% of it is filler (roughly 94 episodes), so the mountain is smaller than it looks. Even better, fresh filler basically stopped in 2026.

When the Elbaph Arc began, Toei switched One Piece to a seasonal schedule that adapts Oda's manga almost one-to-one, and the filler faucet shut off. For the first time in the show's history, the filler list sits still, which means you can finally map the whole thing.

So here's the plan. First, the complete skip list sorted by arc, the kind you can scan in about ten seconds. Then the filler arcs that are genuinely worth a watch, along with the "fake skips" that quietly carry real canon. Skip clean, miss nothing.

One Piece Filler: Quick Stats

StatNumber
Total episodes aired~1,168
Filler episodes~94
Canon episodes~1,070
Filler percentage~8%
Time saved skipping all filler~35 hours
Filler status (2026)Frozen (seasonal 1:1 adaptation since Elbaph)

For context, 8% is remarkably low. Naruto: Shippuden sits around 41% filler, and Bleach's original run climbed to roughly 45%. One Piece has always been kinder to your schedule than its Big Three siblings.

The Complete One Piece Filler List, Every Skippable Episode by Arc

Here's the core skip list in chronological order. The Type column tells you what kind of filler you're dealing with. The Verdict column tells you whether to skip it, skim it, or actually sit down and enjoy it.

The No-Filler Cut (copy-paste TL;DR)

Want the fastest clean run? Skip these ranges, and you'll still catch every core beat of the story:

One Piece Filler Episodes That Are Secretly Peak

Filler doesn't automatically mean bad, and anyone who says otherwise probably hasn't seen G-8. There isn't a deep bench here, so instead of padding a list to hit a round number, here are the five filler entries that genuinely earn a spot in your watch. Everything else on the skip list above you can pass on without a second thought.

One quick warning before the picks. A couple of episodes get flagged as filler on the big trackers but are actually canon, so don't let a skip-list talk you out of them. The Davy Back Fight (207–219) comes straight from the manga, and its characters matter again later. Episode 1084 lands as anime canon on most trackers too. Neither is filler, so keep both in your watch.

1. G-8 Arc (196–206)

The undisputed king of One Piece filler, and it isn't close. Coming down from Skypiea, the Going Merry doesn't splash into open sea. It lands inside the sealed bay of a heavily fortified Marine base run by a sharp Vice Admiral named Jonathan. What follows is eleven episodes of infiltration comedy and slow-building tension as the scattered crew goes undercover to steal their ship back.

The character beats are the draw. Sanji talks his way into the base kitchen and duels the head cook, Usopp invents a fake identity named Condoriano that fans still meme about, and Nami runs a nurse disguise and a wounded-victim bluff to slip past the guards. Jonathan is the glue: a calm, genuinely clever antagonist who keeps predicting the crew's moves and nearly boxes them in, popular enough that fans have wanted him made canon for years. It plays like something Oda himself could have written.

2. Ocean's Dream Arc (220–224)

A seahorse called Noko steals the crew's memories overnight, and one morning they wake up not recognizing each other. On paper, that sounds like a lazy clip-show excuse. It isn't. The crew's bond is the whole engine of One Piece, and stripping it away has real weight. Some of them, memories gone, revert to who they were before they ever joined up, which makes for both comedy and a few genuinely tense moments between crewmates.

Without spoiling how it resolves, the final stretch leans on the crew's history in a way that lands emotionally, and it does it without endless recycled flashbacks. Adapted from an old PlayStation game, it's self-contained, with five tight episodes with no lasting consequences. Verdict: Great.

3. Z's Ambition Arc (575–578)

Set after Fish-Man Island, this is the direct prequel to One Piece Film: Z, one of the most loved movies in the franchise. The crew crosses a vicious stretch of the New World that throws mirage fleets and weather shifting from giant hail to avalanche snow to the sea splitting open beneath them. Along the way, they pick up a giant who can shrink herself and agree to help her out of a jam. In the background, a new group of antagonists is quietly introduced, the pieces that the film then pays off. The action punches above the usual filler grade, and it flows straight into the movie, which picks up almost exactly where these episodes stop. If you plan to watch Film Z (and you should), start here. Verdict: Worth It as a pair.

4. Toriko × One Piece × Dragon Ball Z (590)

For years, this was the "lost" One Piece episode. It's the second half of a one-hour crossover special (paired with Toriko episode 99) that aired in Japan in 2013 to celebrate Toriko's anniversary, back when the two shows shared Fuji TV's Sunday morning "Dream 9" block. Luffy, Goku, and Toriko all enter a gourmet tournament for a legendary cut of meat, which spirals into a three-way team-up against a power-draining sea beast. Watching Luffy and Goku throw hands side by side is the kind of thing that basically never happens in anime. Toonami skipped it for years, Crunchyroll never carried it, and it only reached Netflix with fresh dubs fairly recently, so it's been genuinely tough to track down. Watch it for the novelty and the slice of anime history. Verdict: Fun Detour.

5. Little East Blue Arc (426–429)

The lead-in to One Piece Film: Strong World, and the most "your mileage may vary" pick here, so I'll be straight about it. The crew lands on an island nicknamed Little East Blue because its residents are all East Blue transplants, which means the town is dotted with miniature versions of the places the crew calls home. That nostalgia is the charm. The villains are a mariachi-themed pirate crew, and their captain carries one of the more inventive filler powers, a Devil Fruit that lets him form nets out of anything he eats, including turning his own body into one. The fight gives Luffy a fun problem to solve. It ties into Strong World by setting up the movie's threat. It's not top-tier, and it interrupts the run to a major canon arc, so keep expectations in check. As a warm-up to a great movie, though, it does the job. Verdict: Worth a Look.

What Actually Counts as Filler in One Piece?

Confused about why some filler is safe to skip, and some isn't? Here's the breakdown. One Piece filler comes in four flavors.

TypeWhat it isSkip it?
Pure FillerAnime-original content not in Oda's mangaYes
Canon FillerAnime-original scenes that stay true to canon and expand it without changing outcomesSkim
Mixed CanonCanon episodes padded with anime-only scenesNo, watch
Recaps / CrossoversClip shows and promo tie-ins (Toriko, DBZ, movie prequels)Usually

One Piece keeps its filler percentage so low for a subtle reason. Toei tends to sprinkle small filler scenes inside otherwise-canon episodes instead of building whole filler arcs. That approach stretches the material without bloating the skip list, which is clever even if it occasionally tests your patience.

Hot Take: G-8 Should Be Made Canon

We'll say it a little louder for the folks in the back: the G-8 Arc (196–206) holds its own against plenty of canon arcs. Tight plotting, real character beats for the whole crew, and an "escape the Marine fortress" premise that delivers as much tension and comedy as a lot of the main story around it. A big part of the fandom treats it with the kind of affection usually saved for canon, and there's a long-running wish for Oda to fold it into the official timeline.

Our take? Filler this good challenges the whole "filler equals worthless" idea. The word describes where an episode came from, not how good it is. Plenty of filler is easy to pass on, sure. A blanket "skip all filler" rule, though, would cost you one of the most enjoyable stretches in the series. Watch G-8. That's the hill we'll stand on.

Skip Smart and Enjoy the Voyage

One Piece is one of the most rewarding stories in anime, and with the filler list frozen, it's never been friendlier to newcomers. Use the No-Filler Cut to move quickly, keep the fake skips in mind so you don't lose a thread, and give the strong filler like G-8 a real chance. The point was never to rush the journey. It's to spend your time on the episodes that reward it.

How many episodes of One Piece are filler?

Almost certainly not. The seasonal, one-to-one chapter adaptation that started with Elbaph has effectively closed the filler era.

Title: Naruto Shippuden Filler List: Every Episode to Skip or Watch
Summary: Save 75+ hours with our full Naruto Shippuden filler list for all 500 episodes. 41% is filler, but the best arcs hit hard. 🍥🔥
Meta Title: Naruto Shippuden Filler List: Every Episode Sorted
Meta Description: Naruto Shippuden filler list for all 500 episodes. Save 75+ hours and keep the filler arcs that are actually great. See what to skip.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Naruto Shippuden is 500 episodes long, and roughly 203 of those episodes have absolutely nothing to do with anything Masashi Kishimoto ever put on a manga page. That's 41% of the entire series. Forty-one percent! If you watched every single filler episode back to back, you'd lose over 75 hours of your life to anime-original side quests, recycled flashbacks, and dream sequences where Tenten becomes the main character (yes, really).

You already know you need a Naruto filler guide. The question is which one to trust, because every guide on the internet gives you a different filler count. Some say 196 episodes. Others say 206. A few just shrug and write "about 200." The numbers never match because there are roughly 50 episodes sitting in a gray zone between canon and filler, and every tracker on the planet draws that line somewhere different.

So here's what you're getting below: the verified episode count with a clear explanation of why the numbers vary across trackers, a full arc-by-arc breakdown with honest verdicts on every single filler stretch, three concrete watch paths depending on how much of your life you want to give Shippuden, and (crucially) the filler arcs that are genuinely too good to skip. Because some of them are. Kakashi's ANBU arc has no business being as good as it is for a filler arc, and we need to talk about it.

The skip list table is right below for anyone mid-binge. If you want the full breakdown, keep scrolling.

Naruto Shippuden Filler by the Numbers

StatNumber
Total Episodes500
Pure Filler Episodes203
Mixed Canon/Filler Episodes~50
Manga Canon Episodes~247
Filler Percentage41%
Hours of Pure Filler~78
Canon-Only Runtime~114 hours

Shippuden aired weekly from February 2007 to March 2017. A full decade of continuous production. Studio Pierrot was burning through manga chapters faster than Kishimoto could draw them, so they did what every long-running shonen studio used to do: write original episodes and pray the audience sticks around until the source material catches up. Sometimes that meant a two-episode detour. Sometimes it meant a 24-episode dream arc wedged between two of the most important canon fights in the entire war saga. The results were... inconsistent.

The numbers in this article follow the AnimeFillerList standard of 203 pure filler. It's the most referenced count across the community, and where other trackers disagree, I've flagged the differences so you can make your own call.

Complete Naruto Shippuden Filler List

Here's every filler arc and standalone Naruto filler episode in Shippuden, organized chronologically. Each one gets an episode range, an episode count, and a straight verdict. If something shows up in the "Worth Your Time" section later in the article, it's flagged here too.

ArcEpisodesVerdict
Twelve Guardian Ninja57-71Skip. Solid worldbuilding around the Fire Temple and a pseudo-jinchuriki named Sora, but nothing here connects to anything that happens later. You'll forget this arc existed by the time the Pain arc starts.
Three-Tails' Appearance91-112Skip. The longest filler arc in Shippuden, and it feels every minute of its length. The final episode lands a surprisingly emotional beat if you've gotten attached to the original characters, but asking someone to sit through 22 episodes for one good payoff is a tough sell.
Six-Tails Unleashed144-151Optional. Utakata, the Six-Tails jinchuriki, gets real character development here, and it subtly deepens the emotional weight of the jinchuriki theme right before the Pain invasion begins. At only eight episodes, it won't kill your pacing. Worth a look if you care about the tailed beast hosts as a group.
Past Arc: The Locus of Konoha176-196Skip. Dropping 21 filler episodes directly after the Pain arc is genuinely painful. Most of this content retreads Naruto's childhood and rehashes material from Part 1. If you've already watched the original series, almost nothing here will surprise you.
Adventures at Sea (The Boat Arc)223-242Skip. The infamous boat arc. Twenty episodes of goofy side missions as Naruto sails toward the Fourth Great Ninja War. A handful of comedic episodes have their fans, but most of the community considers this stretch Shippuden's absolute low point. Proceed at your own risk.
Flashback: Sasuke and Naruto257-260Skip. Four episodes recapping Sasuke and Naruto's rivalry. If you've been watching the show, you've already lived through all of this. Twice.
Power Arc (Chikara)290-295Watch. Created to celebrate the franchise hitting 500 combined episodes, and the production team went all out. Movie-quality animation, Kabuto pulling the villain strings, a clone of Nine-Tails Naruto as the final threat. The fights are absolutely gorgeous. Six episodes, clean story, no loose threads. Peak filler.
War-Era Side Missions303-320Skip. Side characters run minor missions while the Fourth Great Ninja War is supposedly raging around them. The return of the Sound Four in episodes 303-305 is a solid nostalgia hit (watching our heroes demolish villains who used to be terrifying is satisfying), but 18 episodes of war-era padding is a lot.
Kakashi's ANBU Arc349-361Watch. The single best filler arc in the Naruto franchise, full stop. I go deeper on this below, but the short version: if you skip every other filler arc on this Naruto Shippuden filler list, keep this one.
Mecha Naruto376-377Optional. A mechanical clone of Naruto attacks the village. It's exactly as ridiculous as it sounds, and it knows it. Love it or skip it, but at two episodes it's essentially free. Solid comic relief between heavy canon episodes.
War Filler Block389-390, 394-413, 416, 422-423Skip. The biggest pacing killer in the entire series. Twenty-four filler episodes scattered across the climax of the war saga. Right when the stakes should be at their absolute highest, you're watching flashbacks and side stories that drain every ounce of momentum. The strongest argument for why filler guides exist.
Infinite Tsukuyomi Dreams427-450Skip. Every major character gets trapped in a dream world and imagines their ideal life. The Tenten dream episodes (427-428) are hilariously awful in a way some fans enjoy ironically. Beyond that, it's 24 episodes of stalling before the finale. The war arc needed a lot of things at this point. Twenty-four dream episodes were not one of them.
Childhood Flashbacks480-483Optional. Quiet, heartwarming stories about young Naruto, young Sasuke, and young Shikamaru. They work beautifully as a soft goodbye to the series if you let them. If you've just finished the final battle and you're feeling emotional, give these four episodes room to breathe. If you're ready for the actual ending, skip to 484.

Standalone Filler Episodes

A complete Naruto Shippuden filler list also needs to account for the scattered one-off filler episodes that don't belong to any arc:

EpisodeTitleVerdict
170-171(Pain arc interruption)Skip. Filler episodes interrupting the Pain invasion. The single best arc in Shippuden gets paused for two episodes of nothing. Criminal pacing.

279-281White Zetsu war fillerSkip.
284-289War-era standalonesSkip. Minor character spotlights during the war. Light on lasting impact.

Naruto Shippuden Filler Episodes Worth Your Time

Most Shippuden filler episodes are skippable. But "most" is doing serious heavy lifting in that sentence, because a few arcs are genuinely, undeniably excellent. If someone told you to skip every filler episode without exception, they'd be pulling you away from some of the strongest material in the franchise. Should you watch Naruto Shippuden fillers? For these five, absolutely.

1. Kakashi's ANBU Arc (Episodes 349-361)

The best filler arc in either Naruto series, and a lot of fans will tell you it belongs in the conversation for best arc in Shippuden, period. The tone shifts dramatically. Kakashi spirals into an emotionless, mission-obsessed state after losing Rin, cycling through increasingly dark ANBU assignments while Gai, Hiruzen, and others try to pull him back from the edge. You get Yamato's full origin story, a young Itachi joining ANBU as a prodigy who's already carrying the weight of the world, and political maneuvering from Danzo that adds genuine layers to the main story.

Episode 350 is a standout even among standouts. It animates the night of Naruto's birth, Minato and Kushina's deaths, and the Nine-Tails attack with an emotional depth that expands on the canon version. Fans consistently rank it as one of the single best episodes in the entire franchise. Filler label or not, these 13 episodes hit harder than half the canon war arc.

2. Power Arc / Chikara (Episodes 290-295)

Six episodes that look and feel like a Naruto movie. Studio Pierrot built this arc as a celebration of the franchise reaching 500 combined episodes, and they treated it like a prestige project. The sakuga is incredible. Kabuto serves as the antagonist, the stakes escalate quickly, and the whole thing wraps in six clean episodes without overstaying its welcome.

A clone of Four-Tails Naruto powers up into a full Nine-Tails form and nearly consumes the original. A child from the destroyed village breaks through to Naruto at the critical moment. Minato's voice urging his son forward. It packs more genuine emotion into six episodes than some canon arcs manage in twenty.

3. Itachi Shinden: Light and Darkness (Episodes 451-458)

No entry on any filler list generates more debate. These episodes adapt Takashi Yano's official "Itachi Shinden" light novels, which Kishimoto supervised. AnimeFillerList classifies them as mixed canon/filler (not pure filler), and a growing number of fans treat them as functionally canon. You get Itachi's childhood, his years at the Academy, his deepening horror at the Uchiha clan's trajectory, and the full, devastating weight of the choice he eventually makes.

If Itachi matters to you (and for most Shippuden fans, he's the emotional center of the entire series), calling these episodes filler feels wrong. They fill a gap the manga left open, and they do it with source material Kishimoto himself blessed.

4. Mecha Naruto (Episodes 376-377)

Hear me out. Mecha Naruto is stupid. It's proudly, aggressively stupid. A Frankenstein robot version of Naruto chases the real Naruto through the village while his friends get picked off one by one. It is also exactly the comic relief the war arc needs at that exact moment in the story, right when everything is at its darkest and heaviest.

Two episodes. Harmless fun. The kind of filler that earns its place not by being important but by being the breather you didn't know you needed.

5. Childhood Flashbacks (Episodes 480-483)

Easy to dismiss, hard to forget once you've watched them. Four episodes revisiting the childhoods of Naruto, Sasuke, Shikamaru, and others. Young Naruto eating ramen alone. Young Sasuke before the massacre. Young Shikamaru getting dragged into his first responsibility.

After hundreds of hours with these characters, after the final valley, after everything, four episodes of their childhood don't feel like padding. They feel like one last quiet moment before the credits roll. If you're emotional at the end of your watch (and you will be), let these breathe.

The Hot Take: Kakashi's ANBU Arc Belongs in the Canon

Every Shippuden fan has a tier list of the arcs that define the series. Pain is usually at the top. The Itachi truth reveal. Jiraiya's last stand. Naruto vs. Sasuke at the final valley. The arcs that made Shippuden what it is.

Kakashi's ANBU arc (349-361) deserves a seat at that table. The only thing keeping it out of the conversation is the word "filler" next to its name on a fan-maintained spreadsheet.

Kishimoto never fully showed what happened to Kakashi between losing Rin and becoming Team 7's sensei. He left a gap. And the anime didn't just fill that gap; it filled it with some of the most psychologically grounded, emotionally devastating character writing in the entire franchise. Kakashi doesn't unlock a new jutsu. He doesn't win a big fight. He breaks down, loses himself in increasingly violent ANBU missions, and slowly, painfully, finds a reason to keep going. The tone is darker and more mature than anything in the main Shippuden storyline.

If Kishimoto had drawn these chapters himself, nobody would question them for a second. The "filler" label is a technicality. The quality is peak fiction.

Save 75 Hours and Keep the Arcs That Earned It

Shippuden's filler problem is real, but it's completely solvable. Use this Naruto Shippuden filler list as your go-to reference: grab the canon-only path if you want the tightest ride, the balanced path if you want Kishimoto's story plus the filler that genuinely deserves to exist alongside it, or the completionist route if 500 episodes sounds like a good time. (It does, honestly, if you've got the weeks to spare.)

The 203 Naruto filler episodes will always be there if you decide to come back for them. But the canon story Kishimoto wrote stands on its own. Knowing which shippuden filler episodes to skip and which ones earned a place in your watch is the difference between 192 hours and 114 hours, between a bloated marathon and a series that never once loses its momentum.

For more anime takes, seasonal guides, and breakdowns that actually say something, the Kaminari newsletter lands weekly. Worth a subscribe if you're the type of fan who likes opinions with their episode lists.

FAQ

What episodes of Naruto Shippuden are fillers?

The pure filler episodes are: 28, 57-71, 91-112, 144-151, 170-171, 176-196, 223-242, 257-260, 271, 279-281, 284-295, 303-320, 347-361, 376-377, 389-390, 394-413, 416, 422-423, 427-450, 464-468, and 480-483. That comes to 203 episodes out of 500, based on AnimeFillerList's classifications. Around 50 additional episodes are classified as mixed canon/filler, meaning they contain some canon material alongside anime-original content.

How many fillers are in Naruto Shippuden?

203 pure filler episodes out of 500 total, putting the filler percentage at about 41%. The count varies slightly between trackers (some list 196, others 206) depending on how they classify mixed canon/filler episodes and whether light novel adaptations like Itachi Shinden get labeled as filler or canon-adjacent material.

Should I watch Naruto Shippuden fillers?

Most of them are easy passes. But a handful of filler arcs are genuinely excellent, and skipping them means missing some of the strongest material in the franchise. Kakashi's ANBU arc (349-361) is widely considered one of the best arcs in the series, filler or otherwise. The Power arc (290-295) has movie-quality animation. The Itachi Shinden episodes (451-458) adapt official light novels that deepen one of the most important characters in the story. A balanced approach (skip most, keep the best) gives you the strongest viewing experience.

What is the best Naruto Shippuden filler arc?

Kakashi's ANBU arc, episodes 349 through 361. It tracks Kakashi's psychological descent after losing Rin, features a young Itachi and Yamato's origin story, and carries a noticeably darker tone than anything else in Shippuden. Episode 350 (Minato and Kushina's deaths on the night of Naruto's birth) is one of the highest-rated individual episodes in the franchise. The writing quality rivals the best canon arcs, and many fans argue it should be considered canon outright.

Can I skip all Naruto Shippuden filler and still understand the story?

Yes. The canon story (approximately 297 episodes including mixed canon/filler) is fully self-contained. You won't miss any plot points, character deaths, or major reveals. The one caveat: mixed canon/filler episodes sometimes contain real plot beats wrapped in anime-original padding. Skipping those can create small gaps in context, especially around major arc transitions. The safest approach is to skip only pure filler episodes and watch every mixed episode.

Title: Bleach Filler List: All 163 Episodes You Can Skip (and the Ones You Shouldn't)
Summary: Cut 45% filler from your Bleach watch with our complete Bleach filler list. The most bloated Big Three run, finally sorted. ⚔️💀
Meta Title: Bleach Filler List: All 163 Episodes You Can Skip
Meta Description: Bleach filler list to cut 45% filler from your watch. Keep the Zanpakuto Rebellion and follow the canon story clean. See what to skip.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Nearly half of Bleach doesn't exist. Not in the manga, anyway. Out of 366 episodes in the original anime, 163 are filler. That's a 45% filler rate, which makes Bleach the worst offender in the entire Big Three. Naruto Shippuden clocks in around 41%. One Piece barely hits 10%. Bleach almost doubles One Piece's entire filler count *in percentage alone*.

And the placement makes it worse. Bleach doesn't dump its filler at the end of a saga where you can see it coming. It drops 46 straight episodes of spiritual vampires right after the Soul Society arc, the best stretch of the entire show. You ride the highest high Bleach ever gives you, and then you crash into the Bount Arc for four months. Studio Pierrot did this to buy Tite Kubo time to stay ahead in the manga, and it worked for production. It didn't work for fans.

This bleach filler list gives you the full breakdown. Every filler arc and standalone episode, sorted and judged honestly. A copy-paste skip list for the people who just want numbers. A section on the filler that's actually worth your time. And a look at the episodes the trackers get wrong, because blindly copying animefillerlist.com will steer you wrong in at least three places.

Bleach Filler by the Numbers

StatNumber
Total episodes (original series)366
Filler episodes163
Filler percentage45%
Canon + mixed canon episodes203
Manga canon only166
Watch time saved by skipping filler~65 hours
Bleach: TYBW episodes (all canon)52
Full canon watch (original + TYBW)~255 episodes

Strip the filler and you go from 366 episodes to 203. That's 65 hours of your life reclaimed! Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War has zero fillers. Studio Pierrot moved to seasonal production, every episode pulls from the manga, and Kubo personally supervises the expansions that fill in gaps from the manga's rushed ending. If you're catching up for TYBW, you can skip every piece of filler in the original series without losing a single plot thread.

Every Bleach Filler Episode, Sorted by Arc

Here's the complete list of all bleach filler episodes. Every arc, every standalone, every verdict.

ArcEpisodesVerdict
"Miracle! The Mysterious New Hero"33Skip. Follows Ichigo's sisters on a throwaway side quest. He doesn't even show up.
"The Reviving Lion"50Skip. Kon wanders Karakura Town solo. Completely detached from everything.
Bount Arc64-109Skip. Spiritual vampires invade Soul Society across 46 painful episodes. The longest and most hated filler block in the series. Kills all the momentum from the Soul Society arc. The single biggest reason fans dropped Bleach during its original run.
Stolen Hogyoku / Arrancar Filler128-137Mostly skip. A grab bag of slice-of-life and a short arc about rogue Arrancar. Episodes 132 and 133 are the exceptions, they're both quietly excellent (see the "Worth Watching" section below).
Forest of Menos147-149Watch. Three episodes in the Menos Forest with a lost Soul Reaper named Ashido. Expands how Hollows organize and evolve. Respects your time, adds genuine texture to Hueco Mundo right before it becomes the main setting.
New Captain Shusuke Amagai Arc168-189Skip. A new Squad 3 captain with a hidden agenda. The structure copies the Soul Society arc (conspiracy, betrayal, dramatic reveal) but none of the emotional beats land. 22 episodes for a villain you won't remember a week later.
Kemari Arc204-205Skip. Ichigo mediates a feud through an ancient ball game. Two episodes of nothing.
Karakuraizer Arc213-214Debatable. Kon and friends form a superhero team. Most trackers call this filler, but these episodes actually adapt manga omake chapters, not anime-original scripts. See "Episodes the Trackers Get Wrong" below.
Beach Episode + One-off228-229Skip. Swimsuit episode and an Ikkaku/Yumichika comedy. You've seen this formula before.
Zanpakuto Unknown Tales / Rebellion Arc230-265Watch. The best filler arc in Bleach by a wide margin. Zanpakuto spirits gain physical forms and rebel against their wielders. Creative, emotionally grounded, visually ambitious. Full breakdown below.
Hueco Mundo Recap266Skip. Pure recap. You already know what happened.
"Ichigo and the Magic Lamp"287Skip. Dream episode Aladdin parody for the manga's 10th anniversary. A curiosity, not a commitment.
Shinigami Film Festival298Skip. Soul Reapers make a movie. Pure comedy filler.
Hell Verse Prologue299Watch if you're watching Hell Verse. Skip if you're not. It's a direct movie prologue, not a standalone episode.
Assorted One-Offs303-305Skip. New Year special, dream episode, hot springs comedy. Momentum killers.
Assorted One-Offs311-316Skip. More standalone comedies. Episode 316 (Hitsugaya in the human world) has mild charm, but nothing here is essential.
Gotei 13 Invasion Arc317-342Optional. Mod Soul imposters replace the captains. Better concept than the Bount or Amagai arcs, and the villain actually feels like a threat. Second-best filler arc overall, but a clear step below the Zanpakuto Rebellion.
"Shinigami at War! New Year Special"355Skip. You're 11 episodes from the finale. Keep moving.

That's every filler episode in Bleach. All 163 of them, sorted, judged, and accounted for.

Bleach Filler Episodes Worth Watching

Most of Bleach's filler earns its skip label. But a handful of arcs and episodes are worth breaking your skip list for, and they're worth it because they do something the rest of the filler never attempts: they feel like they belong.

Zanpakuto Unknown Tales / Rebellion Arc (Episodes 230-265)

The single best filler arc in Bleach, and a genuine contender for best filler arc in shonen anime, period. A rogue zanpakuto spirit named Muramasa severs the bond between every Soul Reaper and their blade, giving the zanpakuto physical forms, unique personalities, and the will to fight back against their masters.

What makes it work is specificity. Senbonzakura manifests as a masked swordsman with his own pride and combat philosophy. Zabimaru splits into two bickering halves who can't agree on anything. Hyorinmaru walks the battlefield as an ice warrior who has forgotten his wielder entirely. Every zanpakuto design became iconic to the fanbase. People forget these characters originated in filler. That's how well they fit Kubo's world.

Muramasa himself carries the arc. His motivation isn't conquest; it's abandonment. He was sealed away by his master and the pain of that rejection drives everything he does. For a filler villain, that's a shocking amount of emotional depth. He has more internal life than some canon antagonists.

The fanbase has argued for years that the Rebellion deserves canon status, and TYBW may have quietly agreed. A Byakuya flashback in the modern anime appears to reference events from this arc as though they happened. More on that in the Hot Take below.

Gotei 13 Invasion Arc (Episodes 317-342)

The runner-up. Mod Soul duplicates of the Gotei 13 captains infiltrate Soul Society, and Ichigo can't rely on his powers. The imposter concept gives the arc more tension than the Bount or Amagai arcs ever managed. Kageroza Inaba, the villain, actually feels dangerous, which is more than you can say for most filler antagonists.

It runs long at 26 episodes and certain fights lose steam, but the overall experience is solid if you're open to more Bleach after the canon run.

Forest of Menos (Episodes 147-149)

Three episodes. That's it. And they accomplish more worldbuilding than arcs ten times their length. Ashido, the lost Soul Reaper surviving alone in the Menos Forest, was a character Kubo originally planned for the manga but cut for pacing. His story fills in how the Hollow ecosystem actually works, and the setting builds atmosphere that the main arcs rarely slow down long enough to create. If you watch one short filler block, this is the one.

Episode 132: "Hitsugaya, Karin, and Soccer Ball"

Ichigo's younger sister Karin bullies Captain Hitsugaya into joining her neighborhood soccer match. On paper, it sounds like throwaway fluff. In practice, it's one of the only times in 366 episodes that Karin gets meaningful screen time and genuine character work. The Hitsugaya/Karin dynamic plays naturally (prodigy captain humbled by a stubborn kid who doesn't care about rank), and the episode avoids the forced melodrama that plagues most filler one-offs.

Episode 133: "Ikkaku: The Hot-Blooded Kendo Tale"

Ikkaku teaches a bullied kid how to fight. Pure character piece. Zero plot relevance. But it captures who Ikkaku actually is (aggressive, blunt, secretly kind) in ways that some of his canon fights don't bother with. Good comfort-food anime.

Hot Take: The Zanpakuto Rebellion Deserves to Be Canon

The Rebellion arc (episodes 230-265) explored a question Kubo's manga never touched: what happens when a zanpakuto gains full autonomy and turns on its wielder?

And the wild part is how naturally the concept fits. Zanpakuto aren't just weapons in Bleach. They have names. They have inner worlds. They communicate with their wielders, argue with them, test them. The idea that they could rebel isn't a stretch of the lore; it's a logical extension of it. Kubo built the foundation. The filler team built the house.

The designs stuck, too. Senbonzakura as a masked warrior. Kazeshini as a violent, chaotic spirit who resents Hisagi's self-control. Sogyo no Kotowari as twin children. These aren't footnotes in the fandom's memory. They're load-bearing images that people associate with the characters permanently. Most fans can picture Senbonzakura's human form faster than they can picture half the canon Arrancar.

Then TYBW dropped a reference that nobody expected. During a Byakuya flashback in the modern anime, the show briefly depicts events resembling the Rebellion timeline, specifically the confrontation between Byakuya and Koga Kuchiki. Kubo is deeply involved in TYBW's production. He hasn't confirmed or denied the nod. The "make it canon" crowd has never been louder.

Would the full arc slot cleanly into continuity? Not perfectly. Some power levels don't align, and a few character positions are off relative to where the manga was at that point. But the thematic core, zanpakuto as autonomous beings capable of rejecting their wielders, fits Kubo's world like a sheath fits its blade. If any filler arc in shonen history earned a promotion to canon, it's this one.

Cut the Filler, Keep the Bankai

Bleach is better without 45% of its runtime. That's not an insult to the show. It's just what happens when a weekly anime outruns its source material for eight straight years. The canon arcs, from Soul Society's legendary twist through the Arrancar saga's emotional crescendo, hit harder when they aren't buried under dozens of episodes about vampires and ball games.

But "skip everything" is a blunt instrument for a series where the Zanpakuto Rebellion exists, where the Forest of Menos quietly fills a real lore gap, and where a soccer episode gives Karin her only meaningful moment in the entire anime. Use the skip list as your foundation. Use the "Worth Watching" picks as your exceptions. And check whether a "filler" episode is actually anime-original before you hit skip, because the trackers aren't always right.

If you want more guides like this (watch orders, seasonal breakdowns, honest verdicts on what to skip across every major anime), the Kaminari newsletter goes out weekly. No filler, just the good stuff.

FAQ

How many episodes of Bleach are filler?

163 out of 366 episodes in the original series are filler, roughly 45%. If you also count the 37 mixed canon episodes (which blend manga scenes with anime-original content), the non-pure-canon number climbs higher, but mixed episodes are generally worth keeping.

Can I skip all Bleach filler and still understand the story?

Yes. Every filler arc and standalone can be cut without losing plot-critical information. The manga storyline flows cleanly across the 203 canon and mixed canon episodes. Filler characters sometimes appear in the background of later canon episodes, but they're never relevant.

Does Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War have filler?

No. TYBW has zero filler across all of its cours. Studio Pierrot adopted a seasonal schedule, and every episode pulls from the manga. Some scenes are anime-original expansions that Kubo supervised to address gaps in the manga's ending, but those are creator-approved additions to the canon, not filler.

Is the Zanpakuto Rebellion arc worth watching?

It's the most widely recommended filler arc in Bleach, and it earns that reputation. The premise (zanpakuto spirits gaining physical forms and rebelling against their masters) fits the show's lore naturally, the villain carries real emotional weight, and the character designs became iconic. If you're watching one filler arc, make it this one.

Why do different Bleach filler lists show different episode counts?

It comes down to how each tracker handles "mixed canon" episodes and whether manga omake adaptations (like episodes 213-214) count as filler. Different sites use different definitions, which produces counts anywhere from 160 to 165. The safest approach: skip only episodes that are entirely anime-original and keep anything with partial manga content.

So, how many filler episodes does Naruto have? The Naruto filler count for the original series lands at roughly 90 out of 220, putting it at the same percentage as Shippuden (also 41%). For context, Bleach comes in at approximately 45% filler while One Piece stays under 10%.

Naruto Skippable Episodes: The Quick-Skip List

If you're speed-running the original Naruto filler list and just want the episode numbers, here they are. These are all Naruto fillers in the original series you can skip without losing a single plot thread:

Episodes 26, 97, 101-106, 136-140, 143-219

A few of those deserve an asterisk, though. Episode 101 (Kakashi's True Face) is one of the most beloved episodes in the entire franchise, filler or not. The Cursed Warrior arc (162-167) has a mystery that genuinely holds up and lets Naruto be clever instead of just loud. Watch those if you have the time. Skip the rest guilt-free.

One more thing: Episodes 107-135 are NOT filler. The Sasuke Recovery Mission is fully canon and covers some of the most important fights in the original series, including the first battle at the Valley of the End. Don't skip those on your way to Shippuden.

The Complete Naruto Filler List

The original Naruto front-loads its canon arcs and backloads almost all of its filler. Everything from Episode 1 through 135 is nearly all manga-adapted storytelling, covering Naruto's journey from academy outcast to a genin willing to risk everything to bring his best friend home. After Episode 135, the anime outpaced Kishimoto's manga and filled the gap with over 80 straight episodes of original content. Below is the complete Naruto filler episode list, covering every filler episode in Naruto grouped by arc.

Arc / EpisodesVerdict

Secretly Peak: The Filler Worth Keeping

Most filler guides treat every non-canon episode as interchangeable background noise. But the original Naruto has a handful of filler arcs that earned their reputation through genuine comedy, sharp writing, or emotional moments the manga never had room to deliver. These are the episodes worth keeping on your schedule even if you're cutting everything else.

Episode 101: Gotta See! Gotta Know! Kakashi-Sensei's True Face!

Zero plot relevance. Pure joy. Team 7 spends an entire episode trying to catch a glimpse of what Kakashi is hiding under his mask, and every attempt fails in increasingly ridiculous ways. Naruto's stubbornness, Sasuke's reluctant curiosity, and Sakura's scheming all fire on every cylinder, and the payoff at the end is the kind of gag that rewards patient viewers. It's one of the most rewatched and most memed episodes in the franchise for good reason. If you only keep one filler episode, this is the one.

The Cursed Warrior Extermination Mission (Episodes 162-167)

Buried deep in the filler stretch that most fans skip on autopilot, the Cursed Warrior arc sends Naruto, Neji, and Tenten to the Land of Birds to investigate a ghostly suit of armor terrorizing a village. What sets it apart is the structure: it plays like a genuine mystery instead of a standard fight-the-villain-of-the-week setup. Naruto gets to be observant and resourceful, Neji's Byakugan can't solve the problem alone, and the twist actually earns its reveal. For a filler arc buried in no-man's-land, it punches well above its weight.

Episode 220: Departure

Classified as mixed canon/filler, Episode 220 is the emotional bridge between Part 1 and Shippuden. Naruto leaves the village with Jiraiya for his two-and-a-half-year training journey, and the episode takes its time showing what that departure means to the people he's leaving behind. Starting Shippuden without it skips the quiet moment that gives the time skip its weight. Treat this one as mandatory, regardless of what any classification says.

Hot Take: Episode 101 Belongs in Every "Best Naruto Episodes" List

Of all 220 episodes in the original series, Episode 101 is the one fans bring up unprompted in "favorite moments" conversations. It tells you more about Team 7's chemistry in 22 minutes than a dozen training arcs spread across entire seasons.

The fact that it has zero plot relevance is exactly why it works. For one episode, Naruto, Sasuke, and Sakura get to exist outside the weight of prophecy and world-ending stakes. The result is the purest snapshot of the team at their most natural, goofing off, bickering, and bonding over something completely pointless. No canon episode in the original series captures that specific energy better. A filler episode being this beloved, this rewatchable, and this quoted says everything about what the show does best when it stops trying to be epic and just lets its characters breathe.

The Fastest Path Through the Hidden Leaf (Without Missing What Matters)

If you're prepping for the 2026 anniversary special, starting the series for the first time, or cutting the fat on a rewatch, this Naruto filler list gives you the map. The canon-only path through the original Naruto runs about 130 episodes. The full ride runs 220. The best version keeps Episode 101, the Cursed Warrior arc, and Episode 220 on the schedule, because all Naruto filler episodes carrying the "filler" tag don't mean they all deserve the same treatment.

Now go get to the Valley of the End. That's where it all starts to matter.

Author: devin-morris
Content:
Boruto: Naruto Next Generations has a reputation problem. Ask the internet how much of it is filler and you'll get answers ranging from 10% to 70%, depending on who you ask and how they define the word. The truth is somewhere in the middle, buried under a classification system that no other anime uses at this scale, and it's the reason every Boruto filler list on the internet gives you a completely different number.

Here's the short version: out of 293 episodes, only about 78 directly adapt the manga. The rest are a mix of anime-original stories and genuine filler, and the line between those two categories is where all the arguments start. But here's what nobody leads with: hiding inside that pile of anime-original content is a time-travel arc where Boruto trains alongside young Naruto under Jiraiya's watch, and it's one of the best things the franchise has ever produced.

Below, you'll get the verified episode count broken into all three categories, a full arc-by-arc breakdown with honest verdicts, and the anime-original arcs that genuinely earned their place.

Boruto Filler Worth Your Time

Most filler in Boruto is easy to pass on. But three anime-original arcs genuinely earn their keep, and one of them might be the best thing Boruto ever did.

1. Time Slip Arc (Episodes 128-136)

Boruto and Sasuke get thrown back in time by Urashiki Otsutsuki and land in the Hidden Leaf Village during Naruto's childhood. Young Naruto is still the village outcast, still eating ramen alone, still training under Jiraiya. Boruto has to work alongside his father without revealing who he is.

The setup is pure fan service, and the arc knows exactly what it's doing. But the payoff is real. Boruto watches his father's loneliness firsthand. He trains with him under Jiraiya's guidance. He sees the version of Naruto who had nothing and fought for everything, and it fundamentally changes how he understands his own dad. Jiraiya's presence alone makes this arc worth it for any Naruto fan who still misses the old pervy sage.

The fights against Urashiki are solid, the callbacks land, and the emotional core actually works. For anime-original content, it has absolutely no business being this good.

2. Kara Actuation Arc (Episodes 157-175)

Anime-original content that bridges directly into the manga's most important storyline. The Kara organization, Boruto's central villain group, gets its anime introduction through stories involving the Hashirama Cell and rogue scientific experiments. When the manga-canon Kara arc begins at episode 181, everything hits harder because this arc laid the groundwork.

Skipping it is technically possible, but the transition into the manga story feels abrupt without it.

3. Parent and Child Day (Episodes 93-95)

Three episodes adapted from the Naruto Shinden light novels. Naruto and Himawari spend the day together. Sasuke tries (and fails spectacularly) to connect with Sarada. Shikamaru deals with Shikadai. Warm, funny, and one of the rare moments Boruto lets these characters just be parents and kids.

For fans who grew up watching Naruto and Sasuke, seeing them figure out fatherhood is the kind of content only this series can deliver.

The Hot Take: The Time Slip Arc Is the Blueprint

Every long-running anime produces filler. Most of it is forgettable. The Time Slip Arc is proof that anime-original content can be something genuinely special.

It works because it's built on an emotional question that only Boruto can ask: what happens when a kid who resents his famous father gets to see exactly what that father went through? The answer isn't a speech or a flashback montage. It's Boruto standing next to twelve-year-old Naruto, watching him eat alone, train alone, and smile anyway. Jiraiya teaching them both. Boruto quietly realizing that the Hokage he's been angry at was once a lonely kid who had it worse than he ever will.

If the Naruto franchise ever returns to long-form anime-original storytelling, the Time Slip Arc is the template. Find the emotional question only your characters can answer. Boruto found it once. It was enough to justify everything around it.

78 Episodes of Canon, One Arc That Justifies Everything Else

Boruto's filler reputation is earned. A series where only 27% of episodes adapt the manga is a hard sell, and no Boruto filler list can change the underlying math. But the manga story itself (Kawaki, Kara, the Otsutsuki threat) is genuinely excellent, and the anime-original highlights prove the format can produce real quality when the writing commits to it.

Use this Boruto filler list to find your way through 293 episodes. The canon is worth the trip. And the Time Slip Arc is worth the detour. For weekly anime takes, seasonal guides, and opinions that come with receipts, the Kaminari newsletter has you covered.

Content:
Black Clover ran for 170 episodes as a weekly shonen anime, and only 18 of them are filler. That's roughly 10%, which is absurdly low for a show that aired nonstop from 2017 to 2021. Asta's anti-magic apparently extends to padding.

If you're watching (or rewatching) and want a clean path through the canon story, this is the only Black Clover filler list you need. So how much filler is in Black Clover, really? The accurate count is 18 pure filler episodes. The number floats anywhere from 17 to 45 depending on how you classify one category that trips everyone up: anime-canon episodes.

Black Clover has 22 episodes (3, 13, 55-56, 130, 132-133, 136-141, 149-157) that were created exclusively for the anime but supervised by series creator Yuki Tabata. They fill the six-month timeskip between the Elf Reincarnation arc and the Spade Kingdom setup. These are not filler. Tabata approved them; they develop the characters during a period the manga skipped entirely, and they set up storylines that Season 2 will pay off. We count 18 pure filler episodes in our Black Clover filler list and treat the anime-canon block as what it is: canon that just wasn't drawn in manga panels.

Black Clover Skippable Episodes: The Quick-Skip List

If you're speed-running and just want the episode numbers, here they are. These are all 18 Black Clover filler eps you can skip without losing a single plot thread:

Episodes 29, 66, 68, 82, 123, 124, 125, 131, 134, 135, 142, 143, 144, 145, 146, 147, 148, 149

Three of those deserve an asterisk, though. Episode 68 (Yami vs. Jack), Episode 131 (return to Hage), and Episode 135 (Finral's dating chaos) are all genuinely entertaining, and fans consistently single them out as filler worth keeping. If you have the time, watch those three. Skip the rest guilt-free.

One more thing: the anime-canon episodes from 130 to 157 are NOT filler. Don't skip them on a first watch. They bridge two major arcs and include captain training, squad development, and Tabata-approved character moments that the manga simply didn't have room for.

Secretly Peak: The Filler Episodes Worth Protecting

Some filler pages in the grimoire have real power. These three are the ones fans argue should never be skipped, even on a pure-canon run.

Episode 68: Yami vs. Jack

Every fan who's seen it defends it. Captain Yami and Captain Jack turn a festival food-stall competition into an all-out brawl, and the animation team clearly had fun with it. The fight has no plot consequences and absolutely no reason to exist, which is exactly why it works. It captures the ridiculous competitive energy between Black Clover's captains better than some canon episodes do.

Episode 131: A New Resolve

Asta and Yuno return to Hage village between arcs, and the episode trades action for atmosphere. Their old home has changed. They've changed more. It's a small, quiet beat that earns its emotions without forcing them, and the fan community consistently ranks it among the best filler the show ever produced.

Episode 135: The One Who Has My Heart, My Mind, and Soul

Finral gets the spotlight in a dating-focused side story that doubles as a love letter to the Black Bulls' squad chemistry. If you fell for the cast because of how they bounce off each other, this is 20 minutes of exactly that.

The Fake Skip: Episodes 142-148

The Devil Believers arc is the most polarizing filler stretch in all of Black Clover. The fan community is genuinely split on it. The arc asks an interesting question (what happens to ordinary people when devils show up?) but takes seven episodes to answer something that needed three. Watch the bookends if the premise hooks you. Skip the middle without guilt.

The Real Hot Take: Asta's Anti-Magic Extends to Filler

Black Clover is the show that embodies its own protagonist. Asta had no magic in a world that runs on it, and his series had almost no filler in a production pipeline that practically runs on it. Studio Pierrot's weekly shonen model historically turns padding into an inevitability, but Black Clover resisted it the same way Asta resists spells: through sheer, stubborn refusal to follow the pattern. Eighteen filler episodes across 170. That's not a production strategy, that's a character statement. The show's identity and its main character's identity are the same thing, and the filler rate is the proof.

Asta Never Needed the Padding

Black Clover ran weekly for three and a half years out of the same studio that turned filler into an art form (or a war crime, depending on your Naruto experience). It came out the other side with one of the lowest filler rates in long-running shonen history. The manga wrapped in May 2026 at Chapter 392, and Season 2 is confirmed with a new seasonal format. Odds of filler in the new season? Basically zero. Tabata's full story is on the page, and Pierrot has learned from the Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War approach.

That's the complete Black Clover filler list. If you want the same treatment for the rest of the Pierrot lineup, check out our Naruto Shippuden filler list, our Bleach filler list, and our One Piece filler guide.

What Is Filler in Anime (And Why Does It Exist)?

Filler refers to anime episodes that aren't adapted from the original manga. They're original stories created by the animation studio, usually inserted when the anime's production pace catches up to (or threatens to overtake) the manga it's based on.

Why do anime have fillers in the first place?

The answer comes down to production math. A weekly anime needs roughly 40 to 50 new episodes every year. A weekly manga, meanwhile, produces about 48 chapters per year, and most anime episodes burn through one to two chapters of material. It doesn't take long before the anime is knocking on the manga's door, and the studio has to choose between going on hiatus or creating original content to buy time. For decades, studios chose the original content. The result was filler.

The question of why do anime have filler episodes gets more interesting when you look at the three types that exist in practice.

  • Pure filler has no manga basis at all (think Bleach's Bount Arc or the infamous Naruto stretch from episodes 136 to 219).
  • Mixed canon/filler blends manga material with anime-original padding, stretching one chapter across a full episode with added scenes.
  • Anime canon, a newer category that Boruto popularized, where the studio produces original stories considered part of the official continuity even though the manga never told them.

Whether anime canon counts as filler depends entirely on who you ask, and the debate gets heated.

A note on Boruto: The official filler count sits around 26 episodes out of 293 (about 9%), but the community largely considers the massive volume of "anime canon" episodes as functional filler. If you include anime-canon content, the number climbs past 70%. The answer depends on your definition and your patience.

Records worth knowing:

  • Most filler episodes ever: Detective Conan (~569 and still climbing)
  • Highest filler percentage: Trigun 1998 (65%, though it's only 26 episodes)
  • Longest consecutive filler stretch: Naruto, episodes 136 to 219 (83 episodes, May 2005 to February 2007)

Show-by-Show Quick Filler Guide

The leaderboard gives you the big picture. Here's the quick reference for the shows fans search for most on any filler episodes list, with a brief take on what to skip and what to keep.

Naruto + Naruto Shippuden

Filler count: ~294 out of 720 episodes (41%)

The original series back-loads its filler hard. Episodes 1 through 135 are almost entirely canon, and then episodes 136 to 219 are 83 consecutive episodes of filler right before Shippuden begins. Skip that entire block and jump straight to Shippuden. In Shippuden, filler is scattered more evenly, but Kakashi's Anbu Arc (349–361) and Itachi Shinden (451–458) are worth keeping. Everything else is safe to pass on.

Bleach

Filler count: 163 out of 366 episodes (45%)

Bleach drops its filler arcs directly into the middle of canon storylines, which makes them especially disruptive to momentum. The Bount Arc (64–109) is widely considered the weakest stretch of the show. The New Captain Amagai Arc and the Gotei 13 Invading Army Arc are skippable without hesitation. The Zanpakuto Rebellion (230–265) is the exception: watch it if you want the best filler Bleach has to offer. And if you're catching up for the Thousand-Year Blood War finale in July 2026, know that TYBW has zero filler across all four cours.

One Piece

Filler count: ~98 out of ~1,168 episodes (8%)

One Piece has the leanest filler ratio of any classic long-runner. Most filler arcs are short (5 to 15 episodes) and clearly separated from the main story. The G-8 Arc (196–206) is genuinely excellent and worth watching. The Warship Island, Ice Hunter, and Silver Mine arcs are safe to skip. With One Piece moving to a seasonal format in April 2026 (26 episodes per year for the Elbaph Arc), new filler has effectively stopped.

Dragon Ball Z

Filler count: 39 out of 291 episodes (13%)

Relatively clean for its era. The Garlic Jr. Arc is skippable. The Other World Tournament is worth your time for the fun factor alone. Most other filler is scattered across single episodes or brief scene extensions that pad out fights. If you're watching Dragon Ball Z Kai instead, filler is already cut, giving you a tighter 167-episode version of the full story.

Boruto: Naruto Next Generations

Filler count: 26 pure filler out of 293 episodes (9%), or 70%+ if you count anime canon

Boruto is the most polarizing entry on any anime filler list. The official filler count is low, but the show's heavy reliance on "anime canon" episodes that don't adapt the manga makes it feel far more padded than the numbers suggest. Fans who want the core story typically stick to the manga-adapted arcs: the Chunin Exams reimagining, the Kawaki Arc, and the Kara storyline.

Fairy Tail

Filler count: 63 out of 328 episodes (19%)

Fairy Tail's filler is concentrated in a few distinct arcs. The Key of the Starry Sky Arc and the Eclipse Celestial Spirits Arc are the biggest offenders and easy to skip. Canon-heavy stretches like the Grand Magic Games and the Tartaros Arc are where the show is at its best.

Detective Conan

Filler count: ~569 out of ~1,200+ episodes (~47%)

The all-time filler champion. Detective Conan's episodic, case-of-the-week format makes filler less painful than in a serialized story, because many standalone filler cases are genuinely fun mysteries on their own. Early filler episodes are especially well-regarded among longtime fans. If you're only interested in the overarching Black Organization plot, though, you're looking at skipping roughly half the show.

Sailor Moon

Filler count: ~99 out of 200 episodes (~49%)

Nearly half the original anime is filler, but much of it is charming monster-of-the-week content that builds out the characters' daily lives in ways the manga didn't have room for. Fans who grew up with the show often have a real soft spot for these episodes. If you want a leaner experience, Sailor Moon Crystal (2014–2016) adapts the manga directly with no filler, though its early animation quality was a sore point for some viewers.

Anime With Zero Filler: Where to Start if You Don't Want to Skip Anything

If the entire concept of checking filler guides before each viewing session sounds exhausting, these shows have none. Every episode is canon, every minute counts.
