The pattern across all of these is clear: seasonal production (12 to 26 episodes per season) eliminates the need for filler entirely. When studios wait for source material to build a buffer before animating, they never have to invent content to fill airtime.

The Best Anime Filler Arcs Actually Worth Watching

Filler has earned its bad reputation. But a handful of arcs are genuinely great television, and skipping them means missing some of the most memorable moments in their respective series. Here are the ones the fan community consistently champions.

One Piece: G-8 Arc (Episodes 196–206)

After falling from Skypiea, the Straw Hats crash-land inside a heavily fortified Marine base and have to bluff, sneak, and fight their way out. Every crew member gets a spotlight moment. Sanji takes over the kitchen. Robin infiltrates the intelligence division. Luffy hides inside a burlap sack (badly). The filler-original character Captain Jonathan is sharp enough that fans have wished he'd appear in the manga for years. And the Condoriano gag has become one of the most referenced jokes in the entire One Piece community. Fans regularly say they didn't even realize G-8 was filler until they looked it up years later. It's that seamless.

Naruto Shippuden: Kakashi's Anbu Arc (Episodes 349–361)

A deep look at Kakashi's years in ANBU Black Ops after his father's death and before he became Team 7's sensei. The arc builds out his relationship with a young Yamato and a teenage Itachi, both of whom served in ANBU alongside him, and it paints the darker side of the ninja world that the main story only hints at. The emotional weight here rivals any canon arc in the series. Fans on community polls consistently rank it alongside the Pain Arc and the Chunin Exams as peak Naruto. If you skip all other Naruto filler, keep this one.

Bleach: Zanpakuto Rebellion Arc (Episodes 230–265)

Every Soul Reaper's Zanpakuto spirit materializes and rebels against its master, led by the mysterious Muramasa. The concept alone is creative enough to justify the arc, but the execution delivers too. Seeing Byakuya's Senbonzakura and Rukia's Sode no Shirayuki as independent characters adds real texture to the weapon-wielder dynamic that the main story never fully explored. Muramasa himself became a fan-favorite, and the fight choreography holds up well for its era. In a show with 45% filler, the Zanpakuto Rebellion is the one arc fans consistently defend.

Naruto Shippuden: Itachi Shinden (Episodes 451–458)

Based on the Itachi Shinden light novels (which some fans argue makes this "novel canon" rather than true filler), the arc follows Itachi from childhood through the Uchiha massacre. Shisui gets fully realized as a character for the first time. Izumi's relationship with Itachi gives the massacre a personal, heartbreaking angle the main series never achieved. The arc recontextualizes one of anime's most iconic twists by showing every agonizing step that led to it. Even fans who skip every other filler arc tend to make an exception for Itachi Shinden.

Dragon Ball Z: Other World Tournament

After the Cell Games, Goku finds himself in the afterlife competing in a martial arts tournament against deceased warriors from across the universe. It's pure Dragon Ball fun: new opponents with creative abilities, escalating fights, and Goku doing what Goku does best. Some fans call it better than the actual ending of the Cell Saga. At minimum, it's one of the best tonal palette cleansers in any Dragon Ball series.

Saint Seiya: Asgard Saga

An entire filler saga that the fan community treats as honorary canon. Set in the frozen lands of Asgard, the Bronze Saints face the God Warriors in battles with gorgeous choreography and surprising emotional depth. The original characters are well-designed and motivated, and the saga builds to a climax that earns its payoff. For a filler arc, the Asgard Saga punches absurdly far above its weight class.

Honorable mentions

Gintama's filler in general (impossible to separate from the canon because all of it is equally hilarious), the Boruto Time Slip Arc (Boruto meets young Naruto in a love letter to the franchise's 20th anniversary), and Samurai Champloo's baseball episode (the crew plays baseball with Americans, and it's one of the funniest single episodes in anime history).

The Era Ends, the Backlog Remains

The era of anime filler is closing. One Piece went seasonal. Bleach's comeback proved the model works. Every major new anime ships with zero padding. Give it a few more years, and filler might be something only older fans remember wrestling with.

But right now, in 2026, the backlog is still enormous. Naruto still has 720 episodes. Detective Conan is past 1,200. Bleach's original run is still 45% filler. And millions of fans are still starting these shows for the first time, still wondering which episodes matter and which ones don't.

FAQ

Which anime has the most filler episodes?

Detective Conan holds the record with roughly 569 filler episodes out of over 1,200 total. By percentage, the original Trigun leads at 65%, though it's only 26 episodes long. Among long-running shonen, Bleach (45%) and Naruto (41%) have the highest filler ratios.

Is it okay to skip filler episodes in anime?

Yes. Filler episodes are designed to be self-contained, and the main story almost never references them afterward. You can skip every filler episode in Naruto, Bleach, or One Piece and follow the plot without any gaps. The exception is a small number of arcs that add genuine character depth, like Kakashi's Anbu Arc or the G-8 Arc.

What is the best filler arc in anime?

The One Piece G-8 Arc (episodes 196 to 206) is the most widely praised filler arc in anime. Fans regularly say they didn't realize it was filler until they checked afterward. Kakashi's Anbu Arc in Naruto Shippuden and the Zanpakuto Rebellion in Bleach are close seconds.

What is the longest filler arc in anime history?

Naruto holds the record with episodes 136 to 219, a stretch of 83 consecutive filler episodes that aired from May 2005 to February 2007. The entire block aired between the end of the original Naruto story and the beginning of Naruto Shippuden.

Do modern anime still have filler?

Rarely. The shift to seasonal production (12 to 26 episodes per season, with breaks between seasons) has largely eliminated the need for filler. Demon Slayer, Jujutsu Kaisen, Chainsaw Man, and Spy x Family all have zero filler episodes. Even One Piece moved to a seasonal format in April 2026, ending its 27-year weekly tradition and stopping new filler production entirely.

Title: Fairy Tail Filler List: Which Episodes to Skip And Which Are Worth Your Time
Summary: Sort every arc with our complete Fairy Tail filler list and skip or watch verdicts. The filler rate is lower than you'd think. 🧚‍♀️🔥
Meta Title: Fairy Tail Filler List: Which Episodes to Skip
Meta Description: Fairy Tail filler list with skip or watch verdicts for every arc. The rate is lower than you'd expect. See which episodes to pass on.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Fairy Tail ran for 328 episodes across a full decade, and 61 of them are filler. That's roughly 19%, which puts it in the middle of the pack for long-running shonen. But the raw number doesn't tell you the interesting part: Fairy Tail has the widest filler quality gap of any major anime. One filler arc runs 26 episodes, and fans genuinely defend it. Another runs 23 episodes, and the community tells you to run the other way.

Think of them as side quests on the guild request board. Some are S-Class jobs disguised as downtime. Some are D-Class busywork that should have been taken down before anyone accepted them. This Fairy Tail anime filler list covers every filler episode and arc with real verdicts, and we'll sort out the mixed-canon mess that has the internet disagreeing on the actual count.

Fairy Tail Filler at a Glance

StatDetail
Total Episodes328
Filler Episodes61
Filler Percentage~19%
Mixed Canon/Filler10 episodes
Canon Episodes257 (manga canon)
Sequel100 Years Quest (S2 confirmed for early 2027)

So how many filler episodes are in Fairy Tail? The clean answer is 61 pure filler episodes. But you'll see the count listed anywhere from 52 to 61, and the gap comes down to 10 mixed canon/filler episodes (20, 49, 69, 151, 182-183, 201, 255, 260, 270, 312). These episodes weave original anime content around real manga plot points, so they're not pure filler and shouldn't be skipped. Our Fairy Tail filler list keeps them in their own category and counts 61 episodes as the true filler number.

Fairy Tail Skippable Episodes: The Quick-Skip List

Here's the complete Fairy Tail filler episodes list if you just want the numbers. These are all 61 episodes you can skip without losing a single plot thread:

Episodes 9, 19, 50, 69-75, 125-150, 202-226, 268

One asterisk: the Key of the Starry Sky arc (125-150) is 26 episodes of filler that fans consistently call worth watching, especially if you care about Lucy's character arc and Celestial Spirit lore. If you're going to make one exception to the skip list, make it that one.

The 10 mixed canon/filler episodes listed above are NOT included here. Don't skip those on a first watch. They contain real plot beats wrapped in original framing.

The Complete Fairy Tail Filler List (by Arc)

Below is the full Fairy Tail filler list broken down by arc. Every group gets a verdict and a reason, not just a color code.

Standalone Fillers

ArcEpisodesVerdict
Natsu vs. mushroom monsters (Eisenwald arc)9Watch. Natsu and Happy try to eat monsters that turn out to be alive. Pure comedic guild energy in a single episode.

Daphne Arc

ArcEpisodesVerdict
Daphne's artificial dragon plot69-75Skip. The most disliked filler arc in Fairy Tail by a wide margin. The villain is baffling (picture a cowgirl-scientist obsessed with sausages), the plot goes nowhere, and Natsu spends most of the arc trapped inside a mechanical dragon. At 7 episodes it's short enough to feel harmless, but it's still 3 hours you could spend on a canon arc.

Key of the Starry Sky Arc

ArcEpisodesVerdict
The Infinity Clock and Lucy's father's legacy125-150Watch. The longest filler arc in the franchise at 26 episodes, and the one fans consistently defend. Lucy's relationship with her late father anchors the emotional core, while her Celestial Spirit Magic gets genuine spotlight and development. The arc also brings back the Oracion Seis in reformed roles and gives Blue Pegasus meaningful screen time. It's filler by classification, but it feels like a canon Lucy arc that the manga didn't have room for.

Eclipse Celestial Spirits Arc

ArcEpisodesVerdict
Eclipse-corrupted Zodiac battles204-226Skip. The longest skippable block in the series at 23 episodes. The Celestial Spirits turn hostile and challenge the guild to gimmick fights: dance battles, card games, amusement park duels. The premise strips characters out of the guild context that makes them interesting and replaces it with disconnected spectacle. The pacing drags, the stakes feel hollow, and the community consensus is nearly unanimous. If you skip one arc guilt-free, it's this one.

Zero Arc Standalone

ArcEpisodesVerdict
Fairy Tail Zero: Treasure Hunt268Watch. A standalone episode tied to Mavis Vermillion's backstory and the Fairy Tail Zero prequel arc. Light, fun, and rewards anyone who enjoyed learning about the guild's founding.

Secretly Peak: The Side Quests Worth Taking

Some jobs on the request board hit harder than they look on paper. These are the filler entries that the Fairy Tail community argues deserve the guild mark.

Key of the Starry Sky (Episodes 125-150)

Twenty-six episodes is a serious time investment for filler, and honestly, that length scares people off before they give it a chance. But the arc earns its runtime through Lucy's family history. Her father's legacy, the connection between the Heartfilia estate and the Infinity Clock, and the way Celestial Spirit Magic gets developed as an actual combat system rather than a summoning gimmick all land with real weight. The Oracion Seis reborn as antagonists give the arc a villain roster that feels consequential, not throwaway. If you care about Lucy as more than the girl who summons zodiac spirits, these 26 episodes are where the show does her the most justice.

Episode 9: Natsu vs. the Mushroom Monsters

A standalone filler that captures everything fun about early Fairy Tail in 20 minutes. Natsu and Happy take a job that involves eating mushrooms; the mushrooms fight back, and chaos follows. No stakes, no lore, just the guild being the guild. Quick, funny, and exactly the kind of breather episode that works between canon arcs.

Episode 268: Fairy Tail Zero Treasure Hunt

A Mavis-centric episode that ties into the prequel storyline about the guild's founding. If you watched the Fairy Tail Zero arc and wanted one more glimpse at young Mavis and the original guild members, this episode delivers without overstaying. Think of it as a bonus chapter at the end of a volume.

The Fake Skip: Eclipse Celestial Spirits (Episodes 204-226)

Here's the other side of the coin. At 23 episodes, the Eclipse Celestial Spirits arc is the longest block of filler you should actually skip. The concept (corrupted Zodiac spirits turn on their masters) sounds promising on paper, but the execution turns each confrontation into a themed gimmick duel with zero emotional stakes. Gray has a dance battle with Cancer. Cana plays cards against Scorpio. Wendy goes to an amusement park with Aquarius. These episodes pull the characters away from the guild and drop them into disconnected vignettes that feel like a different show entirely. The community opinion is loud and consistent on this one.

The Real Hot Take: Guild Chemistry Is the Filler Barometer

Fairy Tail is a hangout show wearing shonen armor. The fights matter, but the thing that actually keeps you watching 328 episodes is the guild hall. The brawls at the bar, the request board chaos, Natsu kicking in the door. When filler remembers that, it works. When it forgets, it collapses.

Key of the Starry Sky works because it's 26 episodes of the guild being the guild, anchored by Lucy's emotional arc. Eclipse Celestial Spirits fails because it rips the cast out of that context and isolates them in gimmick fights with no guild dynamic. The Daphne arc fails because it traps the protagonist inside a machine and removes him from the very interactions that define the show. The standalone filler that works (episode 9, episode 268) succeeds because it's just the guild hanging out and getting into trouble.

How much of Fairy Tail is filler? About 19%. But the real question is how much of that filler actually feels like Fairy Tail. The answer is roughly 28 out of 61 episodes. The rest is a different show borrowing the character designs.

Some Quests Are Worth the Detour

Fairy Tail's filler request board has S-Class jobs and D-Class busywork, and the gap between them is wider than almost any other shonen. The good news: the best filler arc in the franchise (Key of the Starry Sky) is genuinely great. The bad news: the worst one (Eclipse Celestial Spirits) is 23 episodes long. Knowing which is which before you start saves you a full season's worth of time.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many filler episodes are in Fairy Tail?

Fairy Tail has 61 pure filler episodes out of 328 total. The complete list of Fairy Tail filler episodes includes standalone episodes (9, 19, 50, 268), the Daphne arc (69-75), Key of the Starry Sky (125-150), and Eclipse Celestial Spirits (204-226). An additional 10 mixed canon/filler episodes exist but shouldn't be skipped.

How much of Fairy Tail is filler?

About 19% of Fairy Tail is pure filler. Including the 10 mixed episodes would push the number closer to 22%, but those mixed episodes contain real story beats and are generally worth watching.

Can I skip all Fairy Tail filler without missing the story?

Yes. Every filler episode is self-contained, and skipping all 61 won't create any plot gaps. The one exception worth reconsidering is the Key of the Starry Sky arc (episodes 125-150), which develops Lucy's character in ways the main story doesn't replicate.

Is Fairy Tail: 100 Years Quest filler-free?

Season 1 of 100 Years Quest (25 episodes, July 2024 to January 2025) adapted the manga directly with no filler. Season 2 is confirmed for early 2027, and with J.C. Staff handing production to CloverWorks under a seasonal model, filler is unlikely.

Is the Key of the Starry Sky arc worth watching?

For Lucy fans, absolutely. The arc focuses on her late father's connection to the Infinity Clock, gives Celestial Spirit Magic real development as a combat system, and features the reformed Oracion Seis as villains. At 26 episodes it's a commitment, but the emotional payoff and character depth justify the runtime for most viewers.

Look, you could just watch Dragon Ball Z Kai, which condenses the whole story into 167 filler-free, HD-remastered episodes covering everything from Raditz crashing into Kame House to Kid Buu turning into space dust. But something about that 291-episode original keeps pulling people back, probably because the version of DBZ that taught an entire generation to sit through three episodes of a Spirit Bomb charging is the version that actually lives in your memory. If you're here, you already made your choice, and now you just want to know which episodes to cut so the rewatch doesn't drag.

Good news: there are only 38 pure filler episodes in this Dragon Ball Z filler list, putting the series at roughly 13% filler. Lower than Naruto Shippuden, lower than Bleach, lower than Fairy Tail. The number sounds clean until you remember how the show actually felt to watch, but we'll get to that. For now: every filler episode broken down by saga, real skip-or-watch verdicts, the Kai situation explained, and the reason one chunk of "skippable" filler might contain the most important character work in the franchise.

Secretly Peak: The Filler Worth Protecting

Some Dragon Ball Z fillers carry more weight than their classification would suggest, and these are the episodes fans will fight you about skipping.

Episode 125: Goku's Ordeal

If there's a single filler episode every Dragon Ball fan agrees on, it's this one. Chi-Chi decides Goku and Piccolo need to earn their driver's licenses because she's tired of walking to the grocery store, and what follows is one of the funniest episodes the franchise has ever produced.

Piccolo shows up to driving school wearing Goku's civilian clothes (tight jeans, yellow shirt, backwards baseball cap) looking completely bewildered. Goku panics behind the wheel of a car despite being able to fly faster than jets. The whole thing plays like a slice-of-life comedy starring two planet-busters who have been domesticated against their will, and it captures the original Dragon Ball's goofy humor better than almost anything else in Z.

Other World Tournament (Episodes 195-199)

Five episodes of afterlife tournament action that gave us Pikkon, an anime-original fighter who went blow-for-blow with Super Saiyan Goku and earned a permanent spot in the fan community's heart despite never appearing in a single panel of the manga.

The fights are well-animated, the pacing is tight (rare for this show), and Goku's non-canon Super Saiyan Kaioken remains one of the most visually striking moments in the series. As a breather between the emotional wreckage of Cell and the slow buildup to Buu, these five episodes do exactly what a palate cleanser should.

Gohan's Wilderness Training (Episodes 9-10, 12-15)

The filler that quietly built the most important relationship in the franchise. Where the manga covers Gohan's year under Piccolo in a handful of panels, the anime turns it into six episodes of a four-year-old surviving alone in the wilderness while Piccolo watches from the shadows, gradually cracking under his own reluctant protectiveness. More on why this matters in the hot take below.

The Fake Skip: Garlic Jr. Arc (Episodes 108-117)

Ten episodes, zero consequences, a villain who never comes back. The longest skippable block in DBZ and the safest cut on this list. The arc has been mildly reappraised for letting Gohan, Piccolo, and Krillin run the show without Goku, but the villain feels like a retread of his own movie, the Spice Boys are forgettable, and the whole thing wraps up the same way the Dead Zone did. Worth a look if you loved that film, easy to pass on otherwise.

The Real Hot Take: DBZ's Filler Did More for Gohan Than the Manga Did

Here's the thing about Gohan's arc that nobody talks about when they talk about filler: the manga handed him a destiny (defeat Cell, surpass Goku, become the strongest fighter alive) without building the emotional foundation to make any of it land. His training under Piccolo, the relationship that becomes the beating heart of the entire Dragon Ball franchise, gets a few manga panels. Piccolo takes Gohan, time passes, Gohan is ready, move on.

The anime's filler episodes built everything the manga left out. Six episodes of a kid surviving alone in the wild, earning the respect of the Namekian warrior who kidnapped him, while Piccolo watches from the shadows with his cold exterior breaking down one episode at a time. Those episodes are the reason Piccolo's death against Nappa doesn't just work as a plot moment but absolutely destroys you, and the franchise eventually proved how central that bond is when Dragon Ball Super: Super Hero turned their relationship into an entire movie, decades after filler episodes laid the groundwork.

The Spirit Bomb Was Always Worth the Wait

Dragon Ball Z has 38 filler episodes across 291 total, and most are easy skips. Fake Namek delays the best saga, Garlic Jr. goes nowhere, and the Buu Saga padding tests your patience. But woven between those are filler episodes that became iconic for good reason: a driving test, a dead man's tournament, and a child learning to survive alone. Kai removes all of it in one clean cut. This Dragon Ball Z filler list lets you pick what stays and what goes on your own terms.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many filler episodes does Dragon Ball Z have?

38 pure filler episodes out of 291 total, putting the filler rate at roughly 13%. An additional 8 mixed canon/filler episodes contain both original and manga-adapted content but shouldn't be skipped.

What is the difference between DBZ and DBZ Kai?

Kai removes all filler and trims the in-canon padding, condensing 291 episodes down to 167 with re-recorded voice work, updated visuals, and a different music score (the Bruce Faulconer soundtrack from the US version of DBZ is not in Kai). Same story, dramatically tighter pacing.

Is the Garlic Jr. arc worth watching?

For most viewers, no. Ten episodes of standalone filler with no lasting consequences and a villain who never returns. If you enjoyed the Dead Zone movie the arc expands on that storyline, but strictly for story purposes you can jump from 107 to 118 without missing anything.

Is Dragon Ball Daima filler?

No. Daima (20 episodes, Oct 2024 to Feb 2025) is fully canon, written by Akira Toriyama before his passing, and set between the end of Dragon Ball Z and the beginning of Dragon Ball Super.

What is the best filler episode in Dragon Ball Z?

Episode 125, "Goku's Ordeal," and it's not close. Goku and Piccolo attempt to earn their driver's licenses at Chi-Chi's insistence, and the result is the funniest 20 minutes the franchise has ever produced.

Title: My Hero Academia Filler List: The Complete Guide to Every Episode You Can Skip
Summary: Pin down the few skippable episodes with our complete My Hero Academia filler list for every season. MHA barely has filler. 🦸‍♂️⚡
Meta Title: My Hero Academia Filler List: Every Skippable Ep
Meta Description: My Hero Academia filler list for all 8 seasons. Just 4 pure filler episodes, plus the ones fans wrongly skip. See what to watch and skip.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
My Hero Academia wrapped its eight-season run in December 2025, dropped a bonus epilogue episode in May 2026, and left behind 170 numbered episodes with one of the lowest filler counts in shonen anime history. The My Hero Academia filler list clocks in at just four pure filler episodes, which puts the series at roughly 2-3% filler across its entire run, and for a show that aired over nearly a decade, that number is borderline absurd.

The catch is that "four" isn't the whole picture. Depending on how you define filler (pure anime-original content, recap episodes, or mixed canon/filler hybrids), you could count anywhere from four to nine episodes with non-canon material. The breakdown below covers all of them so you can decide what to skip, what to keep, and which episodes the fandom has been sleeping on.

My Hero Academia Filler: Quick Stats

StatDetail
Total Episodes170 (+1 bonus special)
Pure Filler Episodes4
Mixed Canon/Filler5 (episodes 54, 55, 89, 105, 127)
Filler Percentage~2-3%
Seasons8 (2016-2025)
Series StatusComplete

For comparison, Naruto sits at roughly 41% filler and Bleach at around 45%. MHA earned its low count largely through seasonal production: air a season, go on break, let Horikoshi build a manga lead. The anime never had to stall because it never caught up.

MHA Filler Episodes: The Quick-Skip List

Here's every episode on the My Hero Academia filler list in one clean block, every episode you can skip without losing a single plot thread:

Episodes 39, 58, 64, 104

Four episodes out of 170, and even within that short list, two of them are movie prologues that become required viewing if you plan to watch the films. Episode 58 ("Save the World With Love!") sets up the first MHA movie, Two Heroes, and episode 104 ("Long Time No See, Selkie") feeds directly into the third movie, World Heroes' Mission. Episode 32, which constantly gets mislabeled as filler, is actually anime-original canon that gives Froppy her single best character moment in the series, and you can read more about why below.

You might also see episode 13.5 ("Hero Notebook") counted as a filler episode. It's a Season 1 recap numbered as a half-episode, and most streaming platforms don't even include it in their count. If you're binging from episode 1, you already know everything it covers.

Every My Hero Academia Filler Episode, Explained

Not every filler episode is created equal, and MHA's short list includes everything from harmless breathers to movie tie-ins that quietly become essential depending on how much of the franchise you want to experience. Here's the full breakdown.

TitleSeasonVerdict
Hero Notebook (Ep 13.5)Season 2Skip. Pure recap of Season 1 events with nothing new added. If you watched the first season, you've seen all of this before.
Everyone's Internships (Ep 32)Season 2Watch. Constantly mislabeled as filler, but this is anime-original canon. It follows Froppy on a mission with pro hero Selkie and his sidekick Sirius against the villain Innsmouth, and it's one of the few episodes where a female character gets a full spotlight and genuinely delivers.
Game Start (Ep 39)Season 3Skip. Pool day with Class 1-A, mostly a padding episode between seasons. One caveat: the opening two minutes feature Tomura Shigaraki in the League hideout, articulating his hatred for All Might and planting the motivation for the Forest Training Camp attack. That scene is canon even though the rest of the episode is not.
Save the World With Love! (Ep 58)Season 3Watch if you're doing the movies, skip if you're not. Serves as the prologue to the first MHA film, Two Heroes. Class 1-A trains at a resort island with an investigation subplot that ties directly into the movie's opening act, and it's entertaining enough as a standalone even if you never plan to watch the film.
The Scoop on U.A. Class 1-A (Ep 64)Season 4Skip. A freelance journalist named Taneo visits U.A. trying to figure out which student inherited All Might's power. Charming and completely self-contained, but it has zero impact on anything that follows. The perfect "watch it if you have 20 minutes to kill" episode.
Long Time No See, Selkie (Ep 104)Season 5Watch if you're doing the movies, skip if you're not. Ochaco, Tsuyu, and Nejire team up with Selkie for a sea-rescue mission that sets up the third MHA movie, World Heroes' Mission. Without the movie context, it's the weakest filler episode in the series by a comfortable margin.

The mixed canon/filler episodes (54, 55, 89, 105, and 127) blend manga material with anime-original scenes, and you should watch all of them since the canon portions contain setup that pays off later.

Seasons 1, 6, 7, and 8 contain zero filler of any kind. Season 1 adapted the manga nearly panel-for-panel, and Seasons 6 through 8 were locked into the Paranormal Liberation War and Final War arcs with no room for detours.

The MHA Filler Episodes That Are Actually Worth Your Time

Four skippable episodes across 170 means you could watch every single one of them in under 90 minutes and lose nothing from your afternoon, but three entries on the list deserve a closer look before you press skip.

Episode 32: The One Everyone Gets Wrong

"Everyone's Internships" gets written off as filler constantly, but it's actually anime-original canon, a category that means Studio Bones created the episode specifically to expand the story rather than pad runtime. The episode follows Tsuyu Asui during her internship with the pro hero Selkie, and her mission against the villain Innsmouth gives Froppy one of the most capable and independent hero moments she gets in the entire series. MHA frequently struggled to give its female cast sustained spotlight outside of group battles, and this episode quietly did what the main arcs often didn't make time for. Skipping it means missing one of Tsuyu's defining scenes, and that's a loss that hits harder than you'd expect from a "filler" episode.

Episode 58: The Movie Prologue That's Better Than It Needs to Be

As a standalone My Hero Academia filler episode, "Save the World With Love!" is a well-animated resort-island training exercise with fun Class 1-A dynamics. As a movie prologue, it's the connective tissue between Season 3 and the first MHA film. The investigation subplot feeds directly into the opening act of Two Heroes, and skipping it means the movie's first scene will feel like you walked in late. Even outside the movie context, the animation quality makes this one of the more enjoyable MHA filler episodes.

Episode 39: Canon Hiding Inside Filler

The pool day episode is pure breather content with no stakes and no plot advancement, except for the first two minutes. The episode opens with Tomura Shigaraki sitting in the League of Villains hideout, watching an All Might broadcast, and articulating exactly why All Might, Deku, and Stain all infuriate him. That monologue crystallizes his motivation heading into the Forest Training Camp attack and sets the emotional tone for Season 3's villain escalation. The full episode is labeled filler, but those opening minutes aren't, and they're worth seeing even if you skip the pool shenanigans that follow.

The Real Filler Problem Nobody Talks About

Here's what the My Hero Academia filler list conversation always misses: the actual filler episodes were never this show's real pacing problem.

Ask any fan which stretch of MHA felt the most like filler and the answer comes back almost unanimously: the Joint Training arc in Season 5, roughly episodes 89 through 101. Every fight, every Quirk showcase, every flashback in that stretch is straight from the manga, one hundred percent canon, and the community still treats it like a ten-episode endurance test. Forums are packed with fans calling it a dragged-out filler arc despite the fact that every frame of it has a corresponding manga panel.

The frustration had nothing to do with anime-original content. It came from pacing stretched thin with repeated flashbacks (Endeavor's abuse backstory showed up at least four times that season), an arc reorder that killed dramatic tension by pushing My Villain Academia to the back half, and animation quality dipping while Studio Bones split resources with movie production. The one actual filler episode in Season 5 (episode 104, the Selkie movie tie-in) played a role in that reorder too, because the season needed room for the movie prologue, and carving out that space contributed to rearranging canon arcs in a way that drained everything around them.

Meanwhile, episode 64 (the journalist filler episode) aired right before the Overhaul arc and almost nobody resents it. It landed at exactly the right moment as a lighthearted palate cleanser, and it did what good filler should do: give you a breath before the story hits hard again.

The label tells you surprisingly little about whether an episode is worth your time. Some canon episodes will test your patience more than any filler ever could, and some filler episodes earn their spot in the watch order more than they get credit for.

Plus Ultra: The Complete MHA Filler Verdict

My Hero Academia wrapped up 170 episodes and left behind fewer skippable MHA filler episodes than most shows produce in a single season. The complete My Hero Academia filler list fits on a Post-it note, and whether you skip the four pure filler episodes or watch them all (it's under 90 minutes of content), the difference in your viewing experience is genuinely negligible.

The bigger favor you can do yourself: watch episode 32 even though it keeps getting written off, catch episodes 58 and 104 if you're planning to watch the movies, and brace yourself for the Joint Training arc regardless of how clean the show's filler record looks.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many filler episodes does My Hero Academia have?

There are 4 pure filler episodes (39, 58, 64, and 104), but the count rises to 5 if you include the recap episode 13.5, and to 6 if you add episode 32, which is more accurately classified as anime-original canon rather than traditional filler. The mixed canon/filler episodes (54, 55, 89, 105, 127) contain plot-relevant material and should be watched.

Is there a time skip in My Hero Academia?

Yes. The series finale features an eight-year time skip, and the bonus "More" episode (May 2, 2026) adapts Chapter 431 of the manga, showing the adult lives of Class 1-A working as pro heroes. The "More" special is fully canon.

Does MHA Season 8 have any filler?

No. The 11-episode final season adapted the Final War and Epilogue arcs with zero filler. Horikoshi was heavily involved in production and personally supervised anime-original scenes that were added to expand the finale beyond what the manga covered.

Which MHA filler episodes are worth watching?

Episode 32 ("Everyone's Internships") is the standout for Froppy's character development, and episodes 58 and 104 are worth watching if you plan to see the MHA movies since they serve as direct prologues to Two Heroes and World Heroes' Mission.

What is MHA's filler percentage compared to Naruto and Bleach?

MHA sits at roughly 2-3% filler across 170 episodes, compared to Naruto at approximately 41% and Bleach at around 45%. MHA's seasonal production model (air a season, take a break, let the manga build a comfortable lead) is the structural reason it never needed to pad its episode count with original arcs.

Title: Dragon Ball Super Filler List: Every Episode to Skip; Ones You Should Actually Watch
Summary: Trim the fluff between sagas with our full Dragon Ball Super filler list. Most of DBS is canon, but the gaps have skippable filler. 🐉✨
Meta Title: Dragon Ball Super Filler List: Every Episode Sorted
Meta Description: Dragon Ball Super filler list, sorted by saga. Most of DBS is canon, but the gaps hide filler you can skip. See the watch-or-skip guide.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Dragon Ball Super has 14 filler episodes out of 131. At 11% filler, it's the cleanest Dragon Ball anime ever made. You can skip everything non-essential and lose barely five hours of content. The number isn't the problem.

The problem is that DBS also has 15 anime-original episodes that aren't in the manga and aren't filler. They're anime canon, and they matter. Some of them directly set up the Tournament of Power. Skip them because a color-coded list told you to, and you'll walk into the show's best arc missing context you can't get back.

Below is the complete Dragon Ball Super filler list with verdicts for every episode, plus the honest calls on which "filler" is actually worth your time. Consider it a Dragon Ball Super filler guide from someone who's watched every episode and has opinions about all of them.

Dragon Ball Super Filler at a Glance

Stat
Total Episodes131
Filler Episodes14
Filler Percentage11%
Anime-Canon Episodes (not in manga, but essential)15
Mixed Canon/Filler Episodes3
Watch Time Saved by Skipping All Filler~5 hours
AiredJuly 2015 to March 2018

Every Dragon Ball Super Filler Episode, Arc by Arc

Here are all the Dragon Ball Super filler episodes broken down by saga. Skip means you lose nothing. Watch means I'd keep it even on a lean rewatch. Your Call means it's fun but not essential.

God of Destruction Beerus Saga

EpisodeTitleVerdict
4"Aim for the Dragon Balls! Pilaf Gang in Action!"Skip. Pilaf gang filler. Nothing connects to Super's plot.

Golden Frieza Saga

EpisodeTitleVerdict
15"Make a Miracle, Satan the Hero!"Skip (but it's funny). Mr. Satan fights aliens to protect his reputation. Zero consequences, pure slapstick.

Post-Universe 6 Tournament (Copy-Vegeta Arc)

EpisodeTitleVerdict
42"Monaka vs. Son Goku!"Your Call. Beerus disguises himself as Monaka. A gag episode paying off the tournament joke.
43"Looking After Pan is a Lot of Trouble!"Your Call. Goku babysits Pan. Cute if you like slice-of-life Goku, easy to pass on.
44"Secret of the Superhuman Water is Unleashed!"Your Call. Copy-Vegeta mini-arc starts. Weird detour, fun fight at its core.
45"The Menace of Duplicated Vegeta!"Your Call. Copy-Vegeta continues. Low stakes, quick resolution.
46"Goku vs. Duplicated Vegeta!"Your Call. Arc wraps up. Goku punches the problem away. If you skipped 44-45, you missed nothing.

Post-Future Trunks Saga

EpisodeTitleVerdict
68"Come Forth, Shenron!"Skip. Everyone argues over a Dragon Ball wish. Setup for nothing.
69"Goku vs. Arale!"Watch. One of the best standalone episodes in DBS. Breakdown below.
70"This Time We Fight With Baseball!"Watch. The baseball episode. Yamcha's death pose. A meme was born.

Pre-Universe Survival Saga

EpisodeTitleVerdict
73"An Unexpected Great Saiyaman Movie?!"Your Call. Gohan gets rare screen time in a lighthearted Saiyaman story. Thin plot.
74"The Unbeatable Great Saiyaman!"Your Call. Wraps up the Saiyaman arc with an alien parasite fight. Better than 73, still skippable.
75"Back to the Old Training Grounds!"Watch. Krillin's best two episodes start here. Do not skip.
76"Krillin's Fighting Spirit Returns!"Watch. The payoff to 75. See below.

Secretly Peak: DBS Filler Worth Watching

Three filler episodes in Dragon Ball Super that aren't just "good for filler." They're good episodes, full stop.

1. Episode 69: Goku vs. Arale

Before Dragon Ball, Toriyama created Dr. Slump, a gag manga about a hyperactive robot girl named Arale who could punch the planet in half. Episode 69 brings her into the DBS power structure, and the results are beautiful chaos. Arale fights evenly with Super Saiyan Blue Goku. She one-shots Vegeta. She cracks the Earth in half and treats it like a joke, because in her world, it is one. Vegeta breaks the fourth wall to complain about "gag characters," which might be the single funniest moment in the series. A love letter from Toriyama to his own creative roots that works whether you know Dr. Slump or not.

2. Episode 70: Baseball

Champa challenges Universe 7 to a baseball game. Goku doesn't understand the rules. Vegeta takes it too seriously. Yamcha, borderline irrelevant since the Saiyan Saga, finally gets his moment in Dragon Ball Super. And then the moment kills him (sort of): he makes the game-winning play and ends up collapsed in the dirt in his iconic death pose from Z, a callback that became one of the most shared memes in the show's run. Beerus and Champa close it out with a full god-of-destruction fistfight over the score.

3. Episodes 75-76: Krillin's Fighting Spirit

Krillin hasn't fought seriously in years. He's a cop now. Then Goku asks him to train, and the show does something it almost never does: it lets a side character sit with real emotion. The training generates illusions of past enemies. Krillin faces Tambourine, who killed him in the original Dragon Ball. Frieza, who killed him on Namek. Cell. Nappa. The Ginyu Force. Every villain who ever ended his life is standing in front of him again. The payoff isn't a power-up. It's Krillin deciding to keep fighting anyway. For anyone who's been watching since the original series, these episodes are a character payoff decades in the making.

Dragon Ball Super's Best Writing Is in Its Filler

Hot take: the standalone episodes in Dragon Ball Super have better character writing than most of its canon arcs.

Think about it. The main arcs belong to Goku and Vegeta. Everyone else holds the line until the Saiyans show up. But the filler? The filler belongs to Krillin, Gohan, Yamcha, and the rest of the roster that gets sidelined the second a real villain appears. Episodes 75-76 give Krillin more genuine character development than the entire Tournament of Power does. The baseball episode gives Yamcha more personality in 22 minutes than he gets across the rest of the series. The Arale crossover lets Vegeta be funny in a way no serious arc ever allows.

DBZ taught fans to dread the word "filler." The Garlic Jr. arc earned that reputation. But DBS was never stalling for the manga to catch up. Its standalone episodes were written on purpose, as breathers between arcs, and Toei used them to give screen time to characters who'd otherwise get nothing. Skip them if you want. Any Dragon Ball Super filler list, including this one, exists so you can make that call. But the best episodes on the skip list are better than some of the canon surrounding them, and that's not something you can say about Goku learning to drive.

Your Dragon Radar for the Rewatch

The whole point of this Dragon Ball Super filler list is the gap between a spreadsheet and a guide. The numbers get you through the series faster. The verdicts make sure you don't lose anything worth keeping.

Fourteen filler episodes are safe to skip. The anime-canon episodes (especially 71-72 and 78-81) are not filler, no matter what label they're wearing. And the secretly peak picks, episodes 69, 70, 75, and 76, are the kind of standalone Dragon Ball the franchise doesn't make often enough. Treat this DBS filler list like a Dragon Radar. It finds the real Dragon Balls and filters out the rocks. A Scouter would just give you a reading and explode the second it hits something it can't classify.

FAQ

How many filler episodes are in Dragon Ball Super?

Fourteen out of 131 episodes, putting DBS at an 11% filler rate. That number jumps to 22 if you count anime-canon episodes (original to the anime but important to the story), which this guide treats separately.

Can I skip Dragon Ball Super episodes 1 through 27?

If you've seen the Battle of Gods and Resurrection F movies, yes. Episodes 1-27 retell both films. Skip to episode 28 (Universe 6 Saga) without losing new plot. If you haven't seen the movies, watch the episodes instead.

Is Dragon Ball Super worth watching without skipping filler?

Yes. Five hours of extra content at 11% filler is nothing for a 131-episode series, and several of those filler episodes (69, 70, 75, 76) are among the most entertaining in the show.

What's the difference between filler and anime canon in Dragon Ball Super?

Filler is standalone content that doesn't affect the plot. Anime canon isn't in the manga either, but it was written for the anime and feeds into the main story. The Hit assassination arc (71-72) and the Universe Survival recruitment (78-81) are anime canon, and skipping them means losing setup for the Tournament of Power.

Does Dragon Ball Super have less filler than Dragon Ball Z?

Yes. DBS is at 11% (14/131) versus DBZ's 13% (38/291). The bigger difference is why the filler exists: DBZ needed it because the anime caught up to the manga. DBS chose it as intentional breathers between arcs.

Title: Dragon Ball Filler List: Every Episode to Skip (and Why You Probably Shouldn't)
Summary: Uncover hidden filler in Goku's early journey with our complete Dragon Ball filler list. More filler than most fans realize. 🐉🟠
Meta Title: Dragon Ball Filler List: Every Episode to Skip
Meta Description: Dragon Ball filler list for Goku's early journey. More filler than most fans expect. See which episodes to skip and the few worth keeping.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Here's the truth about looking up a Dragon Ball filler list: you barely need one. The original Dragon Ball has a filler rate of just 14%, one of the lowest of any classic shonen anime. That's 21 episodes out of 153, or roughly eight hours of content. Compare that to Naruto's 41% or Bleach's 45%, and you'll understand why Dragon Ball fans don't talk about filler the way other fandoms do.

But those 21 episodes aren't all throwaway padding. Several of them rank among the show's most inventive standalone adventures. One of them forces Goku to fight an exact copy of himself and confront his own weaknesses for the first time. And one of them is literally the series finale. The "filler" label works differently here than you'd expect coming from longer-running anime, and this Dragon Ball filler episodes list breaks it all down so you can decide for yourself what stays and what goes.

Dragon Ball Filler by the Numbers

StatValue
Total Episodes153
Filler Episodes21
Filler Percentage14%
Canon Episodes132
Time Saved Skipping All Filler~8 hours
Current StatusComplete

So, how many filler episodes are in Dragon Ball? Twenty-one by the standard classification. Some breakdowns count as high as 31 when including episodes that mix canon material with anime-original scenes, but 21 is the consensus number for pure filler. Either way, at 14%, Dragon Ball is remarkably lean compared to most long-running anime of its era.

Dragon Ball Skippable Episodes: The Quick-Skip List

If you're speed-running the Dragon Ball filler list and just want episode numbers, here they are. These are the filler episodes you can skip without losing a plot thread:

Episodes 29-33, 45, 79-83, 127-132, 149-153

A few of those deserve an asterisk, though. Episode 130 (Goku's Doll) is widely considered one of the best episodes in the entire series, filler or not. Episode 129 (The Time Room) gives Goku a training arc with a young Master Roshi that's both fun and surprisingly meaningful. And Episode 153 is the actual series finale, so skipping it means ending the show without its ending. Watch those three at minimum. The rest you can cut guilt-free.

One more thing: Episodes 127-132 bridge a three-year timeskip that the manga jumps over entirely. The anime fills that gap with real training content. If you want context for how Goku shows up to the 23rd Tournament as powerful as he does, these episodes provide it.

The Complete Dragon Ball Filler List

Dragon Ball's filler clusters into five clean blocks, all sitting in natural gaps between the show's major story arcs. Unlike longer-running anime where filler interrupts canon storylines mid-battle, Dragon Ball's original content occupies the breathing room between tournament sagas. Below is the complete Dragon Ball filler list, covering every filler episode grouped by arc.

Arc / EpisodesVerdict
Eps 29-33: Post-Tournament AdventuresSkip. Standalone episodes and a minor Pilaf subplot sitting between the first World Tournament and the Red Ribbon Army saga. Harmless fun, but none of it affects the story going forward.
Ep 45: Red Ribbon Army StandaloneSkip. A one-off episode during the Red Ribbon arc that adds nothing to the larger conflict. Easy to pass on.
Eps 79-83: Pre-22nd Tournament TrainingWatch. Goku's training adventures before the Tien Shinhan saga. Episode 81 (Goku Goes to Demon Land) is a charming standalone where Goku rescues a princess from a demon king, and the arc gives Goku's tail subplot some needed development. Light, fun, and faithful to the show's adventure-first spirit.
Eps 127-132: Training Before the 23rd TournamentWatch. The strongest filler block in the series. Goku trains at Kami's Lookout with Mr. Popo, including a time-travel episode where he meets a young Master Roshi (129) and a fight against an exact duplicate of himself (130). These six episodes bridge a three-year timeskip and contain some of the show's most inventive standalone content.
Eps 149-153: The Wedding ArcWatch. Goku and Chi-Chi prepare for their wedding after the 23rd Tournament. The Ox King's castle catches fire, leading to a quest for a fireproof wedding dress. Episodes 149-152 are a mixed bag (the dress hunt drags in spots), but Episode 153 is the series finale: the wedding itself and a proper sendoff for the entire cast. Skipping this arc means skipping the show's actual ending.

Secretly Peak: The Filler Worth Keeping

With only 21 filler episodes across 153, Dragon Ball doesn't have the "needle in a haystack" problem that most anime filler guides exist to solve. But even in a short list, a few episodes stand clearly above the rest. These three go beyond "decent time-filler" and genuinely add something you won't get from the manga alone.

Episode 130: Goku's Doll

The consensus pick for Dragon Ball's best filler episode. Mr. Popo creates an exact duplicate of Goku and forces him to fight it. The catch: the doll knows every move Goku will make because it fights exactly like him. For a character who usually punches his way through problems without much reflection, being forced to identify and exploit his own blind spots makes for a surprisingly revealing episode. Watching Goku wrestle with the concept of self-awareness (not his strong suit) is both funny and genuinely satisfying. The fight itself holds up, too.

Episode 129: The Time Room

Mr. Popo sends Goku back in time through the Pendulum Room at Kami's Lookout, and he lands in the middle of a rivalry between a teenage Master Roshi and a teenage Master Shen. Goku ends up training under Mutaito (Roshi and Shen's master) and learns about spirit energy for the first time. The episode fleshes out Roshi's backstory in a way the manga never does, and seeing Goku interact with a version of his teacher before he became the old pervert fans know is a genuinely fun premise that the episode delivers on.

Episode 153: The End, The Beginning

The series finale. Goku and Chi-Chi get married, surrounded by the cast of characters who have been part of the journey since Episode 1. It's a warm, simple ending for a show that started as a gag manga riff on Journey to the West and evolved into something that would reshape anime forever. The manga handled the wedding in a single panel. The anime gave it the breathing room the moment deserved. Skipping it means walking away from Dragon Ball without its goodbye.

Hot Take: The Series Finale Being Labeled "Filler" Is Absurd

Episode 153 is called "The End, The Beginning." It is the final episode of Dragon Ball. It depicts the wedding of the show's main character, a moment the series spent over a hundred episodes building toward. The manga covered this in roughly one panel. The anime gave it a full episode with ceremony, warmth, and a proper farewell to the cast.

And the filler classification system calls it skippable.

If any single episode proves that "filler" is a broken label, it's this one. The classification only measures whether an episode adapts specific manga chapters, not whether the content matters. By that standard, the ending of Dragon Ball doesn't matter. Anyone who has watched the series knows better. If you use a filler guide for this show, at least have the sense to ignore it for the finale.

Eight Hours, and Most of Them Are Good

The entire Dragon Ball filler list adds up to roughly eight hours. You could watch all of it on a lazy Saturday and still have time for dinner. At 14%, Dragon Ball is one of the leanest classic anime ever produced, and the filler it does have ranges from harmless to genuinely great. The quick-skip list is above if you want it, but the honest recommendation is that Dragon Ball might be the one anime where skipping filler costs you more in lost charm than it saves you in time.

Enjoy the adventure. Toriyama built it to be worth every episode.

FAQ

How many filler episodes are in Dragon Ball?

Twenty-one by the standard classification, putting the show at a 14% filler rate. Some breakdowns count up to 31 when including episodes that blend canon and anime-original scenes.

Is Dragon Ball filler worth watching?

Most of it, yes. At only 21 episodes (~8 hours), the time investment is small, and several filler episodes (particularly 129, 130, and 153) rank among the show's best standalone content.

What is the best Dragon Ball filler episode?

Episode 130, "Goku's Doll." Goku fights an exact copy of himself and has to figure out how to beat his own fighting style. It's widely considered the best filler in the original series and one of its strongest episodes overall.

Can I skip Dragon Ball filler without missing anything important?

You won't miss any core plot points, but you will miss the series finale (Episode 153), which is classified as filler because the manga barely covered it. You'll also lose the training arc (127-132) that bridges a three-year timeskip.

Is the Dragon Ball wedding arc filler?

Technically, yes. Episodes 149-153 are anime-original. But Episode 153 is the series finale depicting Goku and Chi-Chi's wedding, and skipping it means ending the show without its actual ending.

Title: Gintama Filler List: Every Episode You Can Skip
Summary: Decide which episodes earn their runtime with our full Gintama filler list. Even the filler in this show is often peak absurdity. 🍡🤣
Meta Title: Gintama Filler List: Every Episode You Can Skip
Meta Description: Gintama filler list where the filler is often as funny as the canon. See which episodes actually earn their runtime and which you can skip.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Most filler lists exist to save you time. The Gintama filler list exists to make a point: filler doesn't mean what you think it means when the show you're watching is 80% standalone comedy regardless of whether it came from the manga or not.

Gintama ran from 2006 to 2021 across 367 television episodes, three movies, and a handful of OVAs. Out of that run, only 23 episodes are classified as filler, putting the series at roughly 6%. But that number is almost meaningless: the vast majority of Gintama's canon episodes are self-contained comedy sketches that advance the plot exactly as much as the filler does. The serious story arcs (Benizakura, Yoshiwara, Four Devas, Shogun Assassination, Silver Soul) make up maybe 20% of the series, and none of them are filler. Everything in between is comedy, and the comedy is the whole point.

So does Gintama have filler? Technically yes. Should you skip it? Almost certainly not. But you came here for a Gintama filler guide, so here it is.

Gintama Filler: Quick Stats

StatDetail
Total Episodes367 (+2 Semi-Final OVAs, +3 movies)
Filler Episodes23
Mixed Canon/Filler4 (episodes 82, 111, 120, 367)
Filler Percentage~6%
Seasons10 parts (2006-2018)
Series StatusComplete (concluded with The Very Final movie, 2021)

For context, Naruto sits at around 41% filler and Bleach at 45%. Gintama's 6% is low by any standard, but the comparison falls apart because in most anime, filler feels different from canon. In Gintama, it doesn't.

Gintama Filler Episodes: The Quick-Skip List

Here's every episode on the Gintama filler list in one clean block, every episode you can skip without losing a plot thread:

Episodes 1-2, 50, 57, 75, 106, 114, 124-125, 135, 137, 150, 155, 164, 166, 171, 173-174, 176, 185, 189, 209, 252

Twenty-three episodes out of 367. Before you skip all of those, three quick notes. Episodes 1 and 2 are the very first episodes of the entire series, and skipping them means starting a 367-episode anime on episode 3 with zero introduction (more on why you should actually do that below). Episode 135 is a filler episode where the characters break the fourth wall and discuss why anime has filler in the first place, which is so aggressively Gintama that skipping it feels wrong. And episode 252 is the legendary Gintama finale "We're Sorry," where the cast apologizes for the show ending, and the episode descends into increasingly unhinged chaos. It is technically filler and culturally essential.

The mixed canon/filler episodes (82, 111, 120, and 367) blend manga material with anime-original content and should be watched, especially 367, which contains Silver Soul finale setup.

Every Gintama Filler Episode, Explained

Because Gintama scatters its filler across 10 seasons rather than clumping it into arcs, the list below is long but each entry is light. Most of these are one-off comedy episodes that match the show's tone perfectly, and unless you're watching exclusively for the serious arcs, you won't notice a quality difference between filler and canon.

TitleSeasonVerdict
You Guys!! Do You Even Have a Gintama? Parts 1 & 2 (Eps 1-2)Year 1Skip, then come back later. These were made as a premiere special for manga readers and spoil characters you haven't met yet. Start at episode 3. Return to these after episode 50 if you're curious.
Pending Means Pending, It's Not Final (Ep 50)Year 1Watch. Funny standalone that fits naturally between arcs. No reason to skip.
When Looking For Things You've Lost... (Ep 57)Year 1Watch. Another solid comedy episode right before the Benizakura arc. Good warm-up.
Don't Complain About Your Job At Home (Ep 75)Season 2Skip. One of the weaker standalones, light on memorable gags.
Love Often Played Out In Sudden Death (Ep 106)Season 3Watch. Fun character dynamics, entertaining enough to justify its runtime.
Soy Sauce On Pudding Tastes Like Sea Urchin... (Ep 114)Season 3Watch. Peak Gintama absurdity with one of the most unhinged episode titles in the series.
When Nagging Goes Too Far (Ep 124)Season 3Skip. Passable but forgettable. Easy to move past.
Beware Of Those Who Use An Umbrella On A Sunny Day! (Ep 125)Season 3Skip. Same energy as 124, nothing essential.
The Even More Endangered Future Of 'Gintaman' (Ep 135)Season 3Watch. A filler episode about filler. The characters discuss why anime studios make filler episodes, breaking the fourth wall with the kind of meta-comedy that only Gintama gets away with. Skipping this one is like skipping the joke that's aimed directly at you.
99% Of Men Aren't Confident In Confessing... (Ep 137)Season 3Watch. Strong comedy episode with good character moments.
If You Can't Beat Them, Join Them (Ep 150)Season 3Skip. A clip show recap. Safe to pass on during a binge.
The Other Side Of The Other Side... (Ep 155)Season 4Skip. Middling standalone.
Two Is Better Than One (Ep 164)Season 4Watch. Good pair-up comedy that deepens side character dynamics.
A Beehive The Size Of A Stadium... (Ep 166)Season 4Skip. Lighter comedy, easy to skip without regret.
There Are Things You Can't Cut With A Sword (Ep 171)Season 4Watch. Surprisingly solid standalone with heart.
Eps 173-174 (Two-parter)Season 4Skip. Two-parter that doesn't land as well as most Gintama comedy.
Can You Memorize A Driving Manual...? (Ep 176)Season 4Watch. Strong physical comedy, one of the funnier filler standalones.
Eps 185, 189Season 4Skip. Forgettable standalones that blend into the surrounding episodes.
There's A Thin Line Between Stubbornness... (Ep 209)Gintama'Watch. Good comedy with Yorozuya vs. Shinsengumi energy.
We're Sorry (Ep 252)Gintama'Watch. The Gintama' season finale. The cast apologizes for the anime ending, and the episode spirals into escalating absurdity and self-parody. One of the most iconic filler episodes in anime history. Do not skip.

Seasons that contain zero filler: Gintama': Enchousen (253-265), Gintama° (266-316), Gintama. (317-328), Porori-hen (329-341), and Shirogane no Tamashii-hen (342-367). Once the series enters its back half, filler disappears entirely and the show locks into its most sustained serious arcs.

The Gintama Filler Episodes That Are Actually Worth Your Time

In most anime, "secretly worth watching" filler means a hidden gem buried in forgettable padding. Gintama inverts that ratio entirely.

Episodes 1-2: The Worst Starting Point (That You Should Come Back To)

"You Guys!! Do You Even Have a Gintama?" was a two-part premiere special for manga readers who already knew the cast. Characters appear without introduction, and jokes reference events that haven't happened yet. Every Gintama guide tells you to skip to episode 3, and they're right. But once you've watched 50 or so episodes and know who everyone is, coming back to episodes 1 and 2 lets you appreciate the jokes that flew past you the first time.

Episode 135: The Filler Episode About Filler

The characters discuss why anime has filler episodes, why studios produce them, and what it means for a show's future when the anime catches up to the manga. It's Gintama at its most fourth-wall-demolishing, and the fact that the episode itself is filler makes the whole thing land even harder.

Episode 252: The Legendary Goodbye That Wasn't

"We're Sorry" is the Gintama' finale. The cast apologizes to the audience for the show ending, the episode escalates into a gag about seppuku, and from there it spirals into increasingly unhinged absurdity before closing with yet another apology. Pure, uncut Gintama chaos, and the single best argument that filler can be art when the right show makes it.

The Real Issue Nobody Talks About

Here's what every Gintama filler list gets backward: the Gintama filler episodes are not the problem, and they never were.

The actual barrier for newcomers is the first 25 episodes. Gintama opens with slow, episodic character introductions that don't showcase the show's full range. The comedy is still finding its voice, the serious arcs haven't started, and the callbacks that make later episodes legendary don't have enough setup to land. Fans who stuck with the show universally say it clicks around episode 25 and becomes something entirely different by the Benizakura arc at episode 58.

Filler has nothing to do with that. The slow early episodes are almost all canon. Skipping all 23 filler episodes saves you roughly 8 hours. Knowing that the show transforms after episode 25 saves you from dropping it entirely.

And here's the deeper truth: the show is a comedy first, and around 80% of its canon episodes are standalone bits with zero plot advancement. A manga-adapted episode about Gintoki losing a bet to Hijikata at a ramen shop advances the story exactly as much as a filler episode about the same scenario. The filler/canon line disappears because Gintama's default mode is already episodic. The only time the distinction matters is during serious arcs, and none of the serious arcs contain filler.

Strawberry Milk and Silver Souls: The Complete Gintama Filler Verdict

Gintama left behind 367 episodes, and the Gintama filler list adds up to 23 that are functionally identical to the show around them. Skip them if you want a marginally faster binge, but know you're saving 8 hours out of a 150-hour series and potentially missing some of the funniest episodes it ever made.

The actually useful advice: start at episode 3, give the show until episode 25, and once it clicks, stop worrying about which episodes are canon and which aren't. The comedy is the canon.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Gintama have filler?

Yes, but the distinction barely matters. Gintama has 23 filler episodes out of 367, putting it at roughly 6%. Because the show is primarily episodic comedy, the filler episodes match the tone and quality of the canon episodes surrounding them, and most fans can't tell the difference without checking a guide.

How many episodes of Gintama are there in total?

The main television series has 367 episodes across 10 parts (2006-2018). Including the two Semi-Final OVA episodes from 2021, the total reaches 369. The franchise also includes three movies, additional OVAs, and Jump Festa specials.

Should I skip Gintama episodes 1 and 2?

Yes, for your first watch. Episodes 1 and 2 were created as a premiere special for manga readers and assume familiarity with characters who haven't been introduced yet. Start at episode 3 and come back to episodes 1 and 2 after you've watched around 50 episodes.

What episode does Gintama get good?

The comedy finds its rhythm around episode 25, and the first major serious arc (Benizakura) begins at episode 58. Most longtime fans say the show hits its stride in the second half of Season 1, roughly episodes 50 onward, though individual mileage varies depending on your tolerance for early character setup.

What is Gintama's filler percentage compared to other long-running anime?

Gintama sits at approximately 6% filler, compared to Naruto at 41%, Bleach at 45%, and One Piece at around 10%. My Hero Academia comes in at 2-3%, though MHA's much shorter run (170 episodes) makes the comparison less direct.

Title: Demon Slayer Filler List: Every Episode Explained + 3 Ways to Catch Up Fast
Summary: Find the few padded episodes with our complete Demon Slayer filler list. Nearly zero filler, but we flag what's skippable. 🔥⚔️
Meta Title: Demon Slayer Filler List + 3 Ways to Catch Up Fast
Meta Description: Demon Slayer filler list for all 63 episodes. Nearly zero filler, plus three catch-up paths to finish fast before Infinity Castle.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Does Demon Slayer have filler? Barely any. Across 63 episodes and four seasons, most filler databases put the count at zero. One pegs it at a single episode, roughly 2%. Either way, Demon Slayer holds one of the cleanest adaptation records in shonen anime history.

But the full Demon Slayer filler list tells a more interesting story than that stat suggests. The anime's final TV season, the Hashira Training Arc, stretched eight or nine manga chapters into eight full episodes, with almost 90% of the season consisting of anime-original content that Koyoharu Gotouge's manga never included. Technically filler-free. Practically debatable.

Since there's genuinely nothing to skip, a traditional filler guide isn't much help. What you actually need is a plan for catching up efficiently, whether you're prepping for the Infinity Castle trilogy (Part 1 hit digital streaming in July 2026, Part 2 confirmed for 2027) or you just want to know enough about Demon Slayer to hold a conversation without watching all 63 episodes. The Demon Slayer filler list is short. The catch-up guide below is where the real value lives.

Demon Slayer Filler Quick Stats

StatDetail
Total Episodes63 (4 seasons, 2019–2024)
Filler Episodes0 full filler episodes
Mixed Canon/Filler2–3 episodes depending on the guide (Eps 27, 58, 59)
Filler Percentage0–2%
Anime-Original ConcentrationSeason 4, Hashira Training Arc (Eps 56–63)
Manga StatusComplete (205 chapters, 23 volumes)
Anime StatusTV series complete; Infinity Castle film trilogy in progress

So, how much of Demon Slayer is filler? The number floats between 0% and 2% depending on who's counting. Does Demon Slayer have filler episodes at all? Only if you classify anime-original scenes (content Ufotable wrote that doesn't appear in the manga but doesn't contradict it) as filler. Most guides don't. Here's the season-by-season breakdown:

SeasonEpisodesVerdict
S1: Unwavering Resolve1–26All Canon
S2: Mugen Train + Entertainment District27–44Canon (Ep 27 is anime-original)
S3: Swordsmith Village45–55All Canon
S4: Hashira Training56–63Canon + heavy anime-original content (Eps 57–61 mixed)

Every season is canon. The only variation is how much Ufotable expanded beyond the manga, and that question only matters in Season 4. Since there's almost nothing to skip, the real question is how to use your time.

How to Catch Up on Demon Slayer Fast

A Demon Slayer filler list can't do what a Naruto or Bleach filler list does, because there's nothing to cut. Every episode across all four seasons is canon (or close enough), so the traditional "skip these, watch those" approach breaks down immediately. What actually helps is a plan based on how much time you have.

Here are three watch paths depending on your situation. Pick the one that fits and you'll walk away understanding the story, the characters, and why Infinity Castle matters.

The Crash Course (~5 Hours)

For the person with a movie night coming up, or anyone who wants to understand Demon Slayer well enough to follow the conversation without watching all 63 episodes. These eight picks are the episodes people reference when they talk about Demon Slayer at all, not just the ones tied to a specific movie release. You'll miss character nuance and slower buildup, but you'll know who everyone is, what they're fighting for, and why the stakes in Infinity Castle are as high as they get.

EpisodeRuntimeWhy It's Here
Ep 1: "Cruelty"~24 minThe foundation. Tanjiro's family is massacred, Nezuko transforms into a demon, and the entire premise clicks into place in one episode.
Ep 19: "Hinokami"~24 minThe episode that turned Demon Slayer into a global phenomenon. Tanjiro unlocks the Hinokami Kagura (Sun Breathing) against Lower Rank demon Rui while Nezuko unleashes her Blood Demon Art. Rated 9.7 on IMDb. The r/anime discussion thread for this episode held the record for most upvoted episode post on the subreddit. If you watch one episode of Season 1, make it this one.
Ep 26: "New Mission"~24 minMuzan Kibutsuji, the Demon King, annihilates the remaining Lower Rank demons for being too weak. A single scene that resets the power scale and makes every threat going forward feel existential.
Mugen Train (movie)~1h 57mFlame Hashira Kyojuro Rengoku vs. Upper Rank Three Akaza. The emotional core of the franchise. Rengoku's death defines Tanjiro's motivation for the rest of the series, and Akaza's return in Infinity Castle Part 1 lands harder if you've felt this loss firsthand. If you'd rather not watch the full movie, Episodes 32–33 of the TV arc cover the Akaza fight and aftermath.
Ep 43: "Never Give Up"~24 minThe Entertainment District Arc climax. Tanjiro, Zenitsu, Inosuke, and Sound Hashira Tengen Uzui push past their limits to behead Upper Rank Six. The highest-rated episode in the entire series on IMDb. Also the first time the Demon Slayer Corps successfully kills an Upper Rank demon in over a century, which changes the balance of power heading into the final arc.
Ep 44: "No Matter How Many Lives"~24 minThe immediate aftermath. Gyutaro and Daki's backstory reframes them as tragic figures, and the cost of the Upper Rank victory becomes clear. Tengen retires from combat permanently. The episode also introduces former Upper Rank Six, Doma, who becomes a major villain in Infinity Castle.
Ep 55: "A Connected Bond: Daybreak and First Light"~24 minThe Swordsmith Village Arc finale. Nezuko conquers sunlight, something no demon has done since Muzan himself. The moment changes the entire war: Muzan shifts his target to Nezuko, and the final confrontation becomes inevitable. Best-rated episode of Season 3 on IMDb.
Ep 63: "The Hashira Unite"~48 minThe Season 4 finale, extended length. Muzan arrives at the Ubuyashiki estate, the Hashira converge, and the entire Corps is pulled into the Infinity Castle. The last scene before the movie trilogy begins. Watching this cold, without any context, would be confusing. Watching it after the seven episodes above gives you the full picture.

Total runtime: approximately 5 hours. You'll skip the slower training arcs and most of the character-building episodes, but every major plot beat, power reveal, and emotional turning point is covered. Enough to follow Infinity Castle without being lost, and enough to talk about the show with anyone.

The Weekend Binge (~12 Hours)

For the person who wants to actually feel the story, not just know the plot. The Crash Course gives you the skeleton. The Weekend Binge gives you the muscle and nerve. You'll watch full arc segments here, which means you'll experience the pacing and buildup that makes the payoff episodes hit the way they're supposed to.

Arc SegmentEpisodesRuntimeWhat You Get
Season 1: SetupEps 1–5~2 hrsTanjiro's origin, training under Urokodaki, Final Selection, and his first Nichirin blade. The emotional and mechanical foundation for everything.
Optional: Trio BondingEps 11–14~1.5 hrsIntroduces Zenitsu and Inosuke properly through the Tsuzumi Mansion arc. Without these, two of the three main characters show up at Episode 15 as strangers. Add this block if you want to feel invested in the full team, not just Tanjiro.
Season 1: Spider Mountain + Hashira MeetingEps 15–22~3.2 hrsThe Mount Natagumo arc through the Hashira trial. Includes Episode 19 (Hinokami Kagura), the Rui fight, Giyu Tomioka stepping in, and the full Hashira meeting where the Corps power structure is established.
Season 1: Stakes ResetEp 26~24 minMuzan's Lower Rank massacre. Necessary bridge to Mugen Train.
Mugen TrainMovie~2 hrsFull Rengoku arc. Don't split this into episodes; the movie's pacing is tighter.
Entertainment District (full arc)Eps 34–44~4.4 hrsAll 11 episodes. Tengen Uzui's arc, the Gyutaro/Daki fight, and the aftermath. The Entertainment District is the most consistently highly rated arc in the series, and its finale is the highest-rated episode overall. Watching it in full is worth every minute.
Swordsmith Village: Key EpisodesEps 45, 55~48 minSeason 3's premiere (Upper Rank demon meeting, establishes the remaining threats) and finale (Nezuko conquers sunlight). The arc between those episodes focuses on Muichiro Tokito and Mitsuri Kanroji, which enriches the story but isn't essential for Infinity Castle Part 1.
Hashira Training: FinaleEps 62–63~72 minGyomei Himejima's backstory (Ep 62) and the season finale where Muzan attacks the Ubuyashiki estate and triggers the Infinity Castle confrontation (Ep 63).

Total runtime: approximately 12 hours without the optional block, 13.5 with it. Two long evenings or one dedicated weekend day. You'll skip the early Season 1 mission-of-the-week episodes, most of Swordsmith Village, and the middle stretch of Hashira Training. What you keep is every arc that directly shapes the final battle.

The Full Run (~26 Hours)

All 63 episodes. No trimming, no tough calls.

At 26 hours, Demon Slayer is shorter than a single season of many long-running shonen. You can finish it in a week of evening sessions or a dedicated long weekend. The only decision is how you handle the Mugen Train arc: the movie (1h 57min) or the TV version (Episodes 27–33, roughly 2h 45min). The TV version includes Episode 27, an anime-original Rengoku prelude that adds backstory to the Flame Hashira before the train mission. Both options work. Pick one, not both.

Skip the recap compilation films (To the Swordsmith Village, To the Hashira Training). They condense season transitions into theatrical packages and contain nothing you won't see in the episodes themselves.

If you have the time, the full run is the path we'd recommend. The series earned its zero-filler reputation by making every episode count, and the character moments you'd skip in the shorter paths are the ones that make Infinity Castle's sacrifices land at full force.

Is the Hashira Training Arc Filler?

No. And the question itself reveals a gap in how the anime community talks about adaptations.

Traditional filler exists because a running anime catches up to its manga and needs to stall for time. Naruto invented entire villages and villains to buy chapters. Bleach sent Ichigo on side quests. The content contradicts nothing, but it also leads nowhere. You can pull it out of the timeline and the story doesn't flinch.

The Hashira Training Arc doesn't fit that definition. Ufotable didn't add anime-original content because they ran out of manga. They added it because the manga's version of the arc was too thin to support a full season and too important to compress into a movie or a few throwaway episodes. Nine chapters of training montage became eight episodes of character work, and the result is a season that asks you to invest in every Hashira before sending them into the deadliest battle of the series.

Critical reception was divided. One review called it "a filler-filled season" and compared its pacing to One Piece at its slowest. Others argued the expanded scenes set a new benchmark for what anime-original content can achieve when a studio actually commits to it. Fan response, measured by the specific scenes people share and discuss, sides firmly with the expansion. The Tengen training sessions, the Giyu and Tanjiro soba eating contest (an entirely anime-original scene that fans called one of the best moments in the series), and the extended Hashira backstories are among the most talked-about moments from the franchise's final year on television.

The Season 4 finale, Episode 63 "The Hashira Unite," earned some of the strongest fan reactions of any episode in the show. Muzan's attack on the Ubuyashiki estate, Gyomei Himejima stepping into combat, and Tamayo's return gave the season a closing stretch that justified the slower buildup. If you watch only two episodes from Hashira Training, make them 62 and 63.

If you skip Season 4 entirely, you can follow Infinity Castle's plot. You'll know who's fighting and why. You'll know Gyomei Himejima is the strongest Hashira. You won't know what it cost him to become one. And when he steps into the Infinity Castle, that difference between knowing and feeling is the difference between watching a fight and caring who walks out of it.

The Hashira Training Arc is anime-original content done well. It's not filler. It's Ufotable forging the blade with extra folds in the steel.

The Cleanest Blade in Shonen

The Demon Slayer filler list might be the shortest one you'll read on this site, and that says everything about how Ufotable handled the adaptation. Across 63 episodes and four seasons, there are zero full filler episodes, two or three entries that some guides classify as "mixed," and one final season of anime-original content that most fans consider essential viewing.

Whether you speed-run the Crash Course or commit to all 63 episodes, the takeaway is the same: nothing here is wasted. Even after the Infinity Castle trilogy wraps, these are the episodes that explain why Demon Slayer became the biggest anime of the 2020s. The filler list is empty because Ufotable never let the story breathe idle air. Every episode is a focused cut, the way every swing of a Nichirin blade is supposed to be. Pick the path that fits your schedule, and if you land on the shorter ones, know that the full run is always there when you're ready to go deeper.
