FAQ

Does Demon Slayer have filler?

Technically, no. Demon Slayer has zero full filler episodes across its entire 63-episode run. The closest the series gets is a handful of anime-original scenes in the Hashira Training Arc (Season 4) and Episode 27, which is an entirely original Rengoku story not found in the manga. Some guides classify these as "mixed canon/filler" or "anime canon," but none of them are traditional filler in the way Naruto or Bleach fans would recognize the term.

Is the Hashira Training Arc filler?

No, though it's the most debated season in the series. The Hashira Training Arc adapted only eight or nine manga chapters into eight episodes, meaning the majority of its runtime is anime-original. Ufotable used the extra space to expand character backstories and training sequences that the manga condensed or skipped. The content doesn't contradict the original story, and most of it adds real depth to characters who play major roles in the Infinity Castle films. Anime-original, yes. Filler, no.

How much of Demon Slayer is filler?

Between 0% and 2%, depending on which filler guide you check. The disagreement comes down to whether anime-original scenes (content created by the studio that doesn't appear in the manga but doesn't contradict it) count as filler. Most databases say they don't, putting Demon Slayer at 0%. One counts a single episode, landing the percentage at 2%. Either way, Demon Slayer is one of the lowest-filler shonen anime ever produced.

Can I skip the Mugen Train TV arc if I saw the movie?

Yes. The Mugen Train movie (2020) and the TV arc (Episodes 27–33) tell the same core story. The only exclusive content in the TV version is Episode 27, an anime-original Rengoku prelude that follows him on a solo mission the night before the train. If you watched the movie, start the Entertainment District Arc at Episode 34. Consider going back for Episode 27 when you have time; it's a strong standalone episode that adds real texture to Rengoku's character.

What's the fastest way to catch up on Demon Slayer?

The Crash Course path above covers 8 episodes and the Mugen Train movie in roughly 5 hours. It hits every turning point: Tanjiro's origin, the Hinokami Kagura reveal, the Rengoku fight, the first Upper Rank kill, Nezuko conquering sunlight, and the Infinity Castle setup. You'll miss slower character-building episodes, but you'll understand the full story and every major player. If you have a full weekend, Path 2 at around 12 hours gives you the emotional weight that the Crash Course skips. Check our Demon Slayer filler list quick stats above for the full episode breakdown.

Anime StatusParts 1–6 complete; Part 7 (Steel Ball Run) airing on Netflix

There are no JoJo filler episodes in the David Production anime. Zero. The debate isn't about filler in the traditional sense. It's about whether every Stand battle in Part 3 needs to be watched, whether Parts 1 and 2 can be skipped, and how much backstory Steel Ball Run actually requires. Any JoJo filler list worth reading should answer those questions, and that's what we'll cover below.

Three Routes Through the Joestar Bloodline

A JoJo filler list can't trim episodes the way a Naruto or Bleach guide can, because there's nothing flagged as filler. What it can do is help you plan a route through 190 episodes that fits the time you have. JoJo's Part structure actually makes this easier than most long-running anime, since each Part works as a semi-standalone story with its own beginning and end.

Here are three paths. Pick the one that matches your situation.

The Highlight Reel (~10 Hours)

For the person who wants to understand JoJo well enough to follow conversations, get the memes, and know why the Joestar bloodline matters. These are the episodes people reference when they talk about JoJo at all. You'll skip the slower stretches and most of the monster-of-the-week encounters, but you'll meet every JoJo, see every major villain fall, and understand why Part 7 is generating the hype it is.

The Part Sampler (~30 Hours)

For the person who wants to actually live inside JoJo's world, not just visit. The Highlight Reel gives you the skeleton. The Part Sampler gives you the full experience where it matters most and a trimmed version where it drags.

The Full Bizarre Adventure (~75 Hours)

All 190 episodes. Every Part. No skips, no trims.

At 75 hours, JoJo is a genuine long-haul commitment. But unlike most anime at this length, the Part structure gives you natural stopping points. You can finish Part 2 on a Monday, take a week off, and start Stardust Crusaders fresh without losing the plot. Each Part is its own story with its own resolution. Think of it as six connected short series rather than one continuous marathon.

Skip the recap specials. Skip the older 1993–2002 Stardust Crusaders OVAs (they tell the same story the TV anime tells better). The 2007 Phantom Blood movie is lost and unavailable anyway. The Thus Spoke Kishibe Rohan OVAs are a fun spin-off set during Part 4, but they're optional viewing, not required.

If you have the time, the full run is our recommendation. Part 3's monster-of-the-week stretch tests your patience, but the standalone episodes people love to skip include some of JoJo's most creative battles. You lose nothing by watching everything, and you gain the full weight of a story that's been running since 1987.

Steel Ball Run note: Part 7 is set in an alternate universe. It shares thematic DNA with the original six Parts (Joestars, Zeppelis, the concept of fate) but not a continuous plot. You can start Steel Ball Run without watching Parts 1–6. If you've seen at least Parts 1 and 2, you'll catch the parallels that make Steel Ball Run richer. But it's not required.

The Part 3 Problem: When Canon Feels Like Filler

Stardust Crusaders has 48 episodes and zero filler. Every fight is manga canon. And fans have been skipping half of them for years.

The issue is structural. Parts 1 and 2 told tight, continuous stories. Part 3 introduced Stands and, with them, a formula: the crew encounters a new enemy Stand user, figures out the gimmick, defeats them, and moves on. Some of those encounters are all-time classics (D'Arby the Gambler, the Oingo Boingo brothers, Vanilla Ice). Others are standalone puzzles that don't advance the plot, develop the characters, or raise the stakes.

One popular fan breakdown cut the 48 episodes down to 27 essentials. Others go further, arguing you can watch the first two episodes and the final four and miss nothing plot-critical. The community is genuinely split: some fans consider Part 3 the most iconic JoJo experience, while others call it the weakest stretch in the franchise because of its repetitive structure.

Our take: Part 3 isn't filler, but it is the one Part where the distance between "essential" and "skippable" is widest. If you're watching JoJo in full, lean into the monster-of-the-week format and enjoy the creative problem-solving. If you're on a shorter path, trim confidently. The plot-critical episodes are easy to identify, and skipping a few self-contained Stand fights won't break your understanding of the DIO confrontation.

The Stands you skip might include one of your future favorites. But you can always go back.

190 Episodes, Zero Filler, One Bizarre Legacy

The JoJo filler list is the shortest page on this site, and it belongs to one of the longest-running anime adaptations in modern history. Across Parts 1 through 6, there's nothing to cut, nothing flagged as non-canon, and nothing that contradicts the manga. David Production gave Araki's work a faithful adaptation from start to finish.

Whether you speed through the Highlight Reel or settle in for the full 75-hour Bizarre Adventure, the takeaway is the same: JoJo earned its zero-filler record by building a story where each Part stands on its own, and the generational thread connecting them never breaks. Even after Steel Ball Run wraps, these 190 episodes are the reason the Joestar name carries the weight it does.

FAQ

Does JoJo's Bizarre Adventure have filler?

No. JoJo's Bizarre Adventure has zero filler episodes across its entire 190-episode run. David Production adapted Hirohiko Araki's manga faithfully across all six completed Parts. The only content sometimes considered "optional" is the Stardust Crusaders OVAs from the 1990s and the Thus Spoke Kishibe Rohan spin-off, neither of which is part of the main TV anime.

Is Stardust Crusaders filler?

No, but it's the one Part where fans most commonly skip episodes. All 48 Stardust Crusaders episodes are manga canon, but the monster-of-the-week format means roughly half are standalone Stand battles that don't advance the main plot. The DIO confrontation at the end is essential. Many of the encounters along the way are great but individually skippable if you're short on time.

Can I skip Parts 1 and 2?

You can, but you'll lose more than you think. Phantom Blood (9 episodes) introduces the Joestar-Dio rivalry, the Stone Mask, and Hamon. Battle Tendency (17 episodes) introduces the Pillar Men and Joseph Joestar, who returns as a major character in Part 3. Skipping them means starting at Stardust Crusaders without understanding why DIO matters, who Joseph is, or what the Joestar bloodline represents. At 26 episodes combined, Parts 1 and 2 are shorter than many single-cour anime. Watch them.

Do I need to watch Parts 1–6 before Steel Ball Run?

No. Steel Ball Run takes place in an alternate universe with a separate continuity. You can start watching it on Netflix right now with zero prior JoJo knowledge. The story follows Johnny Joestar and Gyro Zeppeli in a cross-country horse race across 19th-century America, and it stands completely on its own. Fans who've seen Parts 1 and 2 will catch thematic parallels and name callbacks, but they aren't required to follow the plot.

What are the JoJo filler episodes?

There are none. Every episode in the David Production anime (Parts 1–6, Episodes 1–190) is adapted from the manga. The JoJo's Bizarre Adventure filler count cited by every major database is 0%, making it the longest zero-filler streak of any major shonen anime currently running.

Title: Hunter x Hunter Filler List: Every Episode to Skip (and the Ones Worth Watching)
Summary: Spot the only two filler episodes in 148 with our complete Hunter x Hunter filler list. One of anime's cleanest adaptations. 🎯🐾
Meta Title: Hunter x Hunter Filler List: Every Episode to Skip
Meta Description: Hunter x Hunter filler list for the 2011 and 1999 anime. Only two filler episodes in 148, and one is worth watching. See what to skip.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
The manga clawed its way back into Weekly Shonen Jump on June 28, 2026, with Chapter 411 landing after nearly two years of silence. Volume 39 dropped five days later, and Togashi has manuscripts ready through Chapter 421. If you're rewatching the anime before catching up on the Succession Contest Arc, you're going to want a Hunter x Hunter filler list.

You're going to want a very short one.

The 2011 anime has two filler episodes out of 148. A 1% filler rate. The 1999 version has five out of 92, sitting at roughly 5%. No filler arcs in either version. No anime-original sagas dragging on while the manga catches up. Just a handful of recaps scattered across two adaptations that stayed remarkably faithful to Togashi's source material. But even with a count this small, trackers still disagree on Episode 12, mixed episodes inflate the 1999 numbers, and one "filler" episode might actually deserve a spot in your watchlist.

Hunter x Hunter Filler at a Glance

2011 (Madhouse)1999 (Nippon Animation)
Total Episodes14892 (62 TV + 30 OVA)
Filler Episodes2 (Ep 13, Ep 26)5 (Ep 2, 7, 18, 19, 20)
Mixed Canon/Filler1 (Ep 12)11
Filler Percentage1%~5%
Filler ArcsNoneNone

The No-Filler Cut

Here's every episode on the Hunter x Hunter filler list in one clean block, every episode you can skip without losing a single plot thread:

  • 1999: Episodes 2, 7, 18, 19, 20
  • 2011: Episodes 13, 26

Seven episodes across both anime. Before you skip all of them, three quick notes.

Episode 12 (2011) gets tagged as filler or mixed depending on which tracker you check, but it adapts real manga material for Gon's Hunter Exam finale. Skipping it leaves a gap you'll notice. Watch it.

Episode 13 (2011) is technically a recap, but the framing through Aunt Mito's perspective gives it more emotional weight than any recap episode has a right to. Calling it filler feels reductive once you know where Gon's story goes (more on that below).

The 1999 version has 11 additional episodes with anime-original scenes mixed into canon stories, which is why some trackers report a higher filler count than five. Those mixed episodes should be watched. The canon material in them matters.

Every Episode on the Hunter x Hunter Filler List

ArcEpisodesVerdict
Gon's letter to Aunt Mito13 (2011)Skip. Aunt Mito reads a letter from Gon recapping the Hunter Exam. Surprisingly moving for a recap, but you won't miss plot.
Post-exam recap26 (2011)Skip. Bridges the Hunter Exam and Heavens Arena. Nothing new, nothing memorable.
Gon's exam showdown (mixed)12 (2011)Watch. Trackers can't agree on this one, but it adapts manga material from Gon's final exam confrontation. Canon content is load-bearing.
Leorio encounter2 (1999)Skip. Anime-original expansion of Gon's journey to the exam. The 2011 version covers everything that matters.
Hunter Exam detour7 (1999)Skip. Another exam-phase expansion. Light character moments, zero consequences.
Sea voyage mini-arc18-20 (1999)Skip. Three shipboard adventure episodes between exam phases. Fans of the 1999 version's atmosphere sometimes defend these, but they're filler through and through.

The Filler Worth Watching

Episode 13 (2011): "Letter x From x Gon"

Every tracker labels this filler, and technically, they're right. But the whole episode is Aunt Mito reading a letter Gon sent home, and it turns a standard recap into the last quiet, grounded moment the series gives you. After this, it's Heavens Arena, Yorknew, Greed Island, and then the Chimera Ant arc, where Gon stops being the bright-eyed kid who left Whale Island and becomes something harder to watch.

On a first viewing, it's a nice breather between arcs. On a rewatch, knowing what Gon becomes during his confrontation with Neferpitou, this episode reads less like a recap and more like a goodbye to the version of Gon who still wrote letters home. The fan community keeps circling back to it as a hidden emotional beat, and honestly, they're right.

Episodes 18-20 (1999): The Sea Voyage

The 1999 adaptation took its time, and these three episodes are the most obvious example. Anime-original shipboard adventures, added crew interactions, a slower rhythm that lets the Hunter Exam breathe. If you're watching the 2011 version exclusively, these don't exist and you won't miss them. But if you're doing a 1999 run for the darker atmosphere and deeper character work that version is known for, these episodes are part of that identity. The Hunter Exam feels more like an actual journey in the 1999 version, and these episodes are a big reason why.

The Fake Skip: Episode 12 (2011)

The one trackers keep getting wrong. AnimeFillerList tags it mixed. Some guides skip it entirely. Others pretend it doesn't exist. The reality: it adapts manga material covering Gon's final Hunter Exam confrontation with anime-original padding wrapped around it. Skip this and you'll have a visible gap in how the arc resolves. It belongs in your watchlist, full stop.

Hot Take: The 2011 Anime's 1% Filler Rate Came at a Cost

A 1% filler rate sounds like a pure win until you look at what Madhouse left on the table. The 2011 version cut so aggressively that its first episode skips character-building scenes the 1999 version spent full episodes developing. Gon, Killua, Kurapika, and Leorio feel more like real people in the 1999 adaptation because that version gave them room to exist between plot beats. The ship episodes, the expanded exam interactions, the quieter moments where the core four actually bond before being thrown into life-or-death situations.

Fans on MAL and community forums have argued for years that the 1999 Hunter Exam is the better version because of those added scenes, not despite them. The darker atmosphere, the slower pacing, the sense that the exam is a genuine journey and not a highlight reel.

Hunter x Hunter's filler reputation is that it has none. The more interesting truth is that its best "filler" was never filler at all.

Are the Hunter x Hunter Movies Canon?

Neither Phantom Rouge (2013) nor The Last Mission (2014) is canon. Both are original stories that don't align with the manga or anime timeline. Phantom Rouge includes a canonical flashback to Kurapika's childhood from special manga chapters, worth watching if his backstory interests you. Otherwise, both films are safe to skip.

The Cleanest Binge in Anime

That's the complete Hunter x Hunter filler list: seven episodes across two adaptations and over 240 combined episodes. A filler rate that barely registers. And at least one "skip" episode that earns a genuine case for staying in your rotation.

With the manga back in serialization as of June 2026, there's never been a better time to run through the anime and catch up before the Succession Contest Arc moves forward. For weekly anime takes and guides, the Kaminari newsletter drops at joinkaminari.com.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many filler episodes are in Hunter x Hunter?

Two in the 2011 version (Episodes 13 and 26, both recaps) and five in the 1999 version (Episodes 2, 7, 18, 19, 20). The 2011 anime has a 1% filler rate. The 1999 version sits at about 5%. Neither has filler arcs.

Is Episode 12 of Hunter x Hunter (2011) filler?

Not really. It mixes manga-canon material with anime-original scenes, which is why trackers label it differently. The canon content covers Gon's Hunter Exam conclusion and should be watched.

Should I watch Hunter x Hunter 1999 or 2011?

2011 for completeness (it covers through the 13th Chairman Election arc with almost no detours). 1999 for atmosphere and deeper early character work. Both are faithful to the manga. Most fans start with 2011.

Are the Hunter x Hunter movies canon?

No. Both Phantom Rouge and The Last Mission are original stories. Phantom Rouge has a canonical Kurapika flashback from special manga chapters, but the movie itself is non-canon.

Does Hunter x Hunter have any filler arcs?

No, unlike Naruto and Bleach, which padded their runtimes with entire anime-original story arcs, neither HxH adaptation ever produced one. All HxH filler episodes are standalone recaps or one-offs.

Title: Attack on Titan Filler List: Every Episode Explained + OVAs Ranked Watch or Skip
Summary: Verify what's skippable with our full Attack on Titan filler list. AoT is nearly filler-free, but the OVAs need sorting. 🗡️🏰
Meta Title: Attack on Titan Filler List: Every Episode + OVAs
Meta Description: Attack on Titan filler list with zero pure filler across 89 episodes. Get all 8 OVAs ranked watch, skip, or essential before you start.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Does Attack on Titan have filler? No. Across 89 episodes and four seasons, the anime has zero pure filler episodes. Every main-series installment adapts Hajime Isayama's manga directly, and both studios that handled the adaptation (WIT for Seasons 1 through 3, MAPPA for Season 4) kept the story locked to the source material from first episode to last.

But the Attack on Titan filler list tells a stranger story than that zero suggests. Filler trackers report anywhere from 0% to 6.74% for the exact same anime. The disagreement has nothing to do with the 89 main episodes. It comes down to 8 OVA episodes that sit in a grey zone between canon and filler. One of them was written by Isayama himself and still gets classified as non-canon by some databases. Another was referenced in the manga years after release, quietly folding it into the canonical timeline while trackers kept labeling it filler.

Six main-series episodes contain minor anime-only scenes. None are worth skipping. So the AoT filler list works differently here. The main series is the easy part: watch all of it. The only real decision is what to do about those 8 OVAs, and the guide below is built around that decision.

How many filler episodes are in Attack on Titan? The answer depends on who you ask, and the gap is entirely about OVA classification. animefillerlist.com reports zero filler in the main series by excluding OVAs from the count. BNGLY folds them in and arrives at 6.74%. Neither is wrong. They're answering different questions about the same anime, which is exactly why AoT filler percentages vary so wildly across databases. The season breakdown below shows where the confusion actually lives.

Every Season at a Glance

Seven rows of canon. Zero rows of filler. The six mixed episodes contain minor anime-only additions (extra character interactions, expanded dialogue, small pacing embellishments) that no guide recommends skipping. Even the most aggressive trackers mark these as "mixed canon/filler," not filler outright. The main series is settled. The only question with a real answer is what to do about the OVAs.

The OVA Verdict: Watch, Skip, or Essential

Attack on Titan has 8 OVA/OAD episodes released alongside the main series between 2013 and 2018. They sit outside the 89-episode count and outside the core storyline, which is exactly why trackers disagree on the show's filler percentage. Some databases ignore OVAs entirely and report 0%. Others fold them in, count the non-canon ones as filler, and land somewhere around 5 to 7%. The actual answer is simpler than either approach suggests.

Here's the real Attack on Titan filler list, OVA by OVA, with a clear verdict for each:

OVAYearVerdictWhy
Ilse's Notebook2013EssentialWritten by Isayama. Expands Titan lore. Referenced in Season 2.

Three are essential. Three are worth your time if you want deeper character work. Two you can skip without losing anything. The three that matter most deserve a closer look.

Ilse's Notebook: The "Filler" Isayama Wrote Himself

Ilse's Notebook is the most misclassified episode in Attack on Titan. Hajime Isayama wrote it himself, making it the only OVA in the franchise that the original creator personally authored. It adapts a side chapter from the manga that most trackers file under the OAD category and label non-canon by default.

The episode follows a deceased Scout Regiment soldier named Ilse Langnar, whose journal documents an encounter with a Titan that spoke to her. The Titan called her "Lady Ymir," a detail that foreshadows the Ymir and Historia plotline running through Season 2 and the deeper mythology driving the final arc. Hange's discovery of the journal directly shapes her research approach going forward. CBR ranked it among the greatest filler episodes in all of anime, which says more about the classification system than the episode. If your tracker calls Ilse's Notebook filler, your tracker is wrong.

Watch it after Episode 3 or after completing Season 1.

No Regrets: The OVA That Became Canon

No Regrets is the OVA the fandom argues about the most, and the argument is worth understanding before you decide whether to watch it.

The two-part story adapts a spin-off manga about Levi's life before the Survey Corps. It wasn't written by Isayama. The plot follows Levi, Furlan Church, and Isabel Magnolia as underground criminals recruited by Erwin Smith for a mission beyond the Walls. The mission falls apart. Furlan and Isabel die. And Levi's grief hardens into the stoic, reckless loyalty he carries through all four seasons of the main series.

By the traditional definition, No Regrets is filler. A different author created it, and the main series stands on its own without it. But Isayama later referenced No Regrets directly in Chapter 76 of the manga, incorporating a flashback where Levi remembers Furlan and Isabel during a pivotal moment. The Attack on Titan Wiki debated for years whether to reclassify the OVA, and most fan communities now treat it as effectively canon.

Here's the practical takeaway: you will understand Levi perfectly well without No Regrets. But every time he makes a choice that looks cold or self-destructive in the main series, No Regrets is the context that explains why. Every time he loses someone and keeps moving, you're watching a pattern that started underground in the capital with two people whose names the main series never says out loud. It's 50 minutes that make 89 episodes hit differently.

Watch after Episode 25 (before Season 2).

Lost Girls: Annie's Side of the Story

Lost Girls is a three-part OVA adapted from light novels by Ryo Suzukaze, produced under Isayama's supervision. The first two episodes follow Annie Leonhart's perspective during and after her mission inside Wall Rose as the Female Titan. The third is a standalone Mikasa story set in an alternate timeline where the Titans never attacked Shiganshina.

The Annie episodes are the highlight. Attack on Titan rarely gives extended screen time to its villains' inner lives, and seeing the toll of Annie's infiltration through her own eyes adds real weight to her eventual return in Season 4. The Wall Sina episodes won't change the plot for you, but they change how Annie feels as a character when she finally wakes up from her crystal.

The Mikasa episode is the most skippable of the three. It explores what her life might have looked like without the tragedy that shaped her, and it's well-made for what it is. But it connects to nothing in the main timeline, and the emotional resonance depends on how invested you already are in Mikasa specifically.

Watch the Annie episodes after Season 2. Watch the Mikasa episode after Season 3 Part 1 (after Episode 49).

Three Ways to Watch Attack on Titan

Since the Attack on Titan filler list has nothing to cut from the main series, the watch paths here work by addition instead of subtraction. The 89-episode run is the baseline, and it's already complete and self-contained. The paths below vary only by how many OVAs you fold in and where you place them.

Path 1: Main Series Only (~37 Hours)

All 89 episodes in release order. Season 1 through the Final Chapters, no interruptions, no OVAs. Every minute is canonical manga-adapted story.

Pick this if you want the cleanest possible run. The main series never assumes you've seen the OVAs. No character introduction, no plot point, and no emotional beat depends on outside material. You can always circle back for the OVAs later, and some fans prefer it that way: experiencing the core story first, then adding context on a rewatch.

Path 2: Main Series + Essential OVAs (~38 Hours)

All 89 episodes plus three OVAs placed at the moments where they land hardest:

Three OVAs. Roughly 75 extra minutes. Ilse's Notebook plants a seed about talking Titans and the name "Ymir" that pays off across the next three seasons. No Regrets gives you Levi's emotional foundation before the main story asks you to watch him lose people over and over. The community consistently calls these three essential, and the extra hour and change is the best return on time in the franchise.

Path 3: The Complete Experience (~40 Hours)

All 89 episodes plus all 8 OVAs, placed in chronological order to avoid spoilers:

Lost Girls: Wall Sina Parts 1 and 2Episode 37 (after Season 2)
Lost Girls: Lost in the Cruel WorldEpisode 49 (after S3 Part 1)

For the viewer who wants every expedition beyond the Walls, including the ones that never made it into the official report. A Sudden Visitor and Distress are lightweight, but they round out the early Survey Corps atmosphere in a way that's enjoyable on a first watch and easy to skip on a rewatch. The full run at roughly 40 hours is still shorter than a single arc of several long-running shonen. Attack on Titan is a dense series, but it is not a long one.

Beyond the Walls, the Sea

The Attack on Titan filler list might be the shortest guide on this site, and it earned that distinction the hard way. Zero pure filler across 89 episodes. Six entries with minor anime-only scenes that you'll barely notice while watching. Eight OVAs where the only difficult calls are the three you should probably watch anyway.

Isayama plotted the ending before the first chapter was published, and both WIT and MAPPA treated the source material like a sealed blueprint. There's nowhere in this story where the animation team needed to stall for time, because the manga stayed ahead and the seasonal format gave the adaptation room to pace itself without padding. The result is a series that runs tight for a decade and never wastes a single episode on anything that doesn't move the story forward or deepen a character who matters.

If you've been putting off the series because you expected a bloated commitment with filler arcs to skip, the reality is simpler. Attack on Titan is 89 episodes of unbroken story. Add the essential OVAs and it's 92. The entire thing fits inside two weeks of evening sessions or one very committed long weekend. At the end of Season 3, the surviving characters reach the ocean for the first time. Everything they fought for lived inside the Walls. Everything that comes next exists past the horizon. The show works the same way. Once you start, the only direction is forward, and there is nothing in your path that isn't supposed to be there.

FAQ

Does Attack on Titan have filler?

No. Attack on Titan has zero pure filler episodes across its 89-episode run. Six episodes (22, 33, 38 through 41) contain minor anime-only scenes, but every one of them adapts core manga plotlines alongside those additions. The only content that could be called filler in the traditional sense lives in the OVA/OAD episodes, which are separate from the main series. Even among those, several OVAs (Ilse's Notebook, No Regrets) have strong arguments for being canon.

How many filler episodes are in Attack on Titan?

Zero in the main series. The reported filler percentage varies from 0% to 6.74% depending on the tracker, and the entire difference comes from how each database classifies the 8 OVA episodes. animefillerlist.com excludes OVAs and reports 0%. BNGLY includes them and arrives at 6.74%. Both are defensible. They're counting different things.

Are the Attack on Titan OVAs worth watching?

Three of them are worth making time for. Ilse's Notebook (written by Isayama, enriches Titan lore, referenced in Season 2) and No Regrets Parts 1 and 2 (Levi's full backstory, referenced in manga Chapter 76) are the OVAs most fans consider essential. The Lost Girls episodes following Annie are solid character work and worth watching if you want a deeper read on her motivations heading into Season 4. A Sudden Visitor and Distress are lighthearted side stories that are easy to pass on.

Is No Regrets canon?

It depends on how strictly you define canon. No Regrets was not written by Hajime Isayama, which by the standard definition makes it non-canon supplementary material. But Isayama referenced its events in Chapter 76 of the main manga, where Levi flashes back to his former companions Furlan and Isabel during a critical scene. The AoT Wiki and broader fan community debated the classification for years. Most fans now treat No Regrets as effectively canon, and the story genuinely loses nothing by including it.

What order should I watch the Attack on Titan OVAs?

Place them chronologically to avoid spoilers: Ilse's Notebook, A Sudden Visitor, and Distress after Episode 13. No Regrets Parts 1 and 2 after Episode 25. Lost Girls: Wall Sina Parts 1 and 2 after Episode 37 (end of Season 2). Lost Girls: Lost in the Cruel World after Episode 49 (end of Season 3 Part 1). Title: One Punch Man Filler List: Every Episode Explained + Where to Place the OVAs

Content:
Does One Punch Man have filler? No. Across 36 episodes and three seasons, every episode adapts ONE's webcomic and Yusuke Murata's manga remake directly, and every filler guide on the internet agrees on the count: zero.

But the One Punch Man filler list is only half the story. The franchise also has 13 OVAs and special episodes, all canon, all approved by ONE, and all scattered across Blu-ray releases with no built-in viewing order. Stream the main series on Hulu or Crunchyroll, and you won't see any of them. They exist outside the episode count entirely, and the only way to know where they belong is a placement guide.

One Punch Man Filler Quick Stats

Every filler database says the same thing about One Punch Man: zero. The real question isn't what to skip but where to place the 13 OVAs and whether Season 3's production quality changes your watch plan.

The full OPM episodes list across all three seasons is 36 entries of unbroken canon, and not one is worth skipping for story reasons. The only number that changes across those rows is the MAL score, and that drop from 8.47 to 4.76 is worth understanding before you decide what to do with Season 3.

The OVA Guide: All 13 Specials Placed in Watch Order

One Punch Man has 13 OVA and special episodes released between 2015 and 2020. All were written or approved by ONE, making every one canon. They're side stories set between main episodes, and the Season 1 specials in particular benefit from Madhouse's animation, making them feel like deleted scenes from S-Class production.

Two recap specials also exist (one before Season 2, one before Season 3), but both just rehash prior seasons and are safe to skip.

Season 1 OVAs (Madhouse, 2015-2016)

Three OVAs stand above the rest. Road to Hero is the franchise's only prequel, showing Saitama before he went bald. The Sisters gives Fubuki and Tatsumaki their best joint screen time in the anime. And The Murder Case is a locked-room comedy that plays to OPM's strengths better than most of the main series. If you only have time for a few extras, those three are the ones.

Is Season 3 Worth Watching?

Season 3 is fully canon, same as the rest. But whether it's worth your time comes down to what drew you to One Punch Man in the first place.

Season 1's Madhouse animation was legendary partly because the animation itself was the joke: Saitama's bored expression against absurdly fluid fight choreography. J.C. Staff's takeover for Season 2 was a visible downgrade, but ONE's writing carried it. Season 3 broke something. A clip of Garou walking became the defining meme, spawning nicknames like "One-Frame Man" and "One Slideshow Man." Episode 6 earned a 1.5 on IMDb, reportedly the lowest-rated anime episode on the platform. The MAL community scored the full season at 4.76, nearly half of Season 1's rating.

The story underneath is still ONE's Monster Association arc, one of the manga's strongest. Garou's transformation, the Hero Association's fractures, and the Monster King Orochi confrontation all land as plot beats even when the animation doesn't serve them. Part 2 (2027) will adapt the Saitama vs. Cosmic Fear Garou fight, widely considered the best fight in the entire manga. Skipping Season 3 means skipping the setup for that payoff.

If you watch One Punch Man for the visual spectacle that made Season 1 legendary, Season 3 will frustrate you. If you watch for ONE's writing and the Garou arc, the season delivers what you need before Part 2. Everything in it is canon, and the extended production timeline for Part 2 suggests Bandai Namco knows the presentation needs work.

Three Ways to Watch One Punch Man

Since the One Punch Man filler list has nothing to cut, the watch paths here work by addition. The 36-episode main series is your starting point, and each path adds a layer of OVA content on top of it.

Path 1: Main Series Only (~15 Hours)

All 36 episodes in release order with no OVAs. The main series never references the specials, so you won't miss any plot points or character introductions by saving them for later.

Path 2: Main Series + Best OVAs (~17 Hours)

All 36 episodes plus three standout OVAs woven in where they land best:

Roughly 48 extra minutes, all Madhouse-animated, so they visually match Season 1's quality.

Path 3: The Complete Experience (~20 Hours)

All 36 episodes plus all 13 OVAs in chronological order using the tables above. Skip the two recap specials. At 20 hours total, you can finish everything in a single dedicated weekend.

Class C Ranking, S-Class Punch

The One Punch Man filler list is the emptiest guide on this site, with nothing to skip and nothing to debate across all 36 main-series episodes. OPM earned that record by staying short, staying faithful to the source, and ending each season before the material ran dry. The real decisions live outside the filler count: 13 OVAs that are canon but invisible on streaming platforms, a season that delivered the right story with the wrong production quality, and a Part 2 that could adapt the best fight in the manga if the execution holds up.

Saitama sits at the bottom of the Hero Association rankings despite being the strongest hero alive. The One Punch Man filler list works the same way. It looks like the simplest page on the site, but the questions underneath it punch harder than you'd expect.

Yes. Every OVA and special was written or approved by ONE, and they all fit within the main timeline as side stories between episodes. The standouts are Road to Hero (Saitama's prequel), The Sisters (Fubuki and Tatsumaki), and The Murder Case (the franchise's best comedy OVA).

Title: Sword Art Online Filler List: 0% Filler, But Here's What to Actually Skip
Summary: Skip more than you'd expect with our full Sword Art Online filler list. SAO has more skippable episodes than fans realize. ⚔️🎮
Meta Title: Sword Art Online Filler List: What to Really Skip
Meta Description: Sword Art Online has 0% filler across 96 episodes, but not every arc is essential. Get the honest skip-or-watch guide for the franchise.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Sword Art Online has zero filler. Across 96 episodes of main series content, every single one is adapted from Reki Kawahara's light novels. For an anime franchise that's been running since 2012, that's almost unheard of. Compare it to Naruto's 41% filler rate or Bleach sitting at 45%, and SAO's clean record starts to look like a cheat code.

Every Sword Art Online filler list you'll find stops at "nothing to skip" and leaves you stranded with nearly a hundred episodes and no guidance. The real question was never "which episodes are non-canon?" It was always "which arcs earn my hours, and which ones are safe to pass on?"

With Echoes of Aincrad launching in July 2026 and Reki Kawahara teasing new anime announcements for the year, SAO keeps pulling fans back in. Whether you're starting for the first time or circling back to a franchise you left mid-arc, here's the honest verdict guide that you should know.

Quick Stats

StatDetail
Total Episodes (Main Series)96 (S1: 25, S2: 24, Alicization: 24, War of Underworld: 23)
Filler Episodes0
Filler Percentage0%
Source MaterialLight novels by Reki Kawahara (27 volumes, ongoing)
Additional ContentExtra Edition (OVA), Ordinal Scale (film), 2 Progressive films, GGO Alternative (24 eps), recap specials
Current StatusUnital Ring arc ongoing in novels; new original anime film confirmed (undated)
StudioA-1 Pictures

What makes this Sword Art Online filler list different from the rest is what comes after the stat. SAO's 0% filler rate exists because the franchise never needed padding. A-1 Pictures had a deep well of light novel material to draw from, and the seasonal release schedule meant the anime was never at risk of catching up to the source. When it comes to Sword Art Online filler, the answer really is that simple: there is none. But "canon" and "essential" aren't the same thing, and that's where this guide earns its place.

Sword Art Online Skip or Watch List

Every episode of SAO is adapted from the light novels, so there are no non-canon entries to flag. The verdicts below focus on viewing priority instead: what's essential, what's optional, and what you should absolutely not skip even if you're tempted.

Season 1

EpisodesArcTypeVerdict
1-14AincradCanonWatch. The foundation of everything. Kirito and Asuna's story starts here, the stakes are life-or-death from episode one, and emotional gut-punches like Sachi's story (Episode 3) and the Floor 75 boss fight define the franchise going forward. No skips.
15-25Fairy DanceCanonWatch. The most divisive arc in SAO, and the criticism isn't unfounded. The Sugou plotline is uncomfortable by design, and ALfheim Online doesn't hit the same way Aincrad does. But Fairy Dance resolves the biggest cliffhanger from Season 1, introduces Leafa, and builds the setting for everything that comes after. Dropping SAO here means you never reach Mother's Rosario or Alicization. Push through it.

Extra Edition and Recap Specials

ContentTypeVerdict
Extra Edition (OVA)Anime OriginalSkip. Roughly 80% Season 1 recap with about 20 minutes of new content (a group underwater quest in ALO). The new material is a harmless hangout scene, but it adds nothing you need.
Recap Specials (S2 Ep 14.5, Alicization recaps)RecapSkip. Pure recaps with zero new story content. They exist for broadcast-schedule viewers, not for anyone watching at their own pace.

Season 2

EpisodesArcTypeVerdict
1-14Phantom Bullet (GGO)CanonWatch. SAO trades swords for sniper rifles, and the genre shift works. The Death Gun mystery gives the series genuine thriller energy, and Sinon's backstory is one of the more grounded character arcs in the franchise. A strong stretch that also introduces a character who sticks around for the long haul.
15-17CaliburCanonWatch. Three episodes, zero stakes, pure comfort food. The whole party raids a dungeon in ALO to grab Excalibur, nobody dies, nobody gets trapped. If you're in a rush, Calibur is the easiest canon content to pass on. But it's also the only time the full group just plays a game together without the world ending, and there's something refreshing about that.
18-24Mother's RosarioCanonWatch. Do not skip this. Widely considered SAO's emotional peak, and for good reason. Asuna takes the lead, Yuuki and the Sleeping Knights are among the best characters the series ever introduces, and the ending hits harder than almost anything else in the franchise. If you only have patience for one arc beyond Aincrad, make it this one.

Ordinal Scale (Film)

ContentTypeVerdict
Ordinal ScaleCanon (Film)Watch. Set between Season 2 and Alicization, the movie introduces augmented reality gaming, delivers strong action set pieces, and connects directly to plot threads Alicization picks up. Stands on its own as a solid film, too.

Alicization

EpisodesArcTypeVerdict
1-24AlicizationCanonWatch. SAO's most ambitious arc. The Underworld is a fully realized fantasy setting, Eugeo is the best partner character Kirito has ever had, and the slower pacing pays off in emotional weight that the earlier seasons couldn't always reach.
25-47War of UnderworldCanonWatch. The conclusion of Alicization. Alice's character development carries the first half while Kirito is sidelined, and the war setup feels genuinely earned. The second half gets chaotic with a massive cast and some pacing stumbles near the finish line, but the emotional payoff at the end is worth your patience.

Spin-Offs and Progressive Films

ContentTypeVerdict
SAO Alternative: GGO (S1 and S2, 24 eps total)Canon (Spin-off)Watch if you want more. Completely separate cast, completely separate story. Karen/LLENN is a fun protagonist and the Squad Jam tournaments are entertaining on their own. Not required for the main plot, but worth it if you want to spend more time in the universe.
Progressive: Aria of a Starless Night (Film)Canon (Retelling)Watch if you want more. Retells early Aincrad floors from Asuna's perspective with expanded detail and gorgeous animation. A companion piece to Season 1, not a replacement for it.
Progressive: Scherzo of Deep Night (Film)Canon (Retelling)Watch if you want more. Continues the Progressive retelling with the same strengths and the same optional status.

Secretly Peak: SAO Episodes Worth Protecting

Episode 3: "Red-Nosed Reindeer"

It looks like a standalone early episode. It's actually one of the most devastating emotional beats in the entire franchise. Sachi's story and its aftermath define Kirito's survivor guilt for the rest of the series. People who call SAO emotionally shallow usually haven't sat with this one long enough. The Christmas Eve scene alone justifies the Aincrad arc's time-skip pacing, because it proves the series can make you feel the weight of two lost years in a single episode.

Mother's Rosario (Season 2, Episodes 18-24)

The arc that converts SAO skeptics. Yuuki challenges Asuna to a duel, and what follows is a story about found family, terminal illness, and what it means to leave a mark on a world (virtual or otherwise). The Sleeping Knights guild is a better ensemble than most full-season casts manage, and the ending is a top-tier anime cry. Fans who dropped SAO after Fairy Dance or GGO genuinely missed the best content the show ever produced.

The Calibur Arc (Season 2, Episodes 15-17)

The wildcard pick. Three episodes of zero drama, pure group energy. Nobody dies, nobody gets trapped in another world, nobody angsts about anything. The whole party goes on a dungeon raid and has fun together. In a franchise defined by life-or-death stakes at every turn, Calibur is oddly the most honest version of what SAO's original premise promised: friends logging in and playing a game. It won't rank on anyone's "best of" list, and that's exactly why it belongs on this one.

Hot Take: Fairy Dance Is SAO's Toll Booth, Not Its Grave

The community consensus treats Fairy Dance as the arc where SAO loses people, and the Sugou storyline is genuinely hard to defend on its own terms. But the arc does structural work that the rest of the franchise depends on. It establishes Alfheim Online as a recurring setting, resolves the cliffhanger that would have eaten you alive after Aincrad, and gives Suguha a character arc the show at least tries to handle with care.

The argument isn't "Fairy Dance is secretly great." It's that dropping SAO at its lowest point means you never see it at its highest. Mother's Rosario, Alicization, Eugeo, Alice, Yuuki: all of it lives on the other side of those eleven episodes. Fairy Dance is a toll booth. Pay it, and the rest of the highway opens up.

Log In to What Matters

The Sword Art Online filler list is the shortest one in anime: zero episodes to skip across the entire franchise. But the number alone doesn't help you decide how to spend your time, and that's the gap every other guide leaves open.

Every arc is canon. Not every arc hits the same way. Use the verdicts above to build the watchthrough that fits your patience, skip the recaps and Extra Edition without a second thought, and whatever you do, don't bail before Mother's Rosario. SAO rewards the hours once you know where they matter most.

FAQ

Does Sword Art Online have filler episodes?

No. SAO has a 0% filler rate across all 96 episodes of the main series. Every episode is adapted directly from Reki Kawahara's light novels. The only non-essential content is the Extra Edition OVA (mostly a recap) and various recap specials scattered throughout the franchise.

Is the Calibur arc filler?

Technically, no. Calibur (Season 2, Episodes 15-17) is adapted from Volume 8 of the light novels, making it fully canon. It plays more like a low-stakes side quest than a main story arc, though, and it's the easiest content in the series to pass on if you're short on time.

Can I skip SAO Extra Edition?

Yes. Extra Edition is roughly 80% recap of Season 1 with a short new sequence at the end. It doesn't set up any plot points the main series requires you to know.

What order should I watch Sword Art Online?

Release order works best: Season 1, then Season 2, then the Ordinal Scale film, then Alicization and War of Underworld. GGO Alternative and the Progressive movies are optional and fit naturally after the main series.

Is SAO Alternative: Gun Gale Online required viewing?

No. GGO Alternative follows a completely different cast and story within the same universe. It has no impact on the main SAO timeline. Worth watching on its own merits if you enjoy the setting, but entirely optional for following Kirito and Asuna's story.

Title: Death Note Filler List: 37 Episodes, Zero Filler, One Massive Debate
Summary: Spot the pacing dips with our complete Death Note filler list for all 37 episodes. Zero traditional filler, one massive debate. 📓💀
Meta Title: Death Note Filler List: 37 Episodes, Zero Filler
Meta Description: Death Note filler list for all 37 episodes. Zero traditional filler, plus the one recap and the pacing dips to know before you rewatch.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Does Death Note have filler? No. Zero filler episodes. Across all 37 entries, every single one is adapted from Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata's manga. For a franchise that consistently ranks among the most popular anime ever made, the 0% filler rate is almost comically clean. Compare that to Naruto at 41% or Bleach at 45%, and Death Note looks like it showed up to the exam already knowing every answer.

Death Note's infamous shift after Episode 25 is one of the most debated quality drops in anime history. Near and Mello replace L, the pacing changes, and the community has been arguing about whether the final twelve episodes earn their place since 2007. Fans searching for a filler guide are often looking for someone to tell them whether they can stop at Episode 25 with a clear conscience.

With Death Note: The Musical getting a full revival at London's Barbican Theatre this summer (July 30 through September 12, 2026) and the Duffer Brothers' Netflix live-action adaptation still sitting in development limbo, the franchise stays in the conversation even without new anime on the horizon. Here's the honest, phase-by-phase verdict guide that you've got to know.

Death Note Episode Quick Stats

StatDetail
Total Episodes37
Filler Episodes0
Filler Percentage0%
Mixed Canon/Filler Episodes4 (Eps 1, 25, 26, 37 contain minor anime-original changes)
Source MaterialManga by Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata (108 chapters, completed)
StudioMadhouse
Additional Content2 Relight compilation films
Current StatusOriginal story complete. No sequel anime announced.

Death Note had an even bigger structural advantage than most 0% filler shows: the manga was already finished before the anime wrapped its run. Madhouse never had to stall for time or invent material, which is why Death Note filler simply doesn't exist in any meaningful form. Four episodes contain minor anime-original additions (small scene changes, a recap segment, an altered ending), but none qualify as filler by any standard definition.

Death Note: The Complete Skip or Watch List

Since there are no Death Note filler episodes to flag, a traditional Death Note filler list would be one line long. The verdicts below do the job that actually matters: they cover the show's three structural phases, flag the moments fans genuinely debate, and give you honest viewing guidance for all 37 episodes.

The L Era (Episodes 1-25)

EpisodesPhaseTypeVerdict
1-15The Cat-and-Mouse GameCanonWatch. The stretch that made Death Note legendary. Light finds the notebook, L enters the frame, and the psychological chess match between them is as tight as anime gets. Episode 1 ("Rebirth") has minor anime-original additions (Light hesitates before picking up the notebook, a killing montage absent from the manga), but they strengthen the setup rather than pad it. Episode 7 ("Overcast") has a reputation as the weakest in this run, with the Naomi Misora resolution feeling a bit too convenient, but it's still essential to the plot. No skips.
16-24The Yotsuba Group ArcCanonWatch. The pacing shifts here. Light surrenders the Death Note and loses his memories, the Yotsuba corporate conspiracy takes over, and the show becomes more of an ensemble thriller than a two-person duel. Some fans find this stretch slower without the direct Light-vs-L tension, and the criticism is fair. But the arc does crucial work: it tests whether Kira's ideology can survive without Light consciously driving it, and the payoff when his memories come flooding back is one of the most iconic moments in the series. Worth every minute of the slower build.
25"Silence"Canon (Mixed)Watch. The episode that changed everything. L's death plays out slightly differently than in the manga (no final inner monologue, added symbolic imagery), but the emotional devastation lands either way. The anime's version arguably hits harder visually. If you're reading this guide because you've heard "Death Note falls off after L dies," this is the hinge. Keep going.

The Transition (Episode 26)

EpisodePhaseTypeVerdict
26"Renewal"Canon (Mixed)Watch. The closest thing Death Note has to filler. The first half recaps the events of Episodes 1-25, making it the only recap content in the entire series. But the second half introduces Near and Mello, jumps five years forward, and sets up the final act. You cannot skip this episode. The recap is the price of admission for the new characters and time jump waiting on the other side.

The Near/Mello Era (Episodes 27-37)

EpisodesPhaseTypeVerdict
27-36The Final GameCanonWatch. Here's where the community fractures. Near and Mello step into L's role, the psychological warfare shifts from personal to institutional, and the pacing runs hotter with time jumps and parallel storylines. The common criticism: Near reads like a copy of L without the magnetism, and Mello's mafia subplot tests your patience. The counterargument: these episodes show Light at the peak of his corruption, manipulating entire systems instead of outdueling one detective, and his slow unraveling is compelling if you're watching for character rather than just the chess match. The quality does dip from the first 25 episodes. Pretending otherwise would be dishonest. But it doesn't dip enough to justify abandoning the story twelve episodes from its conclusion.
37"New World"Canon (Mixed)Watch. The finale diverges from the manga more than any other episode. Light's death plays out differently (shot and cornered in the anime, killed by Ryuk writing his name in the manga), and Misa's fate is changed entirely. The anime's ending is more cinematic. The manga's is more thematically clean. Either way, you need to see how the notebook closes.

The Relight Films

ContentTypeVerdict
Relight 1: Visions of a GodRecap CompilationSkip. Covers Episodes 1-26 with some new Ryuk framing scenes. If you've watched the series, nothing here is essential. Completionists may enjoy the new material, but it doesn't add story value.
Relight 2: L's SuccessorsRecap CompilationSkip. Covers Episodes 27-37 in condensed form with minor additions. Same verdict: for completionists only. Neither Relight film replaces or improves on the series itself.

Secretly Peak: Death Note Episodes Worth Defending

Death Note doesn't have filler to rehabilitate, but it does have episodes and stretches that get unfairly dismissed or rushed past. These three picks are the ones worth slowing down for, whether you're watching for the first time or coming back to a series you think you already figured out.

Episode 2: "Confrontation"

The real start of the show. Where Episode 1 sets up the premise, "Confrontation" is the moment Death Note becomes Death Note. L's broadcast trap, Light's furious reaction, and the instant escalation from "teenager with a notebook" to "global psychological warfare" all land in 23 minutes. If the first episode is the cover of the notebook, Episode 2 is the first name written in ink.

The Yotsuba Stretch (Episodes 16-24)

The arc that tests people's patience is also the one doing the heaviest thematic lifting. A memory-wiped Light working alongside L to catch a Kira he doesn't remember being is the most interesting version of the character the show ever produces. He's genuinely likable here, which makes the moment his memories return and the "good Light" vanishes forever one of the coldest beats in anime. Fans who rush through this section to get back to the duel miss the point entirely: the duel was already decided before Light remembered he was playing.

Episode 25: "Silence"

Most fans already know why this episode matters, but its craft deserves closer attention. The anime's choice to strip L's final inner monologue and replace it with silence, rain, and a foot-washing scene is a genuine artistic decision that divides even manga loyalists. The stillness of L's death, set against Light's internal victory, is the kind of storytelling restraint that Death Note rarely gets credit for. Regardless of where you land on the Near/Mello era, Episode 25 is the emotional peak, and it earns that in every frame.

Hot Take: The Post-L Episodes Aren't Filler, They're the Bill Coming Due

The most popular take in the Death Note fandom is that the show peaks at Episode 25 and everything after is a lesser version of itself. The quality does dip. Near lacks L's magnetism. Mello's arc strains credulity. The pacing trades intimacy for scope. All true.

But the post-L stretch serves a purpose the first 25 episodes couldn't: it shows what happens when Light actually wins. The L era is the chess match. The Near/Mello era is the aftermath, where Light has to maintain a god complex without the only person who ever made him feel mortal. His arrogance compounds, his mistakes multiply, and his downfall becomes inevitable because he stopped being challenged at his level.

Skipping Episodes 26-37 doesn't preserve a perfect show. It leaves a story without its closing argument. Light's death is the thesis statement the whole series builds toward. Without it, Death Note is just a villain who got away with it, and that's a worse story than the one Ohba actually wrote.

The Last Name on the Page

The Death Note filler list is the easiest one in anime: zero filler episodes across the entire run. But the number alone is not why you searched for this guide, and pretending otherwise would be a waste of your time.

Every episode is canon. Not every episode hits the same heights. Use the verdicts above to know what you're walking into, watch the Yotsuba stretch with the patience it deserves, and whatever you do, don't stop at Episode 25. Death Note's ending is divisive for a reason, and that reason is worth experiencing for yourself.

FAQ

Does Death Note have filler?

No. Death Note has a 0% filler rate across all 37 episodes. Every episode is adapted from the manga. Four episodes (1, 25, 26, and 37) contain minor anime-original additions or changes from the source material, but none are filler by any standard definition.

Which Death Note episodes are mixed canon and filler?

Episodes 1, 25, 26, and 37. Episode 1 adds a hesitation beat and a killing montage. Episode 25 changes small details of L's death scene. Episode 26 includes recap material alongside the Near/Mello introduction. Episode 37 alters how Light and Misa's stories end. All four are still essential viewing.

Can I stop watching Death Note after Episode 25?

You can, but the story isn't finished. Episode 25 ends L's arc, not Light's. The final twelve episodes show Light's corruption reaching its peak and his eventual downfall. The quality does shift, but the ending gives the series its thematic weight. Stopping at 25 leaves you with half a story.

Is Death Note: Relight worth watching?

Only for completionists. The two Relight films are recap compilations that condense the series with a handful of new scenes. They don't replace the full anime and don't add essential story content.

How many episodes of Death Note are there?

37 episodes in the main series, aired from October 2006 to June 2007. There are also two Relight compilation films, but the core experience is the 37-episode run.

Title: Fullmetal Alchemist Filler List: Both Series Covered with Every Episode Ranked
Summary: Compare filler across 2003 and Brotherhood with our complete Fullmetal Alchemist filler list. Two versions, one essential guide. ⚙️🔥
Meta Title: Fullmetal Alchemist Filler List: Both Series Covered
Meta Description: Fullmetal Alchemist filler list for 2003 and Brotherhood. Two versions, one clean guide. See exactly what to skip and watch in each.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Fullmetal Alchemist is one of the few anime franchises adapted twice, and both versions have almost no filler. FMA 2003 has 3 filler episodes out of 51 (6%). Brotherhood has 1 filler episode out of 64 (2%). Across 115 total episodes, you could count every skippable entry on one hand.

The list can get confusing because roughly half of FMA 2003 diverges from Hiromu Arakawa's manga entirely, and those episodes keep getting mislabeled as filler. They're not. They're the actual ending of a different story, told because the manga wasn't finished when the 2003 anime aired. Calling them filler is like calling an alternate ending a deleted scene.

With Arakawa's new anime Yomi no Tsugai premiering on Netflix in July 2026 (animated by Bones Film, the same studio family behind both FMA series), fans are circling back to her original masterpiece. Whether you're starting fresh or revisiting the Elric brothers, here's the only FMA filler list that covers both anime in one place with honest verdicts.

Fullmetal Alchemist: Quick Episode Stats

StatFMA 2003Brotherhood
Total Episodes5164
Filler Episodes3 (Eps 4, 10, 37)1 (Ep 27)
Filler Percentage6%2%
Source MaterialManga (partially adapted)Manga (fully adapted)
StudioBonesBones
Aired2003-20042009-2010
FilmsConqueror of Shamballa (2005)Sacred Star of Milos (2011)

Fullmetal Alchemist filler barely exists because both adaptations had strong source material to draw from, and neither studio padded the runtime with throwaway content. The 2003 version ran ahead of the manga and wrote its own ending rather than inserting filler arcs. Brotherhood waited until the manga was nearly complete before starting, which is why it adapts all 27 volumes with almost nothing added. For context, Naruto sits at 41% filler and Bleach at 45%. FMA's combined rate across both series is under 4%.

One critical note: FMA 2003's anime-original episodes (roughly Episodes 29 onward) are labeled "Anime Canon" in the tables below, not filler. They tell a complete alternate storyline with its own ending. Treating them as filler misrepresents what the 2003 series actually is.

Complete Fullmetal Alchemist Filler & Skip/Watch List

Since the Fullmetal Alchemist filler episodes across both series total only four, a pure skip list would barely fill a sentence. The tables below cover FMA 2003 and Brotherhood arc by arc, with verdicts on every stretch and clear labels for the actual filler.

FMA 2003: The Shared Canon (Episodes 1-28)

EpisodesContentTypeVerdict
1-3Introduction, Liore, BackstoryManga CanonWatch. A stronger, slower introduction to the Elric brothers than Brotherhood's version. Takes its time establishing the world and the brothers' bond. Many fans recommend experiencing these episodes in FMA 2003 even if you plan to switch to Brotherhood afterward.
4"A Forger's Love"FillerSkip. A standalone about a counterfeiter. Mildly entertaining but completely disposable. The first of only three pure filler episodes in the entire series.
5-9Tucker Arc, Hughes, Laboratory 5Manga CanonWatch. Includes the Nina Tucker episode, one of the most devastating sequences in anime history. FMA 2003 spreads the Tucker story across more episodes than Brotherhood does, giving you time to care before the horror. Essential viewing.
10"The Phantom Thief"FillerSkip. A lighthearted thief-of-the-week story. Fun tone but zero impact on the plot.
11-28Continuing Shared CanonManga Canon / MixedWatch. The stretch where both anime cover roughly the same ground: the Hughes tragedy, the Fifth Laboratory, and the introduction of Greed. FMA 2003 gives several of these beats more room to breathe than Brotherhood's faster pace allows.

FMA 2003: The Divergence (Episodes 29-51)

EpisodesContentTypeVerdict
29-36Anime-Original Storyline BeginsAnime CanonWatch. The manga hadn't finished, so the anime forges its own path. Different Homunculi origins, a darker tone, and storylines that connect the Homunculi personally to the main cast. The shift is jarring if you know Brotherhood's version, but the 2003 interpretation asks genuinely different questions about the same premise.
37"The Flame Alchemist, The Bachelor Lieutenant & The Mystery of Warehouse 13"FillerSkip. The third and final pure filler episode. A comedic Mustang standalone that's completely disconnected from the story.
38-51Anime-Original ConclusionAnime CanonWatch. The 2003 series builds to an ending that splits the brothers across parallel worlds. It's controversial, it's bleak, and it's the story this version chose to tell. Conqueror of Shamballa (2005) serves as the true finale if you make it here. Skipping Episodes 29-51 means you watched half a show.

FMA Brotherhood (Episodes 1-64)

EpisodesContentTypeVerdict
1"Fullmetal Alchemist" (Ice Alchemist)Anime OriginalWatch. An anime-exclusive prologue not in the manga. Introduces the cast and tone through an original conflict. Some fans call it filler, but it functions as a cold open and sets the stage well.
2-26Early Arcs (Liore through Greed)Manga CanonWatch. Brotherhood moves through the early arcs faster than FMA 2003, condensing material like the Tucker arc into fewer episodes. If you watched FMA 2003 first, this stretch will feel like a speedrun of familiar ground. It still works as a first exposure, but the emotional beats hit harder with FMA 2003's pacing as a reference point.
27"Interlude Party"FillerSkip. The one undisputed filler episode in Brotherhood. A recap of the first 26 episodes framed as a party. Offers minor Hohenheim characterization but nothing you need.
28-64The Complete StoryManga CanonWatch. Every single episode. This is where Brotherhood becomes the definitive adaptation and one of the greatest anime ever made. The Promised Day, Father's plan, the nationwide transmutation circle, and a finale that earns every emotional beat it reaches for. No skips. Not one.

Films and OVAs

Conqueror of Shamballa (2005)Sequel to FMA 2003Watch if you watched FMA 2003. Completes the 2003 storyline. Essential for that version, irrelevant to Brotherhood.
Sacred Star of Milos (2011)Brotherhood side storySkip. A standalone adventure that doesn't connect to Brotherhood's main plot. Fine on its own, but entirely optional.
OVAs (both series)Bonus contentWatch if you want more. Short side stories and extras. None essential, all enjoyable for fans who want more time in the world.

Secretly Peak: FMA Episodes Worth Defending

Any Fullmetal Alchemist filler list can give you the four episodes to skip. These three picks are the ones worth protecting.

FMA 2003's Tucker Arc (Episodes 6-7)

Brotherhood handles Tucker in a single devastating episode. FMA 2003 gives the story two, letting you spend more time with Nina and Alexander before the betrayal. The extra runtime makes the horror land harder because you've had the space to care. Fans who only know Brotherhood's version have experienced the shock but not the full weight of the grief that follows. The 2003 pacing is the reason this moment became one of anime's most infamous scenes.

Brotherhood Episode 19: "Death of the Undying"

The Lust confrontation. Mustang's flames, Hawkeye's breakdown, and one of the most visually stunning action sequences in the entire franchise. Often cited as the moment Brotherhood shifts from "great adaptation" to "all-time classic." The animation quality spikes, the stakes become genuinely lethal, and the series announces that it's done holding back.

FMA 2003's Homunculi

The 2003 version gives the Homunculi a completely different origin: each one is born from a failed human transmutation attempt. Sloth is the Elric brothers' mother. Wrath is Izumi's son. These connections make the Homunculi personal in a way Brotherhood's "creations of Father" structure doesn't attempt. Neither version is wrong. Brotherhood's Homunculi serve a grander plot. FMA 2003's Homunculi serve the characters. Both work, and experiencing both sharpens your appreciation for what each version prioritizes.

Hot Take: FMA 2003 Isn't the Wrong Version, It's the Other Answer

The community consensus has crowned Brotherhood as the definitive Fullmetal Alchemist, and that's fair. Brotherhood adapts the complete manga, delivers a more satisfying final arc, and earns its permanent seat near the top of every "best anime" ranking.

But framing FMA 2003 as the "lesser" version, or treating its anime-original content as glorified FMA filler, sells it short. The 2003 series handles the early arcs with more patience and emotional weight. Its Homunculi carry personal connections to the Elric brothers that Brotherhood never attempts. Its tone is darker and more willing to sit in grief rather than push toward resolution. And its ending, while divisive, asks a genuinely different philosophical question than Brotherhood's triumphant finale.

The real equivalent exchange isn't choosing one version over the other. It's watching both and letting each one illuminate what the other couldn't reach.

The Law of Equivalent Exchange (Applied to Your Watch List)

The Fullmetal Alchemist filler list is one of the shortest in anime: 3 episodes in FMA 2003, 1 in Brotherhood, and nothing else worth skipping. But the number was never the point of this guide.

The point was cutting through the confusion that surrounds this franchise. FMA 2003's anime-original content is not filler. Brotherhood's Episode 1 is not a waste of your time. And the question of which version to watch has never been "either/or" for anyone willing to invest in both. Use the verdicts above, skip the four episodes that genuinely don't matter, and give both Elric brothers' journeys the time they earned.

FAQ

Does Fullmetal Alchemist have filler?

Very little. FMA 2003 has 3 filler episodes (4, 10, and 37) for a 6% filler rate. Brotherhood has 1 filler episode (27) for a 2% rate. The combined filler across both series is under 4%, making FMA one of the leanest major anime franchises.

Which Fullmetal Alchemist filler episodes can I skip?

In FMA 2003: Episodes 4 ("A Forger's Love"), 10 ("The Phantom Thief"), and 37 ("The Flame Alchemist, The Bachelor Lieutenant & The Mystery of Warehouse 13"). In Brotherhood: Episode 27 ("Interlude Party"). All other episodes are canon or anime canon and contribute to their respective stories.

Should I watch FMA 2003 or Brotherhood first?

Brotherhood is the complete manga adaptation and works perfectly as a standalone watch. However, starting with FMA 2003's early episodes (1-28) gives you a stronger, more patient introduction to the characters and world. Many fans recommend FMA 2003 first for emotional grounding, then Brotherhood for the full story. Either order works.

Is FMA 2003's anime-original content filler?

No. Episodes 29-51 of FMA 2003 tell a complete alternate storyline with its own ending, created because the manga wasn't finished when the anime aired. They are anime canon, not filler. Conqueror of Shamballa (2005) serves as the conclusion to this storyline.

Is Sacred Star of Milos worth watching?

Only if you want a standalone FMA adventure. The film doesn't connect to Brotherhood's main plot and introduces characters who never appear in the series. It's fine as a side story but adds nothing essential.

Title: Inuyasha Filler List: Every Episode Ranked Across All 193 Episodes
Summary: Power through a heavy filler count with our complete Inuyasha filler list for all episodes plus The Final Act. 🏹🌸
Meta Title: Inuyasha Filler List: Every Episode Ranked
Meta Description: Inuyasha filler list for all 193 episodes plus The Final Act. About 20% is filler. See which blocks to skip clean and which arcs to keep.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Inuyasha runs 193 episodes, with 36 of them being filler, roughly 20% of the total run. The filler includes a notorious 13-episode marathon, several multi-episode arcs, and a handful of scattered standalones that pause the Naraku hunt for side stories.

But here's what makes the Inuyasha filler list different from most: the show's episodic travel structure means filler often feels less jarring than you'd expect. The group is always wandering feudal Japan, encountering one-off demons and troubled villages. A filler episode about a random demon encounter doesn't break the format the way a disconnected side arc would in a more plot-driven series. Some of these detours are genuinely fun, and a few are fan favorites.

With Rumiko Takahashi's MAO anime debuting in April 2026 (directed by Teruo Sato, the same director behind Yashahime), fans are circling back to her most iconic work. Whether you're starting fresh or returning after dropping the show mid-run, here's the complete guide covering the original 167 episodes and the 26-episode Final Act in one place.

Inuyasha Quick Stats

StatDetail
Total Episodes193 (167 original + 26 Final Act)
Filler Episodes~36
Filler Percentage~20%
Mixed Canon/Filler~14 episodes
Source MaterialManga by Rumiko Takahashi (56 volumes, 558 chapters, completed)
StudioSunrise
Additional Content4 theatrical films, Yashahime sequel (48 episodes, 2020-2022)
Final Act Filler0 episodes (100% canon)

The key number: the Final Act has zero filler across all 26 episodes. After the original series left the story unfinished in 2004, the Final Act returned in 2009 to adapt the manga's conclusion without a single episode of padding. Every piece of Inuyasha filler lives in the original 167-episode run, and most of it clusters in a few skippable blocks rather than spreading evenly across the series.

The Complete Inuyasha Filler List

Inuyasha's filler falls into three types: standalone one-off episodes scattered throughout the run, multi-episode filler arcs that stall the Naraku hunt, and mixed episodes that blend anime-original scenes with manga content. The tables below list every filler episode with a verdict, organized by the stretch of the series where they appear. If an episode isn't in the tables, it's canon and safe to watch.

The Foundation (Episodes 1-58)

Zero filler in this stretch. The first 58 episodes are canon or mixed canon, covering Kagome's arrival in feudal Japan, the Shikon Jewel shattering, the full group assembling (Shippo, Miroku, Sango), Naraku's emergence, Sesshomaru's arc, and Kikyo's return. Watch all of them.

The Filler Creep (Episodes 59-101)

This is where the filler starts appearing regularly, building to the longest stretch in the series.

EpisodesVerdict
59Skip. Standalone demon encounter with no plot relevance.
63-65Skip. Three standalone demon-of-the-week episodes back to back. Entertaining enough on their own but zero plot advancement.
68Skip. Another standalone.
72Skip. Standalone filler.
75-79Skip. Five-episode filler arc. The momentum starts to sag here, and none of these connect to the main storyline.
89-101Skip. The big one. Thirteen episodes of filler stacked back to back. Mostly demon-of-the-week stories that grind the Naraku hunt to a complete halt. A handful of these are genuinely entertaining (the modern-day comedy episodes, the group dynamics), but the sheer length is what kills it. This is the block where most viewers lose patience with the series. If you skip only one filler stretch in your entire watch, make it this one.

Band of Seven and Beyond (Episodes 102-167)

Episodes 103-126 (the Band of Seven arc) are fully canon and one of Inuyasha's absolute best stretches. Zero filler. The filler returns afterward:

EpisodesVerdict
127-130Skip. Four-episode filler arc arriving right after the Band of Seven high, which makes the quality drop more noticeable.
133-140Skip. Eight-episode filler arc. The second-longest block in the series. Some group comedy moments land, but the arc overstays its welcome by at least four episodes.
162-163Skip. Two standalone filler episodes near the end of the original run. Easy to pass on.

Secretly Peak: Inuyasha Filler Worth Protecting

Not all Inuyasha filler deserves to be skipped. The tables above give you the clean route, but these three picks are worth circling back to.

The Modern-Day Episodes

Inuyasha's best filler happens when the group visits Kagome's modern-day world. The culture clash between feudal-era characters and contemporary Japan is consistently funny, and these episodes give the cast room to breathe outside the Naraku hunt. The school festival episodes in particular are fan favorites. Scattered across the filler blocks, they're worth cherry-picking even if you skip everything else around them.

The Band of Seven Arc (Episodes 103-126)

Not filler at all, but it deserves the spotlight because it's the stretch that proves Inuyasha can deliver when the plot tightens. Seven distinct villains with their own fighting styles, a genuine threat to the main cast, and a pace that never lets up. Fans who dropped the show during the Episodes 89-101 marathon never saw this arc, and that's the real cost of that 13-episode wall.

The Final Act (Episodes 168-193)

26 episodes, zero filler, pure payoff. Every unresolved thread gets its conclusion. The pacing is tight (sometimes too tight), but the emotional weight of the finale earns every beat. Fans who gave up on Inuyasha during the original run's rougher stretches owe themselves these 26 episodes.

Hot Take: The 13-Episode Marathon Ruined Inuyasha's Reputation

Any Inuyasha filler list shows a 20% rate, which is modest by long-running shonen standards.

The real issue isn't volume. It's placement. Scattering standalone filler episodes between canon arcs is fine, and Inuyasha's wandering structure handles it better than most. But stacking 13 filler episodes at Episodes 89-101 creates a wall that kills momentum right when the story should be escalating. Most fans who dropped Inuyasha quit during that stretch, not because the episodes were terrible, but because thirteen in a row is too many for any series to survive.

Strip out that one block and Inuyasha's filler barely registers. The show's reputation took the hit for one scheduling decision.

Through the Well and Out the Other Side

The Inuyasha filler list runs about 36 episodes across 193, and most of it concentrates in a few skippable blocks. Skip 89-101 without hesitation. Pass on 75-79, 127-130, and 133-140. The scattered standalones barely register.

And when you clear the filler, what's left is a genuinely rewarding journey: a strong first half, the Band of Seven as one of the best villain arcs in long-running shonen, and a 26-episode Final Act that delivers the ending the original series couldn't. Use the verdicts above, skip the blocks that don't earn your time, and come back for the Final Act.
