Title: Sailor Moon Watch Order: The 90s Anime, Crystal, and Every Movie Explained
Summary: Pick your Sailor Moon watch order, the filler-free Crystal run or the beloved 90s anime, with every movie slotted in. 🌙✨
Meta Title: Sailor Moon Watch Order: Crystal, 90s Anime, Movies
Meta Description: The Sailor Moon watch order made simple: choose Crystal or the 90s anime, then follow one path with every movie slotted in.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Short answer: Sailor Moon comes in two versions of the same story, so the first thing to settle is which one you want. For a quick, complete, filler-free run, watch Sailor Moon Crystal (Season 1 through Season 3, then the Eternal and Cosmos films). For the beloved classic, watch the original 90s anime (Sailor Moon, then R, S, SuperS, and Sailor Stars). Pick one continuity and follow it through, since both tell Usagi's whole journey from start to finish.

The reason the Sailor Moon watch order looks scary is the sheer amount of it: two anime adaptations, five differently named 90s seasons, a modern reboot, and a stack of movies. Once you see that it splits cleanly into two paths, the panic fades. Below I break down both versions, help you choose, slot in every movie, and sort out where the Eternal and Cosmos films land.

The two versions of Sailor Moon (the real question)

Here is the knot at the center of the whole Sailor Moon series: there are two complete anime adaptations of Naoko Takeuchi's manga, and they are separate continuities, not sequels.

The original 90s anime (1992 to 1997) is the classic that made Sailor Moon a global icon. It runs about 200 episodes across five seasons, tells the entire story with a warm, character-rich style, and carries plenty of monster-of-the-week filler along the way. It is a big, cozy commitment.

Sailor Moon Crystal (2014 onward) is the modern reboot. It sticks close to the manga, strips out the filler, and tells the same arcs in a fraction of the runtime, continuing into two film duologies that finish the story. It is faster and more faithful, though some fans feel it trades away a little of the original's charm, especially in its early episodes.

Neither is the wrong choice. They are two takes on one legend, and which suits you depends on how much time and nostalgia you are bringing.

Which Sailor Moon should you watch first?

For most newcomers, my pick is Sailor Moon Crystal. It gives you the complete, manga-accurate story (all five arcs, ending included) in around 21 hours, with no filler to wade through and modern animation throughout. If you want to know the whole tale without a marathon, start there.

That said, the 90s anime earns its devotion. Its slower pace gives the characters room to breathe, its humor and heart are hard to match, and for many fans it simply is Sailor Moon. If you love retro animation and do not mind filler and a long runtime, the original is a wonderful place to start instead. In hard numbers, Crystal runs about 21 hours all the way through the films, while the 90s anime is a far bigger commitment at roughly four times that. So the honest answer to what order to watch Sailor Moon is: choose your version first, then follow that path straight through, and the Sailor Moon watch order stays simple once you have picked a lane.

Sailor Moon Crystal watch order (with Eternal and Cosmos)

Crystal is the tidier path, and its later arcs arrived as films rather than TV seasons, which is the part that trips people up. Watch it in this order.

The important thing: Eternal and Cosmos are not optional extras, they are the fourth and fifth chapters of Crystal, just made as movies instead of seasons. Watch Eternal first (both parts), then Cosmos (both parts), and Cosmos brings the whole saga to its close. Three seasons and four films make up the complete Crystal continuity, and it is the smoothest way to learn how to watch Sailor Moon in order. Worth knowing before you start: Crystal's first two seasons drew mixed reactions for their stiff early animation, while Season 3 won fans over with a real jump in quality and pacing.

The original 90s anime watch order

If you go classic, the 90s run is linear too, with the only quirk being that each season has a name instead of a number. Here is the sequence.

All told, the 90s run is roughly 200 episodes, and it covers every arc the manga did, with the final Sailor Stars season wrapping things up. One bit of trivia worth knowing: Sailor Stars went undubbed in English for decades until the modern Viz release finally brought it over, so plenty of older Western fans never saw the original ending. The three original movies (Promise of the Rose, Hearts in Ice, and Black Dream Hole) are fun side stories rather than canon, so they are easy to skip. If you want them, each slots into its matching season: Promise of the Rose around R, Hearts in Ice during S, and Black Dream Hole during SuperS.

Watching both versions

Plenty of fans eventually want both, and there is no strict rule for the order. A common approach is to watch Crystal first for the streamlined, complete story, then go back to the 90s anime to enjoy its slower, richer telling. Others prefer to experience the original the way it aired and treat Crystal as a faithful refresher afterward. Either way works, since the two are separate continuities covering the same events. Just avoid bouncing between them mid-story, so you keep each version's reveals and pacing intact. Handled like that, even the full completionist Sailor Moon watch order stays manageable rather than overwhelming.

Dubs and where to watch Sailor Moon

If you watch dubbed, go with the modern Viz dub rather than the older, heavily edited 90s dubs. The Viz version is uncut, faithful to the original, and covers the whole series, including seasons and movies the earlier dubs never touched.

Streaming is a little scattered. Sailor Moon Crystal's three seasons tend to live on Crunchyroll and Hulu, while the Eternal and Cosmos films stream on Netflix worldwide, which is an easy detail to miss. The original 90s anime turns up on services like Tubi and Pluto in some regions, and on Viz's own platform in the US. Availability shifts by region and over time, so confirm what is live where you are before you plan a viewing.

Fighting evil by moonlight, in the right order

For a franchise three decades deep, the Sailor Moon watch order really comes down to one friendly decision: pick your version. Crystal delivers the full, manga-faithful story in a weekend, capped by the Eternal and Cosmos films, while the 90s anime offers the beloved, filler-and-all classic that made the whole phenomenon. Choose a path, follow it start to finish, and the Sailor Moon series opens right up as one of the most influential magical-girl stories ever made, transformation sequences and all.

FAQ

Which Sailor Moon should I watch first?

For a quick, complete, filler-free version, start with Sailor Moon Crystal, then its Eternal and Cosmos films. If you prefer the beloved classic and do not mind filler or a long runtime, start with the original 90s anime instead. Both tell the full story.

Do I need to watch the original 90s anime before Crystal?

No. Crystal is a standalone reboot that retells the same manga from the beginning, so you can start there with zero prior knowledge. The 90s anime is a separate continuity you can watch before, after, or not at all.

What order do I watch Eternal and Cosmos in?

Watch Eternal (both parts) first, then Cosmos (both parts). They continue directly from Sailor Moon Crystal Season 3 and act as its fourth and fifth chapters, with Cosmos delivering the finale.

Are the original Sailor Moon movies canon, and do I need them?

The three 90s films (Promise of the Rose, Hearts in Ice, and Black Dream Hole) are non-canon side stories. They are enjoyable but skippable, and none are required to follow the main plot.

Where can I watch Sailor Moon?

Most of the panic around the Attack on Titan watch order comes from the final stretch, where the seasons split into parts and specials with confusing labels. Take a breath, because the core path is a straight line from the Fall of Shiganshina to the sea. Below I lay out every season and episode, untangle the Final Season naming, place the OVAs worth your time, and point you to the finale that hits hardest, so you can watch Attack on Titan in order without second-guessing. Fans shorten it to the AOT watch order, but by either name the route is the same.

The full Attack on Titan watch order (all seasons and episodes)

Here is how to watch Attack on Titan in order, season by season, with episode numbers so you always know where you are. The table below covers all Attack on Titan episodes across the four seasons.

For the simplest answer to what order to watch Attack on Titan, just follow that table top to bottom.

Decoding Season 4 and the Final Chapters (the only confusing part)

The Final Season is where the labeling goes sideways, so here is the plain version. Season 4, produced by MAPPA after WIT Studio handled the first three, was released in chunks: Part 1 (16 episodes), then Part 2 (12 episodes), then the ending arrived as two feature-length specials called the Final Chapters. You will see those specials labeled all sorts of ways (Part 3 and Part 4, Special 1 and Special 2, The Final Chapters), but they are simply the last two installments that close the story.

So the whole of Season 4 reads: Part 1, then Part 2, then Final Chapters Special 1, then Final Chapters Special 2. Nothing more to it. Once you know the specials are just the finale under a fancier name, the confusion disappears.

The Last Attack or the Final Chapters specials?

In late 2024, the two Final Chapters specials were re-cut into a single theatrical film, Attack on Titan: The Last Attack, running about two and a half hours with upgraded sound and visuals. It does not change the ending or add new story, it just presents the same finale in one polished cinematic sitting.

For a first-time viewer, either option closes the series just fine. The two specials and the movie tell the same story with only tiny differences. If you can watch The Last Attack, it is the better-looking, better-sounding way to end your run, so I would point a newcomer there. If it is not available in your region, the two Final Chapters specials lose you nothing important.

Which OVAs are worth watching?

Attack on Titan has a handful of OVAs, and they are optional side stories rather than required viewing. Two stand out. No Regrets is the clear pick, a two-part look at Levi's past and how he ended up in the Survey Corps, and it plays great after Season 1. Ilse's Notebook is the other worth-your-time entry, a short, eerie piece of canon Titan lore that rewards watching early.

The rest (Distress, The Sudden Visitor, and the Lost Girls episodes focused on Annie and Mikasa) are pleasant character extras you can take or leave. If you want a precise breakdown of what each one adds and where it falls, our Attack on Titan filler list ranks every OVA watch-or-skip alongside the main episodes. None of them are essential to the plot, so slot them in after their matching season or skip them without worry.

What you can safely skip

A few entries sound important but are not part of the core experience. The recap movies (Crimson Bow and Arrow, Wings of Freedom, The Roar of Awakening, and Chronicle) compress the TV seasons into film form and add no new story, so skip them unless you want a quick refresher before a rewatch. Attack on Titan: Junior High is a non-canon chibi parody that is genuinely funny, but only after you have finished the real thing, never before. The live-action films sit completely apart from the anime and are easy to leave for the curious.

Chronological order vs release order

You may see a chronological Attack on Titan watch order floating around, and it only reshuffles a couple of OVAs to match the in-universe timeline. For a first watch, skip it and stick to release order, which is the cleanest way to watch Attack on Titan in order. The series is built on foreshadowing and slow reveals, and moving side stories earlier risks spoiling moments the main show wants to land on its own terms. Release order keeps every gut-punch intact, which is exactly how the story earns its reputation.

Where to watch Attack on Titan

Crunchyroll is the most reliable home for the series, carrying every season, both Final Chapters specials, and the OVAs with subbed and dubbed options. In some regions the show also lives on Netflix or other platforms, and availability shifts over time, so confirm what is streaming near you before you commit. If you just want to know how to watch AOT in order without hunting across services, Crunchyroll is the one-stop answer in most countries.

Devote your evenings, in the right order

For a series with this fearsome reputation, the Attack on Titan watch order is refreshingly kind: four seasons in a straight line, ending with the Final Chapters or the polished Last Attack film. Add No Regrets and Ilse's Notebook if you want the best of the side stories, skip the recaps and live-action, and let the main run carry you from the first Titan to the final answer. Few stories reward marathoning like this one, and now you can start it without second-guessing a single episode.

Watch it in release order: Season 1, Season 2, Season 3 (Parts 1 and 2), then Season 4, which runs Part 1, Part 2, and the two Final Chapters specials. It covers the entire story from beginning to end.

How many episodes are in Attack on Titan?

The main anime has 89 numbered episodes across four seasons, with the two Final Chapters specials serving as the finale. The optional OVAs and recap films sit on top of that if you want the complete set.

Should I watch The Last Attack or the Final Chapters specials?

Both cover the same ending. The Last Attack is a 2024 theatrical re-cut of the two specials with better visuals and sound, so it is the nicer way to finish if you can access it. The specials work perfectly well otherwise.

Title: Fullmetal Alchemist Watch Order: 2003, Brotherhood, and Every Movie Explained
Summary: Settle the Fullmetal Alchemist watch order: Brotherhood or the darker 2003 series, with every movie placed by path. ⚙️🔥
Meta Title: Fullmetal Alchemist Watch Order: 2003 vs Brotherhood
Meta Description: The Fullmetal Alchemist watch order sorted: Brotherhood or the darker 2003 series, with every movie and OVA placed by path.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Short answer: the real question here is not what order, it is which version. Fullmetal Alchemist has two complete anime adaptations of the same manga, and they are not sequels to each other. For most people, watch Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood (2009), the faithful, complete telling with the author's intended ending. The 2003 series is a darker alternate version you can watch separately (with its own sequel movie). Pick one path and watch it start to finish rather than marathoning both as a single story.

Untie that one knot and the Fullmetal Alchemist watch order gets simple. If you are wondering how to watch Fullmetal Alchemist, the first thing to settle is which of the two adaptations you want. Both shows follow the Elric brothers, Edward (whose sharpest lines the fandom still quotes) and Alphonse, after a forbidden attempt to bring their mother back costs them their bodies. You will also see this searched as the Full Metal Alchemist watch order, spelled as two words, and it means exactly the same thing. Below I lay out both paths, settle the 2003-versus-Brotherhood question, and slot in every movie and OVA.

The full Fullmetal Alchemist watch order at a glance

Here are both routes plus the extras, so you can see how to watch Fullmetal Alchemist in order without cross-wiring the two continuities. You follow one column, not both at once.

EntryTypeYearNote
Fullmetal Alchemist: BrotherhoodTV (64 eps)2009The complete manga adaptation. Start here.
Brotherhood OVAsOVA (4)2009-2010Optional side stories. Watch after.
The Sacred Star of MilosFilm2011Optional non-canon side story.
Fullmetal Alchemist (2003)TV (51 eps)2003Darker anime-original telling.
Conqueror of ShamballaFilm2005The 2003 series' ending. Required for that path.

The top three rows are the modern default. The bottom two are the alternate 2003 experience, complete on their own. So the honest answer to what order to watch Fullmetal Alchemist is: choose a path, finish it, and only then consider the other.

Which version should you watch, 2003 or Brotherhood?

For a newcomer, my recommendation is clear: start with Brotherhood. It adapts Hiromu Arakawa's manga from beginning to end, it has the tighter second half and the more satisfying finale, and it has sat near the top of nearly every anime ranking for over a decade. If you only ever watch one version, this is the one.

The 2003 series is not a lesser option, and it deserves better than the "skip it" treatment it sometimes gets. It aired while the manga was still running, so Studio Bones carried the early arc faithfully and then built an entirely original second half, with a different villain, a darker philosophical streak, and an ending the manga never went near. Plenty of fans who grew up with it prefer it, and they are not wrong to. Think of the two as the same legend painted by two different artists.

If you want both, the smoothest route is Brotherhood first, then a short break to let it settle, then the 2003 series followed by Conqueror of Shamballa. Watching them back to back with no gap tends to blur the shared early arc, so the pause matters. People also ask what order do you watch Fullmetal Alchemist if they plan to see everything, and the answer is still one version at a time, each taken as its own complete story.

Time is worth factoring in too. Brotherhood on its own runs roughly 26 hours, while doing both series plus their movies lands somewhere around fifty. Either way, a clear Fullmetal Alchemist watch order keeps that investment pointed at the version you actually want rather than spread thin across everything at once.

What's the difference between Fullmetal Alchemist and Brotherhood?

Both versions open on the same tragedy and share their early episodes almost beat for beat. Around the middle of the 2003 run, once it caught up to the ongoing manga, the original series branches off into anime-original territory: a reworked origin for the homunculi, a new central antagonist, and a heavier, more melancholic tone that carries through to its own conclusion. Brotherhood, made after the manga finished, follows Arakawa's full story with her intended ending intact, and the payoff in its back half is a big reason it is so beloved. The two lines stay close for roughly their first quarter before splitting, which is another reason the break between them helps and why some rewatchers find the early overlap a little slow the second time through.

Neither version is bloated with filler, though the 2003 series carries a handful of skippable episodes (our Fullmetal Alchemist filler list breaks down both series episode by episode if you want a leaner run). The ensemble cast lands hard in both tellings too, from Scar to fan favorites like Roy Mustang, which is part of why people happily watch both.

Where the movies and OVAs fit

Each film belongs to one version, not the franchise as a whole, so slot them by path.

Conqueror of Shamballa (2005) is the direct sequel to the 2003 series, set two years later in an alternate 1920s Germany. It closes out the original anime's story, so it is essentially required viewing if you take the 2003 path, and it means nothing on its own if you only watched Brotherhood.

The Sacred Star of Milos (2011) is a standalone adventure set during the Brotherhood timeline. It is a fun side trip with original characters, but it is non-canon and changes nothing in the main story, so treat it as optional dessert after you finish the series.

The OVAs are short bonus stories tied to their respective series. The four Brotherhood shorts (including The Blind Alchemist and Simple People) expand backstory and play best once you have finished the show, while the older 2003 bonus shorts are pure extra. All of them are optional.

The live-action films and where to watch

There is also a live-action Fullmetal Alchemist trilogy from Japan (2017, then two films in 2022) that reached most of the world through Netflix. It sits completely apart from the anime and adapts the story with mixed results, so it is safe to leave off your list unless you are simply curious.

For streaming, coverage is fairly good. Crunchyroll carries both series and the major movies, and Brotherhood also turns up on other services in some regions. The older OVAs are the hardest to track down and often live on physical releases only. Availability shifts by region and over time, so confirm what is live where you are before you settle in.

Pick your road through Amestris

For all the debate it inspires, the Fullmetal Alchemist watch order really comes down to one decision: pick a version and commit. Brotherhood is the complete, definitive telling and the right call for almost everyone, while the 2003 series and Conqueror of Shamballa are a genuinely different, darker experience waiting whenever you want it. Add the OVAs and Sacred Star of Milos as extras, keep the two continuities in their own lanes, and one of the most acclaimed stories in anime opens up cleanly in front of you.

FAQ

What order do I watch Fullmetal Alchemist in?

Pick one version and watch it fully. For most people that is Brotherhood (2009), which adapts the complete manga on its own. If you want the alternate take afterward, watch the 2003 series and then its sequel film, Conqueror of Shamballa.

Should I watch Fullmetal Alchemist 2003 or Brotherhood first?

Brotherhood first for most viewers, since it is the complete, faithful adaptation with the strongest ending. The 2003 series is best treated as a separate, darker alternate telling to explore later rather than a prerequisite.

Do I need to watch Conqueror of Shamballa?

Only if you watch the 2003 series. It is the direct conclusion to that version's story. If you only watched Brotherhood, you can skip it, since it is tied to the 2003 continuity.

Where does The Sacred Star of Milos fit?

It is an optional, non-canon side-story film set during the Brotherhood timeline. Watch it after you finish Brotherhood if you want a bit more, since it does not affect the main story either way.

Where can I watch Fullmetal Alchemist?

Crunchyroll carries both series and the main movies, with Brotherhood also available on some other platforms depending on region. The OVAs are the trickiest to find and are often physical-only. Availability varies by region, so check before you start.

Title: Code Geass Watch Order: Every Season, Movie, and OVA in Order
Summary: Map the Code Geass watch order from Lelouch of the Rebellion to R2, with the movie timeline and Rozé sorted out. ♟️🕊️
Meta Title: Code Geass Watch Order: Seasons, Movies, and OVAs
Meta Description: The Code Geass watch order from Lelouch of the Rebellion to R2, with the movie timeline, Re;surrection, and Rozé sorted out.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Short answer: for a first watch, keep it simple. Watch the two TV seasons, Lelouch of the Rebellion, then R2. Those two seasons are the complete, self-contained masterpiece, and for most people they are the whole point. Everything else (the recap movies, the sequel film Re;surrection, the 2024 Rozé of the Recapture, and the Akito side story) is optional extra, with one fork in the road that I will lay out clearly below.

Code Geass earned its confusing reputation honestly, thanks to a pile of similar-sounding subtitles and a set of movies that quietly rewrite the ending. The story of Lelouch, the exiled prince turned masked revolutionary whose coldest, sharpest lines still echo through the fandom, actually has a clean spine once you see how the pieces fit. Below I map the full Code Geass watch order, explain the two timelines, and give you a straight recommendation so you know exactly where to start.

The full Code Geass watch order at a glance

Here is everything in recommended viewing order, with the core story marked apart from the optional extras. If you want the fastest version of how to watch Code Geass in order, this table is it.

#EntryTypeYearNote
1Code Geass: Lelouch of the RebellionTV (25 eps)2006Core. Start here.
2Code Geass: Lelouch of the Rebellion R2TV (25 eps)2008Core. The complete TV story ends here.
3Akito the ExiledOVA films (5)2012-2016Optional side story. Save for later.
4Recap movie trilogy (Initiation, Transgression, Glorification)Films (3)2017-2018Optional. Alternate-timeline retelling.
5Code Geass: Lelouch of the Re;surrectionFilm2019Sequel to the movie timeline.
6Code Geass: Rozé of the RecaptureONA (12 eps)2024Latest entry, set after Re;surrection.

The first two rows are the real Code Geass. The rest is where the choices come in, so let me untangle the part that trips everyone up.

The two timelines, explained (this is the whole trick)

Here is the one thing that makes the Code Geass watch order click: there are two separate continuities.

The original TV timeline is Lelouch of the Rebellion plus R2. Fifty episodes, one continuous story, a complete and genuinely iconic ending. Nothing else is required to enjoy it.

The movie timeline is a different beast. In 2017 and 2018, Sunrise released three films (Initiation, Transgression, and Glorification) that compress the TV run into a trilogy. They look like simple recaps, but they change several key events and adjust the ending, which spins the story off into an alternate timeline. The 2019 sequel film, Lelouch of the Re;surrection, then builds directly on that altered ending, and 2024's Rozé of the Recapture continues from there. So the movies are not remasters. They are revisions with more story attached.

The split is why people get whiplash: watch the TV finale, jump straight to Re;surrection, and the film references an outcome you never actually saw on screen. Once you know the two timelines exist, picking your path is easy.

Where to start (and do you need the recap movies?)

For a newcomer, my recommendation is clean: watch Lelouch of the Rebellion, then R2, and let that be your Code Geass. It is a complete story with one of the best endings in the medium, and you lose nothing by stopping there. If you just want the classic, those two seasons are the honest answer to what order to watch Code Geass.

Caught the bug and want more? You have two ways to continue:

  • The easy path (most people): go straight from the TV series to Re;surrection, then Rozé of the Recapture. You will hit a small continuity bump because the sequel assumes the movies' altered ending, but the gap is minor and easy to roll with.
  • The completionist path: watch the three recap films first as the official bridge, then Re;surrection, then Rozé. It gets you the exact setup the sequel was built on, at the cost of re-watching a condensed version of the story you just finished.

Neither is wrong. If you value your time, take the easy path. If you want every beat to line up perfectly, the trilogy is your bridge. So the answer to what order should I watch Code Geass really depends on how much of a completionist you are, and both routes end in the same place.

Where do Akito, the recap specials, and Rozé fit?

A few odds and ends round out the franchise, and here is the honest placement for each.

Akito the Exiled is a five-part OVA film series set in Europe during the gap between the two TV seasons, following a new cast rather than Lelouch. It is a fun, visually gorgeous side chapter that enriches the world without being essential. Chronologically it slots between the seasons, but for a first-timer it plays best saved until after you have finished the main story, so you are already invested before taking a detour.

Rozé of the Recapture brings in two new leads, the mercenary brothers Rozé and Ash, in a story set years after Re;surrection within the movie continuity. It can work as a standalone, though it lands better once you have the earlier films in your head. Reactions have been mixed, so go in curious rather than expecting a second Zero Requiem.

The recap specials (Black Rebellion and Zero Requiem) are straight summaries of the TV seasons and safe to skip unless you want a quick refresher. The Nunnally in Wonderland OVA is a non-canon comedy bonus with no real home in the timeline, so tuck it in at the very end if you watch it at all.

Is there a Code Geass chronological order?

If you want the in-universe sequence, the original timeline runs Lelouch of the Rebellion, then Akito the Exiled (set between the seasons), then R2. The movie timeline is its own separate branch: the recap trilogy, then Re;surrection, then Rozé of the Recapture. The key rule is not to weave the two together, because they resolve the same events differently and mixing them just creates contradictions. Stay inside one continuity and you keep every reveal intact, which is the smoothest way to take in Code Geass in order.

Where to watch Code Geass in order

Streaming is a little scattered, so here is the lay of the land. In most regions the two TV seasons stream on Crunchyroll, which is the main home for the core story. The four films (the recap trilogy plus Re;surrection) tend to be on Crunchyroll in the US and on Amazon Prime elsewhere, sometimes as a rental or purchase. Rozé of the Recapture is the odd one out, streaming on Disney-operated platforms worldwide and on Hulu in the US. The older OVAs, including Akito, are the hardest to find and often need a physical copy. Availability shifts by region and over time, so confirm what is live where you are before you plan a marathon.

Start the rebellion in the right order

For all the tangled subtitles, the Code Geass watch order comes down to a calm two-step: watch Lelouch of the Rebellion and R2 for the definitive story, then decide whether you want more. If you do, follow the movie timeline into Re;surrection and Rozé, with the recap trilogy as an optional bridge for the completionists. Keep the two continuities separate, save Akito for a rewarding side trip, and you turn a franchise famous for confusing newcomers into one of the sharpest, most rewarding runs in anime.

FAQ

What order should I watch Code Geass in?

Start with Lelouch of the Rebellion, then R2, which is the complete original story. If you want to continue, watch Re;surrection and then Rozé of the Recapture, optionally watching the recap movie trilogy first as a bridge into the sequel's timeline.

Do I need to watch the recap movies before Re;surrection?

Not strictly. The recap trilogy sets up the altered ending that Re;surrection follows, so watching it first makes the continuity line up perfectly. Most viewers skip it, go straight from the TV series to Re;surrection, and simply accept a small gap, which works fine.

Where does Akito the Exiled fit in the watch order?

Akito is an optional side story set in Europe between the two TV seasons, with a separate cast. Chronologically it falls between Season 1 and R2, but it plays best saved until after you have finished the main story.

Is Rozé of the Recapture canon, and where does it go?

Rozé of the Recapture (2024) continues the movie continuity, set years after Re;surrection with new lead characters. Watch it after Re;surrection if you are following that timeline. It can stand alone, but it is richer with the earlier films behind you.

Where can I watch Code Geass?

The two TV seasons are usually on Crunchyroll, the four films are on Crunchyroll in the US and Amazon Prime elsewhere, and Rozé of the Recapture streams on Disney-operated platforms and Hulu. The older OVAs are harder to find. Availability varies by region, so check before you start.

Title: Ghost in the Shell Watch Order: Every Timeline, Film, and Series Explained
Summary: Crack the Ghost in the Shell watch order by continuity, from the 1995 film to Stand Alone Complex and the 2026 series. 🤖🌃
Meta Title: Ghost in the Shell Watch Order: Every Timeline
Meta Description: The Ghost in the Shell watch order by continuity, from the 1995 film to Stand Alone Complex and the 2026 series. Pick a lane.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Ghost in the Shell is not one continuous story, so you do not watch it all in a single line. It is several separate versions of the same world, each self-contained. For a newcomer, start with the 1995 film, then move into Stand Alone Complex, and treat each continuity as its own thread. Make that single change in how you approach it and the whole thing clicks.

The reason the Ghost in the Shell watch order feels impossible is that people try to force every film, OVA, and series into one timeline. They contradict each other on purpose. Once you stop fighting that and pick a lane, learning how to watch Ghost in the Shell gets easy. Below I break down every continuity in order, name the optional recap films you can skip, and give a clear starting point so you are not stuck staring at a wall of titles.

The one rule that makes the Ghost in the Shell watch order simple

Here is the whole trick: the Ghost in the Shell series is a set of separate continuities that share characters and themes but tell different, incompatible versions of Major Motoko Kusanagi and Section 9. Think of it as several shells running the same soul. There are four main ones:

  • The Oshii films (1995, 2004): art-house, philosophical, the works that put anime on the world map.
  • Stand Alone Complex (2002 onward): the most popular and accessible version, a grounded cyber-crime procedural, and the longest-running continuity of the bunch.
  • Arise (2013 to 2015): a reboot that reimagines the Major's origin, more action-forward.
  • The new 2026 series: a fresh manga-based adaptation built as a clean entry point.

Pick one continuity and watch it in its own order. Do not interleave them, because jumping between timelines mid-story means nothing lines up. The real answer to how to watch Ghost in the Shell in order is that simple, and everything below fills in the details for each lane.

Where to start (the best entry point for newcomers)

My pick: begin with the original 1995 film. It runs a tight 83 minutes, it is the definitive version of this world, and nearly every later entry references it. Follow it with its sequel, Innocence, if the philosophical tone grabs you, then move into Stand Alone Complex for the long, rewarding TV run.

If dense, meditative films are not your speed, there is a strong alternative: start with Stand Alone Complex (2002) instead. It is more structured, easier to binge, and does a beautiful job expanding the world with memorable side characters. Neither choice is wrong. The films give you the definitive artistic statement first, while the show gives you the most approachable door in. So the honest answer to "what order should I watch Ghost in the Shell" comes down to taste: the landmark films for the definitive artistic statement, or the accessible series for the smoothest way in. Either path gives you a clean Ghost in the Shell watch order instead of a tangle of titles.

The Oshii films, in order

Mamoru Oshii's movies form the original continuity and the franchise's artistic core.

EntryYearNote
Ghost in the Shell1995The iconic original. Start here.
Ghost in the Shell 2.02008A remaster of the 1995 film with some scenes redone in CG. Optional; the original stays definitive.
Ghost in the Shell 2: Innocence2004Oshii's direct sequel, even denser and more visually lavish.

Two films (plus one optional remaster) and you have the entire Oshii continuity. It is the shortest lane and the most influential, which is why it makes such a clean starting point.

Stand Alone Complex, in order

Stand Alone Complex is the big one, a separate TV continuity that shares the cast but not the films' events. It runs longest and rewards every hour.

EntryTypeYearNote
Stand Alone ComplexTV (26 eps)2002Season 1. The Laughing Man arc.
S.A.C. 2nd GIGTV (26 eps)2004Season 2. The Individual Eleven arc.
Solid State SocietyFilm2006Sequel film that caps the original TV run.
SAC_2045 (Season 1)ONA (12 eps)20203DCG revival set years later.
SAC_2045 (Season 2)ONA (12 eps)2022Concludes the 2045 story.

Two things worth knowing here. The 3DCG look of SAC_2045 split fans hard, so read a few thoughts before diving in if the visual style matters to you. And the various compilation films (The Laughing Man, Individual Eleven, Sustainable War, The Last Human) are recap edits of material you have already seen. They add nothing new to the plot, so they are easy to pass on unless you specifically want a movie-length refresher.

Arise, in order

Arise is a full reboot with its own take on the Major's early years. It reads as a prequel in spirit, but it assumes you already know this world, so it is a poor first stop and a much better later one.

EntryTypeYearNote
Border:1 Ghost PainOVA2013Part 1 of 4.
Border:2 Ghost WhispersOVA2013Part 2 of 4.
Border:3 Ghost TearsOVA2014Part 3 of 4.
Border:4 Ghost Stands AloneOVA2014Part 4 of 4.
Arise: Alternative ArchitectureTV (10 eps)2015Recompiles the four OVAs and adds the new Pyrophoric Cult arc.
Ghost in the Shell: The New MovieFilm2015Closes out the Arise story.

Quick tip: you can watch the four Border OVAs on their own, but the final Pyrophoric Cult arc only exists inside Alternative Architecture (its last two episodes). So the cleanest path is the four OVAs, then just episodes 9 and 10 of Alternative Architecture, then The New Movie to finish the arc.

The new 2026 series and the live-action film

The franchise is not done. A brand-new adaptation from Studio Science SARU, drawn straight from Masamune Shirow's original manga, is arriving in 2026 as its own continuity. Because it starts fresh from the source, it needs no prior knowledge, which makes it a genuine new entry point for first-timers who want to begin with something current. Exact release details are still settling, so check the latest before you plan around it.

One more common question: the 2017 Hollywood live-action film with Scarlett Johansson is completely separate from every anime timeline. It borrows imagery and characters but does not slot into any of the continuities above, so leave it out of your anime run and treat it as a standalone curiosity.

Where to watch Ghost in the Shell

Streaming is the genuinely annoying part, because the franchise is scattered across services. In many regions the 1995 film and Innocence live on Amazon Prime Video, the Arise entries are on Crunchyroll, and SAC_2045 is a Netflix exclusive. The original Stand Alone Complex seasons are the hardest to find and often require a rental or purchase. Availability shifts constantly by region, so confirm what is live where you are before you build your plan around any one platform.

Pick a shell and dive in

For all its reputation as a maze, the Ghost in the Shell watch order comes down to one calm idea: these are separate windows into the same world, not one giant puzzle box. Choose the 1995 film or Stand Alone Complex as your way in, follow that continuity to its end, then explore the others as their own self-contained stories. Do that and a franchise that scares off newcomers turns into one of the richest cyberpunk runs ever made, with a new chapter arriving in 2026 to pull even more people in.

FAQ

What order should I watch Ghost in the Shell in?

Start with the 1995 film, then its sequel Innocence, then the Stand Alone Complex series in its own order. Keep each continuity separate rather than mixing them. If you prefer accessible TV over dense films, starting with Stand Alone Complex first is an equally solid path.

Do the Ghost in the Shell timelines connect?

Not really. The Oshii films, Stand Alone Complex, and Arise are separate continuities that share characters and themes but tell contradictory versions of the story. Watch within one continuity at a time instead of trying to link them.

Is Ghost in the Shell: Arise a prequel I should watch first?

No. Arise reimagines the Major's origin, but it assumes you already know this world, so it lands much better after you have seen the original film or Stand Alone Complex. Treat it as a later reboot, not a starting point.

Is the 2017 live-action movie part of the anime timeline?

No. The Scarlett Johansson film is a separate Hollywood adaptation that does not fit into any of the anime continuities. You can watch it out of curiosity, but leave it out of your anime watch order.

Where can I watch Ghost in the Shell?

Coverage is split across platforms. The original films and Arise are commonly on Amazon Prime Video and Crunchyroll respectively, while SAC_2045 is on Netflix, and the original Stand Alone Complex often needs a rental or purchase. Availability varies by region, so check what is streaming near you before you start.

Title: Re:Zero Watch Order: All Seasons, OVAs, and the Director's Cut

Meta Title: Re:Zero Watch Order: Seasons, OVAs, Director's Cut

Content:
If you're watching it for the first time, watch it in release order. Season 1, then the Memory Snow OVA, then The Frozen Bond OVA, then Season 2, then Season 3, then Season 4 (airing right now). No traditional filler to dodge. The only real puzzle is two OVA films and one Director's Cut, and I'll place all three for you below.

Re:Zero looks messier than it actually is. The confusion comes from a few extras that sit outside the main run: two standalone OVA movies, a Director's Cut that re-edits the first season, and a chronological timeline that doesn't match the release timeline. Sort those out and the correct Re:Zero watch order is straightforward. Learning how to watch Re:Zero in order takes one glance at the list below, and I'll explain the handful of judgment calls (which OVA goes where, whether the Director's Cut is worth it, whether to bother with chronological order) so nothing trips you up.

The full Re:Zero watch order (release order)

Release order is the order Subaru's story was meant to unfold in, and it's the best path for anyone starting fresh. It keeps the big reveals intact and drops the side stories in at the moments they hit hardest. Start at the top and work down.

If you want the pure story with zero extras, the three TV seasons plus the currently airing fourth are the spine, and the two OVA films are the flavor you can add whenever you like. That's the whole of how to watch Re:Zero in order, and it holds for both a first run and a rewatch. The next few sections cover the placement calls that actually matter.

Where Memory Snow and The Frozen Bond actually fit

The two OVA movies are the piece that throws people, so here's the honest placement for each.

Memory Snow (watch after Season 1). A light, mostly self-contained side story set shortly after the events of the first season, full of small character moments and comedy that only land once you know everyone. Some viewers like to slot it between Season 1 episodes 11 and 12 for a breather in the middle of the darkest stretch, and that works too, but dropping it in right after the Season 1 finale is the cleaner call. Either way, it means more once you've spent real time with the cast.

The Frozen Bond (watch after Memory Snow, before Season 2). This one focuses on Emilia's past with Puck, and here's the catch: chronologically it takes place before Season 1. Watching it first sounds logical, but it quietly spoils reveals about Emilia that the main series wants you to discover slowly. Save it until after Season 1 (right alongside Memory Snow works well), and it pays off as backstory instead of stepping on the mystery.

How to watch Re:Zero in chronological order (and why it's a trap for newcomers)

If you want the internal-timeline version, here's how to watch Re:Zero in chronological order: The Frozen Bond first (it's a prequel), then Season 1 episodes 1 to 11, then Memory Snow, then Season 1 episodes 12 to 25, then Season 2, Season 3, and Season 4.

Now the honest part. For a first-time viewer, that order works against you. The Frozen Bond gives away who Emilia is and what her deal is long before the main story wants you to know, and a big part of Season 1's pull is uncovering that slowly alongside Subaru. Chronological order is a genuinely fun rewatch once you already know every twist, and it's worth doing then. On a first pass, release order wins, and it isn't close.

Original Season 1 or the Director's Cut?

Before Season 2 aired, White Fox released a re-edit of Season 1 (officially the New Edition, widely called the Director's Cut) that condenses the 25 original episodes into a smaller run of longer ones, with some scenes tweaked or added. It's an alternate version of the same season, not a new chapter you need to watch on top of the original.

For a first watch, stick with the original 25-episode Season 1. The extra room lets the pacing breathe, and the weekly-episode structure suits how the story doles out its gut-punches. The Director's Cut is best treated as a faster re-entry point for returning fans who want to refresh before Season 2 without redoing the full run. New here? Original season. Coming back after a long gap? The re-edit is a reasonable shortcut.

How many seasons of Re:Zero are there?

As of 2026, Re:Zero has three completed TV seasons and a fourth in the middle of its broadcast, plus the two OVA films. Here's the arc breakdown at a glance:

  • Season 1 (2016, 25 episodes): Arcs 1 to 3. Subaru arrives in a new world and discovers Return by Death, his ability to reset to a checkpoint each time he dies.
  • Season 2 (2020-2021, 25 episodes): Arc 4. Aired split-cour across two halves and digs deep into the Sanctuary and Subaru's hardest emotional trials yet.
  • Season 3 (2024-2025, 16 episodes): Arc 5. The Watergate City stretch, split into an Attack Arc and a Counterattack Arc, and a big jump in scale.
  • Season 4 (2026, airing now): Arc 6. Broadcasting in two cours, with the back half having just started, so this is the current frontier of the story.

The main story is very much still going, which is a big part of why so many people are searching the Re:Zero watch order right now. Anyone catching up has a clear runway from Season 1 straight into what's airing today.

Is there any filler in Re:Zero? (and is Isekai Quartet part of it?)

No, Re:Zero has no traditional filler in the TV seasons. It's a faithful adaptation of the light novels, so every main-series episode moves the story. The extras are the only optional pieces, and even those are canon side stories rather than time-wasters.

A couple of common mix-ups worth clearing up. Isekai Quartet is a separate chibi crossover comedy that puts the Re:Zero cast alongside characters from other isekai shows, and it's a fun spin-off, not part of the main canon or the watch order. The little Break Time chibi shorts fall in the same bucket: pure comedy bonuses you can enjoy whenever, with nothing you'll miss by skipping.

Where to watch Re:Zero

Crunchyroll is the home for the full series, carrying every season and both OVA films with subtitled and dubbed options, which makes watching Re:Zero in order simple in one place. Streaming rights shift by region and change over time, so check what's live in your country before you commit. The main seasons are the widely available part, and those are what matter most for a first run.

Start from zero, in the right order

The good news under all the OVA-and-recut noise: the core Re:Zero watch order is genuinely simple. Three finished seasons, a fourth airing now, and two side-story films you can fold in after Season 1. Go release order on your first pass to keep every reveal intact, save chronological order and the Director's Cut for a rewatch, and let Subaru take the beatings so you don't have to. From his first death to the newest arc, it's one of the most rewarding runs in modern isekai, and now you know exactly how to take it on.

For a first watch, go in release order: Season 1, then the Memory Snow and The Frozen Bond OVA films, then Season 2, Season 3, and Season 4. It keeps the reveals intact and slots the side stories where they read best.

Title: Evangelion Watch Order: The Series, The End of Evangelion, and the Rebuild Films

Meta Description: Untangle the Evangelion watch order across the original series and the Rebuild films. Join Kaminari for more anime watch order guides.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Evangelion has a reputation for being impossible to untangle, but its watch order is one of the cleaner ones once the recaps are set aside. The Evangelion watch order is the original 26-episode series, then The End of Evangelion, then the four Rebuild films in number order. That is the whole thing. The confusion comes from a pile of recap and re-edit films that are safe to ignore.

There are really two Evangelions. The 1995 TV series and its 1997 film ending, The End of Evangelion, are the original story. The Rebuild tetralogy, released from 2007 to 2021, is a reboot that starts familiar and then splits off into its own thing. You watch the original first, then Rebuild, and the recap films like Death & Rebirth add nothing you need.

Below we lay out the full Evangelion series order, sort the essential films from the skippable recaps, and explain what Rebuild actually is. We also cover the odd streaming split. Learn how to watch Evangelion in order once and one of anime's defining works plays out cleanly, mind-melting ending and all.

The Evangelion watch order

The core franchise is two series' worth of story plus a reboot, and it runs in a simple line. This table shows the recommended Evangelion anime order, or how to watch Neon Genesis Evangelion in order at a glance, with the essentials marked and the recaps flagged.

TitleTypeYearWhere it fits
Neon Genesis EvangelionTV, 26 eps1995-1996Core, start here
Death & RebirthFilm1997Skippable recap
The End of EvangelionFilm1997Core, the alternate ending
Evangelion: 1.0 You Are (Not) AloneFilm2007Rebuild, part one
Evangelion: 2.0 You Can (Not) AdvanceFilm2009Rebuild, part two
Evangelion: 3.0 You Can (Not) RedoFilm2012Rebuild, part three
Evangelion: 3.0+1.0 Thrice Upon a TimeFilm2021Rebuild, the finale
Petit Eva: Evangelion@SchoolONA shorts2007Non-canon comedy, skip

Skip Death & Rebirth without a second thought. Its first half recaps the series and its second half is just the opening of The End of Evangelion, so it adds nothing. The same goes for the re-edits floating around, like Death(True) and Revival of Evangelion, which recombine the same footage. The only pieces that matter are the TV series, The End of Evangelion, and the four Rebuild films.

The TV ending, The End of Evangelion, and the recaps

The part that confuses newcomers most is the ending, because there are two of them. The TV series wraps up with episodes 25 and 26, an abstract, introspective finale that landed during a troubled production. The End of Evangelion is the 1997 film that retells that ending on a far bigger canvas, showing the external events the series only hinted at. Watch the full 26-episode series, then watch The End of Evangelion, and you get both halves of one of the most talked-about endings in anime.

Death & Rebirth sits between them by release date, but it is a recap you can skip. If you are a completionist, the Director's Cut versions of episodes 21 to 24 add extra footage worth a look, though they are an enhancement rather than a requirement.

What is Rebuild of Evangelion?

Rebuild is where people get the wrong idea, since it looks like a sequel and is actually a reboot. The four films retell the story of the original series with sharper animation, then deliberately diverge, introducing new characters and a new direction that make the second half its own beast. Watch them in order: 1.0 You Are (Not) Alone, 2.0 You Can (Not) Advance, 3.0 You Can (Not) Redo, and 3.0+1.0 Thrice Upon a Time, which closes the whole saga out.

You could technically start with Rebuild, since 1.0 reintroduces the world from scratch, but we would not. The original series and The End of Evangelion give Rebuild its weight, since so much of it plays as a response to the 1995 story. See the original first, then let Rebuild reframe everything you thought you knew.

Where to watch Evangelion

The streaming split is the one genuine hassle. Netflix carries the original Neon Genesis Evangelion series, Death & Rebirth, and The End of Evangelion in most regions, having rescued them from years of unavailability. The four Rebuild films, though, live on Amazon Prime Video, so you will likely need both services to watch everything. Availability shifts by region, so check what is live where you are before you begin.

Get in the robot and start with episode one

For a series this dense, the Evangelion watch order is mercifully clear: the 26-episode original, then The End of Evangelion, then the four Rebuild films in order, with every recap safe to skip. Watch the original story first and let Rebuild reinterpret it afterward, and do not let the pile of re-edits scare you off. Start with episode one, get in the robot, and let one of anime's most influential works do its work on you.

FAQ

What is the Evangelion watch order?

The Evangelion watch order is the original Neon Genesis Evangelion series (26 episodes), then The End of Evangelion, then the four Rebuild films: 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, and 3.0+1.0. That is the complete story in release order. Recap films like Death & Rebirth are optional and safe to skip.

Do I watch the TV ending or The End of Evangelion?

Both. Watch all 26 episodes of the TV series, which end with the abstract episodes 25 and 26, then watch The End of Evangelion, the film that retells the ending with the external events shown in full. They are two sides of the same conclusion, and seeing both is the intended experience.

Is Rebuild of Evangelion a sequel or a reboot?

A reboot, mostly. The four Rebuild films retell the original story before diverging into new characters and a new ending. They are best watched after the original series and The End of Evangelion, since much of Rebuild works as a response to the 1995 version.

Should I watch Death & Rebirth?

No, you can skip it. Death & Rebirth is a compilation film: the first half recaps the TV series and the second half is the opening of The End of Evangelion. It adds nothing new, so most viewers skip straight from the series to The End of Evangelion.

Where can I watch Evangelion?

Netflix carries the original Neon Genesis Evangelion series and The End of Evangelion in most regions, while the four Rebuild films stream on Amazon Prime Video. You will likely need both to watch everything. Availability changes by region, so check what is streaming near you before you start.

Monogatari has one of the most notorious watch orders in anime, and for good reason: the series tells its story out of chronological sequence on purpose. The one thing that trips people up is Kizumonogatari, the vampire prequel. The rough chronological run is Kizumonogatari, then Nekomonogatari: Black, Bakemonogatari, Nisemonogatari, the Second Season arcs, Tsukimonogatari, Koyomimonogatari, both parts of Owarimonogatari, Hanamonogatari, Zoku Owarimonogatari, and finally Off & Monster Season. Trust the disorder and start with Bakemonogatari

For a series this deliberately tangled, the Monogatari watch order is kinder than its reputation: watch in release order from Bakemonogatari onward, leave Kizumonogatari in its slot for maximum mystery, and save chronological order for a rewatch. The out-of-sequence storytelling is the point, not an obstacle, so lean into it. Start with Bakemonogatari and let one of anime's most distinctive series unspool the way it was meant to.

Title: How to Watch Naruto in Order: Every Series, Movie, and the Filler to Skip

Author: devin-morris
Content:
Naruto has over 700 episodes across two series, so how to watch Naruto in order sounds daunting and mostly comes down to one thing: filler. The order itself is simple. Watch Naruto, then Naruto: Shippuden, then the canon film The Last, and continue into Boruto only if you want the next generation. It is one linear story. The catch is that roughly forty percent of both main series is filler you can skip.

That filler is the real reason people dread a Naruto marathon. The original series pads its 220 episodes heavily in the back half, and Shippuden buries around 200 filler episodes among its 500, including one long stretch late in the run. None of it moves the plot, so a good filler guide turns a 720-episode mountain into a much leaner canon run.

Below we lay out the series in order, break down exactly what filler to skip, and sort the canon movies from the optional ones. We also cover where Boruto fits and where everything streams. Sort the filler once and one of the defining shonen journeys plays out at a pace that respects your time.

How to watch Naruto in order: the series

The franchise is three main TV series that run in a straight line, each picking up where the last left off. This table lays out how to watch Naruto in order across all three, with episode counts and what each covers. The core story, Naruto's own, is complete by the end of Shippuden and the film that follows it.

SeriesYearsEpisodesWhat it covers
Naruto2002-2007220Kid Naruto, Team 7, and the Chunin Exams
Naruto: Shippuden2007-2017500The time-skip saga and the Ninja War
Boruto: Naruto Next Generations2017-2023293The next generation, an optional continuation

For a first watch, go in release order: Naruto, then Shippuden, then the canon movie The Last, with Boruto as an optional extra afterward. That covers how to watch Naruto in order for the complete main story. Naruto and Shippuden together run 720 episodes, but skipping the filler cuts that to roughly 430, the version most fans recommend for a first run.

The filler problem: what to skip

The real time savings hide in the filler. Both Naruto and Naruto: Shippuden are close to forty percent filler, the anime-only episodes studios added to avoid overtaking the manga. In the original series, the canon story runs strong through roughly episode 135, then a long filler block fills much of the way to the finale. In Shippuden, the filler comes in large arcs, with one especially long stretch in the back half.

Most of it is safe to skip, and a good guide makes the ranges obvious. Our Naruto filler list and Naruto Shippuden filler list mark every episode, which is really the key to how to watch Naruto in order without the padding. A few filler arcs are worth keeping, though, like Kakashi's Anbu backstory and the Itachi Shinden arc, which add real depth. And do not skip the closing episodes of either series, since they send the story off properly even where they drift from the manga.

The movies and Boruto: what counts as canon

Naruto has around eleven films, and most are non-canon side stories you can watch any time or skip. Only two are canon. The Last: Naruto the Movie is the important one, set after Shippuden episode 479, and it delivers the Naruto and Hinata story that leads into the next generation. Boruto: Naruto the Movie is also canon, though the Boruto series covers the same events, so you can watch either. Road to Ninja is a fun optional pick if you want more.

As for Boruto: Naruto Next Generations, it is a full sequel about Naruto's son and the new generation of ninja. Title: How to Watch Dragon Ball in Order: Every Series, Movie, and What Counts as Canon

Author: devin-morris
Content:
Dragon Ball has run for almost forty years, so how to watch Dragon Ball in order sounds like a nightmare and mostly is not. The core path is four series: Dragon Ball, then Dragon Ball Z (or its leaner recut, Kai), then Dragon Ball Super, then Dragon Ball Daima. Dragon Ball GT sits off to the side as a non-canon option, and only a handful of the movies actually matter. Everything else is bonus material.

Two questions cause most of the confusion. The first is whether to watch Dragon Ball Z or Dragon Ball Z Kai, since Kai trims the heavy filler and follows the manga more closely. The second is where GT and the two dozen movies belong. Neither is hard once you know that GT is not canon and most films are side stories.

Below we lay out all the Dragon Ball shows in order, settle the Z versus Kai question, and sort the canon movies from the fun detours. We also flag where to stream everything. Sort the order once and the biggest action franchise in anime opens up without the guesswork.

How to watch Dragon Ball in order: the series

The franchise is built from a handful of TV series, and only some are canon. New fans keep asking the same thing: what order do I watch Dragon Ball, or how do I watch Dragon Ball in order without the non-canon detours. This table lays out every Dragon Ball show with its status marked, so the essential path is clear.

ShowYearsEpisodesStatus
Dragon Ball1986-1989153Canon, start here
Dragon Ball Z1989-1996291Canon, the classic run (heavy filler)
Dragon Ball Z Kai2009-2015167Canon, the trimmed remake of Z
Dragon Ball GT1996-199764Non-canon, optional
Dragon Ball Super2015-2018131Canon, the main sequel
Dragon Ball Daima2024-202520Canon, set during the Z era
Super Dragon Ball Heroes2018-202456Non-canon promo, skippable

For a first watch, the clean canon order is Dragon Ball, then Kai (or Z), then Super, then Daima. That is how to watch Dragon Ball in order at the canon level, and everything else is optional. Daima aired most recently but is set back during the Z era, so you can also slot it in right before Super for a strict in-universe timeline. GT is a non-canon alternate ending to save for last or skip, and Super Dragon Ball Heroes is a promotional spin-off you can ignore.

Dragon Ball Z or Dragon Ball Z Kai?

The first real decision is Z or Kai. Dragon Ball Z is the original 291-episode run, famous for filler: long stretches of stalling and side quests that pad the manga's story out. Dragon Ball Z Kai is the 2009 remaster that cuts most of that, tightens the pacing, and sticks close to the manga at around 167 episodes.

For a first watch, we would go with Kai. It tells the same story with far less waiting, which matters a lot across a run this long. Watch full Z instead if you want the complete nostalgic experience, filler included, since some of that filler is beloved. If you do take on Z and want to know exactly what to skip, our Dragon Ball Z filler list marks every episode, and the original series has its own padding covered in our Dragon Ball filler list. This is the biggest single choice in how to watch Dragon Ball in order.

GT, the movies, and what counts as canon

Two things sit outside the main series and confuse people. The first is Dragon Ball GT. The anime made it without Akira Toriyama's manga, so it runs in its own alternate timeline and is not canon. Plenty of fans still enjoy it for Super Saiyan 4 and its ending, so treat it as an optional what-if to watch after everything else, or skip.

The second is the movies. Dragon Ball has more than twenty films, and most are non-canon side adventures you can watch any time for fun. Only four count as canon: Battle of Gods and Resurrection F, whose events Super later retells, then Dragon Ball Super: Broly and Dragon Ball Super: Super Hero, which continue the story after Super's finale. Watch Broly after Super episode 131, then Super Hero after that. Super itself has a little filler too, flagged in our Dragon Ball Super filler list, though far less than old Z.

Where to watch Dragon Ball

Dragon Ball is widely available. Crunchyroll carries the whole main lineup in most regions, from the original series through Z, Kai, GT, Super, and Daima, in sub and dub, while the movies live across streaming and digital storefronts. Netflix also hosts parts of the franchise in some countries. Availability shifts by region, so check what is live where you are before you start the marathon.

For a franchise this old and this large, how to watch Dragon Ball in order comes down to a short canon path: Dragon Ball, then Kai (or Z), then Super, then Daima, with GT as an optional detour and only four movies you truly need. Pick Kai if you want speed or full Z if you want everything, save GT for a curious rewatch, and let Goku's four-decade journey play out in sequence. Start at the very first episode and go from there.

Content:
Made in Abyss looks simple to start and then trips people at one specific spot. The Made in Abyss watch order is short: Season 1, then the movie Dawn of the Deep Soul, then Season 2. That is the entire core, three pieces in a straight line. The catch is that two of the franchise's other films are recaps of Season 1 rather than new story, so knowing which movie actually matters is the whole game here.

The one mistake new viewers make is skipping Dawn of the Deep Soul. It looks like an optional side film, but it is essential canon that bridges the two seasons, covering the Idofront descent and everything Bondrewd sets in motion. Season 2 assumes you have seen it, so jumping straight from Season 1 to Season 2 leaves a gaping hole in the story.

One heads-up before you descend: Made in Abyss pairs an adorable art style with genuinely brutal, disturbing content, so treat it as mature viewing. Below we lay out the Made in Abyss anime in order, sort the recap films from the essential sequel, and point you to where it streams. Get the order right and one of anime's most haunting adventures unfolds exactly as intended.

The Made in Abyss watch order

The whole franchise is only six releases, and half of them are optional. The recap films and the one movie you cannot skip

Three Made in Abyss movies exist, and they are not equal. Journey's Dawn (2019) and Wandering Twilight (2019) are compilation films that re-cut Season 1 into two features, with a few minutes of new animation each. They tell the same story you already get from the series, just compressed, so most viewers skip them. They only make sense as a faster substitute for Season 1 on a rewatch, never as something to watch after it.

Dawn of the Deep Soul (2020) is the opposite. It is a full sequel film with entirely new story, and it is the true bridge between the two seasons. It adapts the Idofront arc, delivers some of the franchise's heaviest emotional turns, and sets up the exact situation Season 2 opens in. Treat it as canon episodes in movie form, not as a bonus. The one rule that matters: watch Dawn of the Deep Soul before Season 2, every time.

For a franchise with only a handful of pieces, the Made in Abyss watch order is easy once the trap is clear: Season 1, then Dawn of the Deep Soul, then Season 2, with the recap films safe to skip. Watch the essential film where it belongs, brace yourself for how dark the Abyss gets, and let one of the most beautiful and devastating stories in anime pull you all the way down. Only one of them. Dawn of the Deep Soul is essential and must be watched between the two seasons. The other two films, Journey's Dawn and Wandering Twilight, are just recaps of Season 1, so they are optional and most viewers skip them.

You can, but only as a shortcut. Journey's Dawn and Wandering Twilight compress Season 1 into two films with minor new footage, so they work if you are short on time or rewatching. The series tells the story with far more room to breathe, so it is the better first experience.

Content:

Roughly 160 of the original 366 episodes are anime-only, padded in while the manga caught up, and four big stretches are pure filler you can pass on without losing the plot. Thousand-Year Blood War: the finale

The Bleach movies (are they canon?)

Content:
Gundam looks like the most intimidating franchise in anime, and newcomers usually ask the wrong question first. There is no single Gundam watch order, because Gundam is not one story. The real question is not what order to watch Gundam in, but which series to start with, and we would point most newcomers to The Witch from Mercury.

The scale is real. Gundam has run since 1979 across more than forty TV series, films, and OVAs, which is why it feels like homework. Those productions are grouped into separate universes, each with its own war and its own cast. Cosmic Era does not connect to After Colony, and you never need one to enjoy another.

There is no one Gundam series order to memorize, only timelines to choose from. Only the Universal Century runs in sequence, its series building on each other across decades. Below we sort out where to start, map every timeline, and lay out the Universal Century in the order to watch it.

Where to start: the best Gundam beginner picks

The best starting point depends on how much you care about modern animation. For most newcomers, we would begin with a recent standalone series, since they need no prior knowledge and look sharp. The Witch from Mercury (2022) is the easiest on-ramp of all, a complete two-cour story with a fresh lead and a school-meets-mecha hook that pulls people in fast. Right behind it sit Iron-Blooded Orphans (2015) for something grittier, Gundam 00 (2007) for a modern-feeling war drama, and Gundam SEED (2002) for the classic that converted a generation.

If you would rather start where the franchise began, the Universal Century is the backbone, and we cover its order below. Just know that the 1979 original shows its age, so plenty of newcomers bounce off it. Beginning with a modern standalone, then circling back to the Universal Century once you are hooked, tends to work far better than forcing yourself through the oldest one cold.

The Gundam timelines at a glance

The whole franchise sorts into a handful of timelines, each its own universe with no required reading, which is why the Gundam watch order comes down to choosing where to start. You can watch them in any order, so pick whichever setting sounds most like your kind of story.

The Universal Century watch order

The Universal Century is the one part of the Gundam watch order that truly runs in sequence, a single sprawling history from UC 0079 onward. For a first watch, production order works best, since it follows how the story was built and spares you jarring jumps in animation quality. Where to watch Gundam

Pick a universe and pilot in

For all its size, the Gundam watch order is freeing once the secret clicks: there is no single path, because each timeline stands alone. Start with a modern standalone like The Witch from Mercury, branch into whatever universe grabs you next, and save the deep Universal Century run for when you want the franchise's full history. There is no wrong door into Gundam, only the one that gets you piloting soonest.

Title: One Piece Watch Order: Every Saga, Movie, and Special in Order
Summary: Map the complete One Piece watch order across all eleven sagas and every one of the fifteen films. ⚓
Meta Title: One Piece Watch Order: Every Saga and Movie
Meta Description: Follow the One Piece watch order saga by saga, with every movie matched to the arc it fits. Get more anime watch order picks from Kaminari.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
One Piece scares people off with its size, not its structure. The One Piece watch order is refreshingly simple: start at episode 1 and watch straight through. It is one continuous story told across roughly eleven sagas and more than 1,140 episodes, from the East Blue to the current Egghead arc, with the fifteen movies as optional side adventures. Watching in order is straightforward, so the length is the only real hurdle.

Two things complicate an otherwise clean run. First, One Piece has filler, the anime-only episodes Toei adds to stay ahead of the manga, much of it skippable. Second, the fifteen movies and dozens of TV specials do not announce where they belong, since most are non-canon side stories set at fuzzy points in the timeline. Neither is a real obstacle once you know the map.

Below we lay out the full saga roadmap, every movie and when to watch it, and how to handle the filler and specials without losing momentum. We also cover the manga shortcut for anyone who wants to move faster. Learn how to watch One Piece in order once and anime's greatest adventure is yours for hundreds of hours.

The One Piece watch order by saga

This is the full One Piece anime watching order, broken into eleven sagas, each made of several arcs. You do not need to track them to watch in sequence, since it is all one line, but they make a useful map of the journey. Episode ranges are approximate, especially for the ongoing final saga.

SagaEpisodesWhat happens
East Blue1-61Luffy forms the crew and enters the Grand Line
Alabasta62-135Baroque Works, Vivi, and the desert kingdom
Sky Island136-206The Straw Hats sail up to Skypiea
Water 7207-325Robin's past and the raid on Enies Lobby
Thriller Bark326-384A haunted ship, and Brook joins
Summit War385-516Sabaody, Impel Down, and the war at Marineford
Fish-Man Island517-574The crew reunites and dives below
Dressrosa575-746Punk Hazard into the fall of Doflamingo
Whole Cake Island747-889Sanji, Big Mom, and a wedding gone wrong
Wano Country890-1085The samurai land and the raid on Kaido
Final Saga1086-presentEgghead and the road to the ending

That is the entire spine of the One Piece watch order. Watch it in that sequence and every reveal lands where it should. The sagas only exist to break a huge story into chapters you can plan around.

Every One Piece movie, and where it fits

Fifteen One Piece movies exist, and almost all of them are non-canon, standalone adventures you can watch whenever you like. We have matched each one to the point in the story you would watch it after, based on which crew members and powers show up. A few carry more weight than the rest, since Eiichiro Oda wrote Strong World and had a hand in Film Z, Stampede, and Film Red, so those four are the ones to prioritize.

TitleYearWatch after
One Piece: The Movie2000the East Blue saga
Clockwork Island Adventure2001the East Blue saga
Chopper's Kingdom on the Island of Strange Animals2002the Alabasta saga
Dead End Adventure2003the Alabasta saga
The Cursed Holy Sword2004the Alabasta saga
Baron Omatsuri and the Secret Island2005the Water 7 saga
The Giant Mechanical Soldier of Karakuri Castle2006the Water 7 saga
Episode of Alabasta2007the Alabasta saga (it retells it)
Episode of Chopper Plus2008the Drum Island arc (it retells it)

Straw Hat Chase2011the timeskip
Film Z2012the Fish-Man Island saga
Film Gold2016the Dressrosa saga
Stampede2019the Wano saga
Film Red2022the Wano saga

If you would rather not watch all fifteen, stick to Strong World, Film Z, Stampede, and Film Red for the best of the bunch. Baron Omatsuri and the Secret Island is also worth a look for its strange, darker tone, a cult favorite among longtime fans. That covers how to watch One Piece in order including movies, each one matched to the arc you watch it after.

Filler, specials, and the manga shortcut

One Piece runs with more filler than most modern shonen, roughly a tenth of the episodes, and most of it is safe to skip. The filler arcs sit between canon arcs and do not touch the main plot, so you can pass on them without confusion. The one exception fans point to is the G-8 arc (episodes 196 to 206), an anime-original stretch after Skypiea that many rank among the best filler in any series. For the full breakdown of what to skip and what to keep, our One Piece filler list marks every episode.

Then there are the specials. One Piece has dozens of TV specials, OVAs, and shorts, and the honest truth is that most are recap episodes or light side stories you can skip entirely. A handful are fun after the matching arc, like the Episode of retellings and the acclaimed 2024 Fan Letter special, and a 2024 remaster of the Fish-Man Island saga re-edits that arc into its own run. None of it is required to follow the story.

If the filler and the sheer length are wearing you down, the manga is the shortcut. It has no filler and stays ahead of the anime, so plenty of fans read the arcs they want to rush and watch the ones they want to savor. On the anime side, the sub stays current with Japan while the dub trails behind, so watchers chasing the newest episodes tend to go subbed.

Where to watch One Piece

Crunchyroll is the main home for One Piece, carrying the run in both sub and dub, though the latest episodes land subbed first. Netflix also hosts large chunks of the series in many regions, which helps if you are working through the early sagas. The movies are scattered across streaming and digital storefronts, so availability depends on where you live. One note to avoid confusion: the Netflix live-action One Piece from 2023 is a separate adaptation, not part of the anime watch order covered here.

Set sail from episode one

For all its intimidating size, the One Piece watch order comes down to one instruction: begin at episode 1 and follow the sagas in sequence, from the East Blue to Egghead. Slot the movies in beside the arcs they match, skip the filler you do not want (G-8 aside), and lean on the manga whenever you feel like moving faster. It is a massive commitment, but it is also the richest adventure the medium has, and there is no wrong time to raise the sails.
