FAQ

What is the One Piece watch order?

The One Piece watch order is simple: watch the anime from episode 1 in sequence, following the sagas from East Blue through the current Egghead arc. The correct order to watch One Piece is just that, one continuous story of over 1,140 episodes, with the fifteen movies as optional side adventures you can add whenever you like.

Do I need to watch the One Piece movies?

No. Almost every One Piece movie is a non-canon standalone story that does not affect the main plot. They are fun extras rather than required viewing, though Strong World, Film Z, Stampede, and Film Red stand out as the ones most worth your time if you only watch a few.

Can I skip the filler in One Piece?

Yes. Most One Piece filler sits between canon arcs and does not touch the main story, so skipping it costs you nothing. The G-8 arc after Skypiea is the one filler stretch many fans recommend keeping. A filler guide makes it easy to see exactly which episodes to pass on.

Should I read the manga instead of watching the anime?

It depends on your patience. The manga has no filler and moves faster, so it is the better pick if the anime's pacing frustrates you. Many fans do both, reading ahead through slower stretches and watching the big arcs animated. Neither is wrong, and both tell the same story.

Where can I watch One Piece?

Crunchyroll streams One Piece in sub and dub and carries the newest episodes, while Netflix hosts large portions in many regions. The movies are spread across various platforms. Availability changes by region, so check what is live near you before you set off.

Title: Berserk Watch Order: Every Anime, Movie, and Where the Manga Takes Over
Summary: Break down the full Berserk watch order, all three Golden Age versions and where the manga takes over. ⚔️
Meta Title: Berserk Watch Order: Anime, Movies, and Manga
Meta Description: Settle the Berserk watch order question by picking one Golden Age version, then the rest in line. Discover more anime guides at Kaminari.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Berserk has a reputation as one of the most confusing franchises to start, and it is half deserved. The story order is straightforward, but the same opening arc got animated three separate times. The clean path: pick one version of the Golden Age arc, watch Berserk (2016), then Berserk (2017), and move to the manga for everything after. That is the whole Berserk watch order once you cut the noise.

The three Golden Age adaptations are where people trip. The classic 1997 series, the 2012 to 2013 film trilogy, and the 2022 Memorial Edition all tell the same story of Guts, Griffith, and the Band of the Hawk, just with different animation and completeness. The CGI-heavy 2016 series then continues from the films, not the 1997 anime, the single most common mix-up in the fandom.

Below we lay out every adaptation at a glance, then the one real choice of which Golden Age to watch. One heads-up before you dive in, Berserk is bleak and extremely graphic, so treat it as mature viewing. Work out how to watch Berserk in order and one of the greatest dark fantasy stories ever drawn is yours.

The recommended Berserk watch order

The whole Berserk watch order at a glance, animated releases only. Five of the seven cover the same Golden Age arc, so you are choosing between those rather than watching all five.

TitleTypeYearWhat it covers
Berserk (1997)TV, 25 eps1997-1998The Golden Age arc, the classic version
Golden Age Arc I: The Egg of the KingFilm2012The Golden Age, part one
Golden Age Arc II: The Battle for DoldreyFilm2012The Golden Age, part two
Golden Age Arc III: The AdventFilm2013The Golden Age, part three, the full Eclipse
Golden Age Arc: Memorial EditionTV, 13 eps2022A re-edit of the three films, the easiest to find
Berserk (2016)TV, 12 eps2016Black Swordsman and Conviction arcs
Berserk (2017)TV, 12 eps2017Hawk of the Millennium Empire arc

For the fullest experience, we would watch Berserk (1997) first for its atmosphere, then the Memorial Edition (or the original films) for the complete Eclipse, then Berserk (2016) and (2017) for the story past that point. If watching the Golden Age twice sounds like a slog, take the short path: start with the Memorial Edition or the films, then go straight into 2016 and 2017. Both routes land in the same spot, facing the same truth. No anime has ever finished Berserk, so the manga is where the story continues.

Watch the 1997 classic, or start with the films?

The 1997 series is the version most longtime fans hold closest. It captures the doomed friendship at the heart of the Golden Age better than any other adaptation, though it sits in a separate continuity and its Eclipse is cut short. The film trilogy and the Memorial Edition tell that same arc with a fuller, far more graphic Eclipse, and they are the official lead-in the 2016 series follows.

For the definitive mood, start with 1997, then let the Memorial Edition fill in the complete Eclipse before continuing. For one clean line with no repeated story, skip 1997 and begin with the Memorial Edition, which is easier to find than the increasingly rare films and adds a few new scenes. Neither choice is wrong. It only changes how much of the Golden Age you watch, not what order to watch Berserk in after the Eclipse.

Continuing past the Eclipse: 2016, 2017, and the manga

Once the Golden Age ends, the only anime continuation is the 2016 and 2017 series, and it comes with an asterisk. The switch to CGI was divisive, and it is fair to say the animation has not aged gracefully, with stiff movement that pulls you out of some big moments. What the two seasons get right is the story: they follow Guts as the Black Swordsman through the Conviction and Millennium Empire arcs faithfully, and for plenty of fans the material carries the rough visuals. If you can meet it halfway, it is worth watching to see those arcs animated at all.

No anime has adapted the whole of Berserk, and none is coming. To continue past where 2017 stops, you read the manga, which is where the series has always been strongest. Kentaro Miura passed away in 2021, and the manga now continues under Kouji Mori and Studio Gaga. Treat the anime as your on-ramp and read the manga for the rest.

Where to watch Berserk

Streaming is scattered, fittingly. The 1997 series, the 2016 and 2017 seasons, and the Memorial Edition tend to move between Crunchyroll and other platforms depending on your region, and the older film trilogy can be tricky to find at all now that the Memorial Edition has largely replaced it. Check what is live where you are before you plan your run, since availability shifts often for this franchise.

Face the Eclipse in the right order

For a franchise this tangled, the Berserk watch order comes down to a simple decision and a straight line after it: choose your Golden Age (the 1997 classic, the films, or the Memorial Edition), then watch Berserk (2016) and Berserk (2017), then pick up the manga for everything the anime never reached. That is how to watch Berserk in order without drowning in duplicate arcs or missing the true continuation. Steel yourself, because it is a brutal ride, but it is also one of the most powerful stories the medium has ever produced.

FAQ

What is the Berserk watch order?

The core Berserk watch order is one Golden Age adaptation, then Berserk (2016), then Berserk (2017), then the manga. For the fullest run, watch the 1997 series and the Golden Age Memorial Edition before 2016. For a shorter one, pick just the Memorial Edition or the films, then continue into 2016 and 2017.

Do I need to watch the 1997 Berserk anime?

Not strictly. The 1997 series and the Golden Age films cover the same arc, so you can watch either one. The 1997 version has the best atmosphere, while the Memorial Edition and films show a more complete Eclipse and lead directly into the 2016 series. Watch 1997 if you want the classic, or skip it if you would rather not repeat the Golden Age.

Is Berserk 2016 a sequel to the 1997 anime?

No, and this is the most common mix-up. Berserk (2016) is a sequel to the 2012 to 2013 Golden Age film trilogy, not to the 1997 TV series, even though the films and the 1997 anime tell the same underlying story. In practice, any Golden Age version leads into 2016 well enough.

Where does the manga pick up after the anime?

The manga is the only complete version of Berserk and goes far beyond where the anime stops. The 2017 season ends partway through the later arcs, and the manga carries on well past that point. After Kentaro Miura's passing in 2021, it has continued under Kouji Mori and Studio Gaga.

Where can I watch Berserk?

The 1997 series, the 2016 and 2017 seasons, and the Memorial Edition move between Crunchyroll and other platforms depending on your region, while the original film trilogy is harder to find since the Memorial Edition replaced it. Check what is streaming near you before you start.

Title: My Hero Academia Watch Order: Every Season, Movie, and OVA in Order
Summary: Map the full My Hero Academia watch order across all eight seasons and every movie's best placement. ⚡
Meta Title: My Hero Academia Watch Order: Every Season, Movie
Meta Description: Follow the My Hero Academia watch order across all eight seasons, with four movies slotted in. Follow Kaminari for more watch order breakdowns.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
My Hero Academia is one of the easiest big shonen to jump into, and the My Hero Academia watch order is a big reason why. Seasons 1 through 8 run in a straight line, so you watch them in plain number order, from Deku's first day at UA to the final war. The only real thinking is where to drop the four movies, and honestly, they are optional side trips.

The reason MHA even has a watch-order question is the extras. Four theatrical movies, a stack of short OVAs, and a prequel spin-off called Vigilantes all orbit the main series, and none slot into an obvious place. The good news is that every one is optional, so you can weave them in or leave them out without losing the core story.

Below we lay out the full lineup at a glance, then the one choice worth making: pure release order or the best order that tucks each movie into its ideal spot. We flag which extras earn your time, which to skip, and where it all streams. Sort that out once and one of the most rewatchable shonen of the decade is yours.

The recommended My Hero Academia watch order

Here is the whole franchise in one place, the eight core seasons up top and the optional movies and extras below. Across those seasons you are looking at roughly 179 episodes, somewhere around 65 to 70 hours, plus four films if you want them. It is a long ride, so most people take it a season at a time rather than in one sitting.

EntryTypeYearWhere it fits
My Hero Academia, Seasons 1 to 8TV, ~179 eps2016-2025Core, watch in number order
My Hero Academia: Two HeroesFilm2018After Season 2
My Hero Academia: Heroes RisingFilm2019After Season 4
My Hero Academia: World Heroes' MissionFilm2021After Season 5
My Hero Academia: You're NextFilm2024After Season 7
OVAs (various shorts)OVA2016-2023Optional, skip on a first watch
My Hero Academia: VigilantesTV spin-off2025Optional prequel, watch anytime

The seasons are the easy part, since they run in order with barely a hiccup. Season 6 is the turning point, where the Paranormal Liberation War tips the whole story into its darker back half, and the Final Season in 2025 carries that straight through to the ending. Everything below the season row is a bonus. The four movies are self-contained adventures, the OVAs are light side stories, and Vigilantes is a street-level prequel you can enjoy whenever the mood strikes.

Release order or best order (where the movies fit)?

Here is the only real fork, and it comes down to the four movies. Release order is the simplest path: watch the seasons as they aired and catch each film around the time it came out. It works fine, because none of the movies are required to follow the plot. The best order just nudges those films into the spots where they make the most sense in the story.

Our recommended placements are simple. Two Heroes fits neatly after Season 2, Heroes Rising lands best after Season 4, World Heroes' Mission slots in after Season 5, and You're Next works well after Season 7. Every one of these is a standalone side story with the main cast, canon-adjacent but self-contained, so the exact placement is forgiving. Watch them where we suggest, save them all for the end, or skip them entirely, and the core My Hero Academia watch order still holds together.

As for the OVAs and a strict chronological order, we would not sweat either on a first watch. The short OVAs are fun bonuses that sit between seasons, easy to save for a rewatch. A chronological cut barely differs from release order here, since MHA runs with almost no filler and adapts the manga closely, which we broke down episode by episode in the My Hero Academia filler list. For most people, seasons in order with the movies tucked in is the smoothest way through.

Where to watch My Hero Academia

Streaming is refreshingly simple for a series this size. Crunchyroll carries every season of My Hero Academia, both subbed and dubbed, so the whole main run lives under one roof. The four movies are on Crunchyroll and the major digital storefronts in most regions. Availability shifts from country to country, so check what is live where you are before you settle in for the long haul.

Plus Ultra, from the first day to the final war

For a franchise this big, the My Hero Academia watch order is about as friendly as they come: Seasons 1 through 8 in number order, with the four movies dropped in after Seasons 2, 4, 5, and 7 if you want the extra adventures. Skip the OVAs on your first pass, save Vigilantes for whenever you are curious about hero society's rougher edges, and let Deku's climb from quirkless kid to Symbol of Peace play out the way it was built to. Start at Season 1 and the whole ride opens up in front of you.

FAQ

What is the My Hero Academia watch order?

The My Hero Academia watch order is Seasons 1 through 8 in number order, with the four movies optional along the way: Two Heroes after Season 2, Heroes Rising after Season 4, World Heroes' Mission after Season 5, and You're Next after Season 7. The seasons carry the full story, so the films and OVAs are bonuses rather than requirements.

Do I need to watch the My Hero Academia movies?

No. Two Heroes, Heroes Rising, World Heroes' Mission, and You're Next are standalone side stories that do not change the main plot. They are well animated and fun, so they are worth folding in if you love the series, but you can skip them without missing anything essential.

Should I watch My Hero Academia in release order or chronological order?

Release order is the easy choice, and it barely differs from chronological here, since MHA adapts the manga closely with almost no filler. The only real adjustment a chronological watch makes is slotting the movies into their story spots, which is exactly what our recommended order above already does.

Should I watch My Hero Academia: Vigilantes?

Only if you want more. Vigilantes is a prequel spin-off about street-level heroes years before Deku reaches UA, and it is optional. It plays as a companion piece rather than a required chapter, so watch it whenever you are in the mood for a grittier side of hero society.

Crunchyroll streams every season of My Hero Academia in both sub and dub, and the four movies are available there and on major digital storefronts in most regions. Availability changes by region, so check what is streaming near you before you start.

Title: Steins;Gate Watch Order: The Series, the Movie, and Steins;Gate 0 in Order
Summary: Cover the entire Steins;Gate watch order: the original series, the movie, the OVAs, and Steins;Gate 0. ⏳
Meta Title: Steins;Gate Watch Order: Series, Movie, and 0
Meta Description: Follow the Steins;Gate watch order so Steins;Gate 0 lands last and never spoils the original. Visit Kaminari for more anime watch order content.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Steins;Gate looks intimidating on a list: a sequel series, a movie, an alternate episode, a scatter of OVAs. It is far simpler than it looks. For a first watch, the Steins;Gate watch order is the original 24-episode series first, then Steins;Gate 0, with the movie and OVAs as optional stops in between. That is the entire core. The only rule that truly matters is that Steins;Gate 0 comes last, never first.

The one wrinkle worth knowing early is Steins;Gate 0 itself. It is not a normal sequel. It follows the worldline where Okabe fails, the dark branch the original series only hints at, so watching it before you finish the original guts the emotional payoff of both. That is why the sequence matters more than the short entry list suggests.

Below you get the full lineup at a glance, then the real choice every fan faces: the simple release order or the ideal interleaved order that the hardcore swear by, including where that infamous alternate episode 23 slots in. Sort out how to watch Steins;Gate once and one of the best sci-fi stories anime has produced is a single weekend away.

The recommended Steins;Gate watch order

Here is how to watch Steins;Gate in order at a glance, the two core entries up top and the optional extras below. The core is a lean 47 episodes, right around 19 hours, and everything animated together lands near 21. For a franchise this beloved, that is a bargain.

EntryTypeYearWhere it fits
Steins;GateTV, 24 eps2011Core, start here
Steins;Gate 0TV, 23 eps2018Core, watch last, never first
Episode 23β: Divide By ZeroTV special2015Optional on-ramp into Steins;Gate 0
Egoistic PoriomaniaOVA, ep 252012Optional epilogue after the original
The Movie: Load Region of Déjà VuFilm2013Optional coda, set after the original
Steins;Gate 0: Valentine's of Crystal PolymorphismOVA2018Optional bonus, once you know the 0 cast
Cognitive Computing (IBM shorts)ONA shorts2014Non-essential promo, skip

The rule to tattoo on your brain: finish the original Steins;Gate before you touch Steins;Gate 0. The original earns an ending that 0 quietly leans on, and flipping the two robs both of their weight. Everything below the core rows is a bonus. The movie is a lovely coda, the OVAs are light extras, and the IBM shorts are a promotional curiosity you can pass on without a second thought.

The simple order or the ideal order?

Here is the choice that splits the fandom over what order to watch Steins;Gate in, and neither answer is wrong. The simple order is plain release order: watch the original Steins;Gate straight through, all 24 episodes, add the movie and the Egoistic Poriomania OVA if you want them, then move on to Steins;Gate 0. It keeps the original's slow-burn pacing and its gut-punch of an ending fully intact, which is exactly why it is the order I would hand a first-timer.

The ideal order is the one longtime fans get misty about. You watch the original up to episode 22, swap in the alternate Episode 23β (Divide By Zero), then play all of Steins;Gate 0 before returning to finish the original's true ending. Done this way, you live through the dark worldline at the precise moment the story branches, so the finale hits with everything the writers loaded into it. It is more work, and it means holding off on the original's payoff, so I would save it for people who already know they love this story, or for a second run. Both roads end in the same place, and both keep Steins;Gate 0 in its rightful spot rather than first.

A quick word on the movie and chronological order, since people always ask. Load Region of Déjà Vu is set about a year after the original's ending, a warm coda focused on Okabe and Kurisu, and it slots comfortably after the original or after Steins;Gate 0. As for a strict Steins;Gate chronological order, the branching worldlines make a single clean timeline impossible, which is rather the point of the show. Should I watch Steins;Gate 0 before or after the original series?

Do I need to watch the Steins;Gate movie?

Title: A Certain Magical Index Watch Order: Every Season & Movie in Order
Summary: Map the full A Certain Magical Index watch order, blending Index and Railgun into one clean line. ⚡

Meta Description: Untangle the A Certain Magical Index watch order across both the magic side and the science side. Stop by Kaminari for more guides like this.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
A Certain Magical Index has a reputation for being a scheduling nightmare, and this time it is fair. The good news: the A Certain Magical Index watch order has one clean path once it is laid out. For a first watch, go Index, then A Certain Scientific Railgun, Index II, the Miracle of Endymion movie, Railgun S, Accelerator, Railgun T, and finally Index III. That is the entire core, in the order that makes the story hit hardest.

The tangle comes from two shows sharing one city. Index follows Touma, a boy whose right hand cancels any power, through the magic side of Academy City. Railgun hands the lead to Mikoto Misaka for the science side, the espers and the politics that run it. The two shows sit on overlapping timelines and keep crossing paths.

So here is how to watch A Certain Magical Index in order without losing the thread: the full lineup at a glance, the two questions every newcomer asks, and where it all streams. One quirk to flag up front, the grand finale actually aired years before two of the seasons that were built to set it up.

The recommended A Certain Magical Index watch order

Here is the whole franchise in one place, core seasons up top and the optional extras below. Eight core entries, a little over 160 episodes, split across the magic side and the science side but telling one connected story.

EntryTypeYearWhere it fits
A Certain Magical IndexTV, 24 eps2008-2009Core, start here
A Certain Scientific RailgunTV, 24 eps2009-2010Core, the science side begins
A Certain Magical Index IITV, 24 eps2010-2011Core
A Certain Magical Index: The Miracle of EndymionFilm2013Core, canon movie
A Certain Scientific Railgun STV, 24 eps2013Core
A Certain Scientific AcceleratorTV, 12 eps2019Core, swappable with Railgun T
A Certain Scientific Railgun TTV, 25 eps2020Core
A Certain Magical Index IIITV, 26 eps2018-2019Core, the finale, watch last
Railgun and Railgun S OVAsOVA2010, 2013Optional side stories
A Certain Magical Index-tan (chibi shorts)ShortsvariousNon-canon parody, skip

The one rule you cannot break: A Certain Magical Index III goes last. It aired back in 2018 and 2019, before both Accelerator and Railgun T, but it is the chronological climax of the whole franchise, so saving it for the end keeps the biggest payoff where it belongs. Accelerator and Railgun T sit close together in the timeline, and you can swap them without hurting a thing. Everything above the OVA rows is essential, and the extras are there only if you want to linger in Academy City a little longer.

Index first or Railgun first?

Here is the first real fork, and it is the one people argue about most. A Certain Magical Index came first and builds the world from the ground up, so it is the natural front door. A Certain Scientific Railgun is technically the spin-off, but it looks sharper, moves faster, and Misaka is one of the most loved leads in the medium, which makes it a tempting place to begin.

My honest read: start with Index. Touma's story explains the rules of Academy City and the magic side that everything else leans on, and Railgun quietly assumes you have picked some of that up. Index does open dense, though, and if the heavy magic lore has you bouncing off, starting with Railgun is a completely fair gateway. You meet Misaka first, fall for the science side, then double back to Touma once you are hooked. Neither choice breaks the story, so pick the entry point that keeps you watching.

Release order or chronological order?

The question of what order to watch A Certain Magical Index in usually comes down to two camps. Release order (the blended path at the top of this guide) is the one I recommend for a first watch, because the reveals were written to land in that sequence and the pacing feels deliberate. Chronological order rearranges everything into strict in-universe time, cutting between Index and Railgun arc by arc. It makes for a fascinating rewatch once you already know the story, but for a newcomer it is fiddly and easy to lose your place in.

There is a third option worth knowing about. If hopping between two casts bugs you, watch by series instead: all of Index, then all of Railgun, or the reverse. You stay with one protagonist the whole way, at the cost of some cross-series timing. Plenty of fans swear by it. For most people, though, the blended release order up top is the smoothest first trip through.

Where to watch A Certain Magical Index

Streaming is simpler than the watch order, at least. Crunchyroll is the main home for the whole franchise now that the old Funimation library has folded into it, so Index, Railgun, Accelerator, and the movie mostly live under one roof. Regional availability still shifts around, so check what is live in your country before you settle in. None of that changes the sequence, only where each piece happens to stream.

Untangle it once, then just enjoy Academy City

For a franchise that looks like a genuine mess from the outside, the A Certain Magical Index watch order really does reduce to one clean line: Index, Railgun, Index II, the Endymion movie, Railgun S, Accelerator, Railgun T, and Index III to close it out. Start with Index for the foundation, save Index III for the finale it was built to be, and let the two sides of Academy City weave together the way they were meant to. Sort the order once and one of the most ambitious worlds in anime opens right up, no notebook required.

Not strictly. Index works on its own for the main plot, and you can follow Touma's story without Railgun. You will miss a lot of Misaka's development and the fuller version of the shared Sisters arc, though, so Railgun is well worth folding in rather than skipping.

Release order for a first watch. The reveals and pacing were designed around it, so it plays smoother. Chronological order interleaves the series by in-universe time and makes a great rewatch, but it is fiddly for newcomers and easier to get lost in.

Title: Sword Art Online Watch Order: Every Season, Movie, and Spin-Off
Summary: Cover the complete Sword Art Online watch order, all five core titles plus where the spin-offs fit. ⚔️
Meta Title: Sword Art Online Watch Order: Every Season, Movie
Meta Description: Follow the Sword Art Online watch order across five core titles and a real, complete ending. Catch more anime watch orders over at Kaminari.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Ask around about Sword Art Online and you get whiplash: one half calls it the show that shaped modern isekai, the other treats it as the genre's punching bag. Here is what nobody leads with: the Sword Art Online watch order is the easy part. For a first watch, go in release order: Sword Art Online, Sword Art Online II, the Ordinal Scale movie, Alicization, and finally War of Underworld. That is the whole core, around 40 hours with a real ending.

At its core, SAO traps players inside a VR game where logging out is impossible and dying in the game means dying for real. The show keeps reinventing that hook across new worlds for years, which is what makes the franchise look bigger and scarier than it really is: four seasons, a movie, a spin-off, and two retellings.

Most of that pile is optional, though, and the spine is short. Below you get the full franchise at a glance, the one fork worth debating, an honest read on which arcs earn the hype and which to sit through, and where each piece streams.

The Sword Art Online watch order at a glance

Here is the whole franchise in one place, core and extras together. The five core entries are the ones you watch in release order for the main story. Everything below them is optional, there for when you want more.

EntryTypeYearWhere it fits
Sword Art OnlineTV, 25 eps2012-2013Core, start here
Sword Art Online IITV, 24 eps2014Core
Sword Art Online: Ordinal ScaleFilm2017Core, canon, do not skip
Sword Art Online: AlicizationTV, 24 eps2018-2019Core
Alicization: War of UnderworldTV, 23 eps2019-2020Core, the finale
Sword Art Online: Extra EditionRecap special2013Optional refresher before season two
Alternative: Gun Gale OnlineTV, 12 eps2018Spin-off, standalone, optional
Gun Gale Online IITV, 12 eps2024Spin-off, optional
Progressive: Aria of a Starless NightFilm2021Optional Aincrad retelling
Progressive: Scherzo of Deep NightFilm2022Optional Aincrad retelling

The core main line is four TV seasons and one canon film, close to 100 Sword Art Online episodes and around 40 hours, all animated by A-1 Pictures, so the look never jolts on you. Each block has its own personality, too. Aincrad is the survival hook that made the show famous, a floating castle where a game over is permanent. ALfheim trades the dread for winged fantasy adventure. The Phantom Bullet arc swaps swords for firearms and a colder edge. Alicization throws all of it out and reaches for a genuinely huge, ambitious epic. Same franchise, four very different moods.

Wait, the death game ends at episode 14?

Here is the twist that catches almost everyone off guard, and I wish someone had told me sooner. The death game everybody shows up for, the trapped-in-Aincrad nightmare where dying in the game kills you for real, wraps up at episode 14. The back half of that first season jumps to a brand new world called ALfheim for what fans call the Fairy Dance arc, and the tonal change is steep. You go from white-knuckle survival to a fairy-winged rescue story almost overnight.

It is where SAO picks up a lot of its "it fell off" reputation, and I understand why. Fairy Dance is a clear step down from the highs of Aincrad, and it leans on a few choices the fandom still grumbles about. It is also fully canon, it carries important characters and plot threads into everything that follows, and skipping it will leave you lost later. Going in already knowing that Aincrad ends early is the real fix, because then the shift reads like a new chapter instead of a bait and switch.

If you want the granular version of what is and is not safe to trim, I mapped every episode in the Sword Art Online filler list, and the short answer is that the show runs with almost no true filler.

Should you watch Progressive first or the main series first?

Here is the one genuine fork in the whole franchise, and it is the only place where the question of what order to watch Sword Art Online in gets interesting. The Progressive films (Aria of a Starless Night from 2021 and Scherzo of Deep Night from 2022) go back and retell the Aincrad arc from the ground up, floor by floor, with cleaner animation and far more room for Asuna. They are excellent. They are also tempting to treat as the new starting line, and that is the trap.

Progressive is not finished. Two films in, it has only worked through the opening floors, while the original season covered that entire world and set up the rest of the franchise in fourteen episodes. Start there and you get a gorgeous, richer version of the beginning that then leaves you stranded before the story connects to anything else. My honest recommendation: if this is your first time, watch the main series in release order and save Progressive for a second lap once you already love Aincrad. If you have seen SAO before, Progressive first is a fantastic way to fall back in. The films sit beside the core either way, never replacing a single required entry.

Which Sword Art Online arcs are actually worth watching

Since the SAO watch order is basically solved, the more honest question is what you are pushing toward. Here is my read, fan to fan.

The peaks are real. The Aincrad arc still holds up as one of the best hooks the isekai boom ever produced. Mother's Rosario, tucked into the back stretch of Sword Art Online II, is the emotional high point of the entire franchise and the arc I would hand to anyone who thinks SAO is all spectacle and no heart. Alicization is where the show finally swings for something enormous and mostly connects, which is exactly why longtime fans point new viewers toward it as proof of what this series can be.

The softer patches deserve a mention too, gently. Fairy Dance is easy to find frustrating. Phantom Bullet, the arc that moves into the Gun Gale Online world in season two, is a slower burn than the arcs around it. None of it is unwatchable, and somebody out there counts each one as their favorite, but knowing the rhythm ahead of time keeps you from bailing right before the payoff hits.

Where to watch Sword Art Online

Streaming is the one part that genuinely is a little messy. Crunchyroll is the main home and carries most of the main line plus the Gun Gale Online spin-off. The Ordinal Scale and Progressive films tend to move around by service and region, and a handful of titles land elsewhere depending on where you are. Availability shifts over time, so check what is live in your country before you commit. None of it changes the order, only where each piece happens to stream.

Log in and start on floor one

For a franchise with a reputation this intimidating, the Sword Art Online watch order comes down to five entries in a row: Sword Art Online, Sword Art Online II, Ordinal Scale, Alicization, and War of Underworld, with the Progressive films saved for a richer rewatch. That is a complete story with a real ending in around 40 hours. Everything else, the spin-off and the specials and whatever that new movie turns out to be, is there for whenever you want to stay a while longer. Go in knowing where it soars and where to be patient, and one of the biggest front doors into isekai swings wide open.

FAQ

What is the Sword Art Online watch order?

The Sword Art Online watch order is five entries in release order: Sword Art Online, Sword Art Online II, the Ordinal Scale movie, Alicization, and Alicization: War of Underworld. That is the full main story. The Progressive films and the Gun Gale Online spin-off are optional and come afterward.

Should I watch Sword Art Online: Progressive first?

It is better saved for later. Progressive retells the Aincrad arc in more detail, but only two films exist so far, so it covers just the early part of the story and does not reach the later seasons yet. First-timers should start with the original series and come back to Progressive for a deeper second pass.

Can I skip the Fairy Dance arc?

You can technically watch around it, but it is not a good idea. Fairy Dance (the back half of season one, after episode 14) is divisive, but it is canon and it carries characters and plot into later seasons. Knowing the setting changes going in makes it land far better than skipping does.

Do I need to watch Ordinal Scale before Alicization?

Yes. Ordinal Scale is a canon film set between Sword Art Online II and Alicization, and later entries build on what happens in it. Keep it in sequence right before Alicization rather than jumping ahead.

Where can I watch Sword Art Online in order?

Crunchyroll carries most of the franchise, including the main seasons and the Gun Gale Online spin-off, while the films can move between services and regions. Check what is streaming near you, then watch Sword Art Online in order starting from the first season.

Title: Fate Watch Order: The 5 Entries That Matter
Summary: Break down the essential Fate watch order, the five titles that matter, and where everything else fits. 🗡️
Meta Title: Fate Watch Order: The 5 Titles That Matter
Meta Description: Narrow the Fate watch order down to the five titles that make up the entire core story. Join Kaminari for more anime watch order picks.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Fate looks impossible, but the essential story is only five entries, and everything else is optional. For newcomers, the cleanest path is Fate/stay night: Unlimited Blade Works, then the three Heaven's Feel films, then Fate/Zero last (which keeps the big reveals intact). If you would rather start with the most action-packed hook, the popular alternative is Fate/Zero first, then Unlimited Blade Works, then Heaven's Feel. Both are great. The rest of the franchise is separate and skippable.

At its heart, Fate is about the Holy Grail War, a secret battle in which mages summon legendary heroes from history and myth as their Servants and fight for a wish-granting Grail. Fate has a reputation as the single most confusing Fate watch order in anime, and honestly, it earns it: three parallel routes, a prequel, alternate timelines, a giant mobile game, and two decades of spin-offs. Here is the calm truth, though. Ignore about ninety percent of it.

The core Fuyuki storyline is a complete, self-contained saga of roughly 26 hours, and once you know how to watch Fate in order at that core, the rest is just bonus material you can explore or ignore. Below I lay out the essential run, settle the famous Fate/Zero debate, explain the three routes, and slot in the optional extras.

The essential Fate watch order (the only 5 entries that matter)

These five entries make up the entire core story, the Fifth Holy Grail War plus its prequel. Consider it the Fate anime series order that actually matters for a first watch.

OrderEntryTypeYear
1Fate/stay night: Unlimited Blade WorksTV (26 eps)2014-2015
2Fate/stay night: Heaven's Feel I. presage flowerFilm2017
3Fate/stay night: Heaven's Feel II. lost butterflyFilm2019
4Fate/stay night: Heaven's Feel III. spring songFilm2020
5Fate/ZeroTV (25 eps)2011-2012

The core runs roughly 26 hours, a complete story with a beginning, a middle, and an ending. Finish those five and you have seen the heart of Fate, which is really all it takes to watch Fate in order. By contrast, watching literally everything the franchise has produced would run well over 100 hours, which is exactly why narrowing to these five matters so much. The animation studio ufotable handles all five, so the look and feel stay consistent throughout, which is a big reason this is the recommended Fate anime watch order rather than the older adaptations.

Fate/Zero first or Unlimited Blade Works first?

Here is the debate that has split the fandom for years, and the honest answer to it. Fate/Zero is a prequel set ten years before Fate/stay night, covering the Fourth Holy Grail War. Watching it first sounds logical, and plenty of people do exactly that, because Zero is gorgeous, action-packed, and an incredible hook.

The catch is that Fate/Zero was written for an audience that had already finished Fate/stay night, so it treats several major reveals from the later routes as ordinary background detail. Start with Zero and you learn a few of Heaven's Feel's biggest secrets before the main story has earned them. It helps to know what Zero even is, too: it follows Kiritsugu Emiya, the adoptive father the main hero Shirou barely remembers, through a bleaker, more adult war of clashing ideals, which is a big part of why it hooks people so hard.

So here is my recommendation: If you want every twist to land the way it was designed to, watch Unlimited Blade Works and Heaven's Feel first, then finish with Fate/Zero. If you care more about the strongest possible opening and do not mind mild spoilers, Zero first is a completely valid and popular choice. Neither camp is wrong, and both orders end with the same five entries, so pick the priority that matters more to you. Beyond that one call, there are no other real forks in the entire Fate watch order.

The three routes, explained

The thing to understand about Fate/stay night is that it began as a visual novel with three routes, each retelling the same Fifth Holy Grail War from a different angle with a different heroine and escalating reveals. Knowing this makes the whole Fate anime order click into place.

  • Fate (the Saber route) is the original path. Its only real anime adaptation is the 2006 Studio Deen series, widely considered the weakest of the bunch.
  • Unlimited Blade Works (the Rin and Archer route) digs into Shirou's ideals and his brutal rivalry with Archer. The 2014 ufotable series is the definitive version and your ideal entry point.
  • Heaven's Feel (the Sakura route) is the darkest path, and it upends much of what the earlier routes set up. The ufotable film trilogy is stunning.

The routes are meant to be experienced roughly in that progression, which is why the Fate/stay night watch order flows Unlimited Blade Works into Heaven's Feel so well. Two quick warnings: skip the 2010 Deen film version of Unlimited Blade Works, which crams a full route into 100 minutes and loses everything, and treat the 2006 series as an optional curiosity rather than a starting point. Unlimited Blade Works was built to be watched without it.

The optional spin-offs and alternate timelines

Once you finish the core, a huge amount of extra Fate awaits, and none of it is required. Most of these are set in entirely separate timelines with their own casts and Grail Wars.

  • Fate/Apocrypha (2017) is a separate Great Holy Grail War with a brand-new cast. Self-contained and easy to enjoy on its own.
  • Fate/strange Fake (2026) is the newest addition, an A-1 Pictures series adapting yet another separate Grail War. It is excellent, but it draws on franchise knowledge, so watch it after at least Fate/Zero and Unlimited Blade Works rather than as a starting point.
  • Fate/Grand Order adaptations (Babylonia, Camelot, Solomon, and more) expand the massive mobile game's story and assume you already know the basics, so save them for after the core routes and watch them in their own release order.
  • Lord El-Melloi II's Case Files (2019) is a mystery spin-off following a Fate/Zero character, best watched after Zero.
  • Fate/kaleid liner Prisma Illya is a magical-girl spin-off in its own lighthearted timeline, Today's Menu for the Emiya Family is a cozy cooking series best enjoyed after Heaven's Feel as emotional recovery, and Carnival Phantasm is a non-canon comedy crossover that only lands once you already know the whole cast.

You genuinely do not need any of these to feel like you have watched Fate. They are desserts, not the meal.

Where to watch Fate

Streaming is scattered, which adds to the confusion. Crunchyroll is the main home for the core, carrying Fate/Zero, Unlimited Blade Works, and many of the spin-offs. The Heaven's Feel films and some older titles tend to live on other services like Hulu depending on region, and Netflix carries Fate/Apocrypha and select Fate/Grand Order content in some countries. Availability shifts by region and over time, so confirm what is live where you are before you build your plan.

Start the Grail War in the right order

For a franchise this intimidating, the real Fate watch order is mercifully small: Unlimited Blade Works, the three Heaven's Feel films, and Fate/Zero, in whichever of the two recommended orders suits you. It is a complete, self-contained masterpiece in about 26 hours. Everything else, from Apocrypha to the newest strange Fake, is optional exploration you can save for whenever the mood strikes. Clear away the noise and one of anime's most rewarding sagas is waiting, no homework required.

FAQ

What order should I watch Fate in?

For the core story, watch Fate/stay night: Unlimited Blade Works, then the three Heaven's Feel films, then Fate/Zero. If you prefer the most action-packed starting point and do not mind mild spoilers, watch Fate/Zero first instead. Both cover the same essential five entries.

Should I watch Fate/Zero first?

You can, but it is a trade-off. Fate/Zero is a prequel that spoils some later reveals, so watching it last preserves the mysteries. Many fans still start with it because it is the most accessible and exciting entry, so it comes down to whether unspoiled twists or the strongest hook matters more to you.

Do I need to watch the 2006 Fate/stay night?

No. The 2006 Studio Deen series adapts the original Fate route but is regarded as the weakest adaptation, and Unlimited Blade Works was made to be watched without it. Save it as an optional curiosity for completionists only.

What are the three Fate routes?

Fate/stay night is built on three routes that retell the same Holy Grail War: Fate (the Saber route), Unlimited Blade Works (the Rin and Archer route), and Heaven's Feel (the Sakura route). Each escalates the reveals, which is why they are meant to be watched in that progression.

Where can I watch Fate?

Crunchyroll carries the core, including Fate/Zero and Unlimited Blade Works, while the Heaven's Feel films and some titles appear on services like Hulu, and Netflix has Fate/Apocrypha and some Fate/Grand Order content. Availability varies by region, so check what is streaming near you before you start.

Title: 15 Beloved Black Anime Characters Who Forever Changed the Game
Summary: Round up 15 black anime characters spanning decades of anime, legends like Yoruichi beside 2025's Gachiakuta breakouts. 🔥
Meta Title: Black Anime Characters: 15 Icons and Scene-Stealers
Meta Description: Meet the black anime characters who carry entire shows on charisma, legends and 2025 breakouts alike. Join Kaminari for more anime lists.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
The best black anime characters do not ask for the spotlight, they just take it. Afro, Yoruichi, Michiko, and Killer Bee are usually the first names people shout, and the bench behind them runs deep. Some anchor entire series on charisma alone. Others show up for a single arc and casually walk off with the whole thing.

We are talking grizzled swordsmen, a sword-swinging rapper, a jaded music kid scraping by on Mars, and a whole crew of professional troublemakers. A few are icons you already have a poster of. A couple are so new the ink is barely dry, and they are already climbing our list of favorites.

Every one of these anime characters that are black earns the spot on pure personality, so expect strong opinions and at least one pick guaranteed to start an argument in the replies. Fair warning: we play favorites, and we are not sorry about it.

Top 15 black anime characters

These fifteen black anime characters span decades of anime, mixing certified legends with a couple of faces from just last season. The most popular black anime characters share space with a few deeper cuts, and there are more than enough black anime dudes and women here to carry a show on charisma alone. It runs past the usual top 10 black anime characters roundups, so here is our list of black anime characters, in no particular order.

Yoruichi Shihoin

Anime: Bleach

Yoruichi could walk into a room full of soul reaper captains and still look like she is the one being inconvenienced. Former head of Bleach's Second Division, fast enough to earn the Flash Goddess nickname, and casual enough to spend chunks of the series as a house cat purely to mess with people. She mentors Ichigo, trades blows with the strongest fighters in Soul Society, and never once breaks a sweat about it. The blueprint for effortless cool, basically.

Afro

Anime: Afro Samurai

Afro barely says ten words a season and still comes across louder than everyone around him. He wears the Number Two headband and hunts the man holding Number One, the one who cut down his father in front of him when he was a kid. Samuel L. Jackson voices both Afro and his motor-mouthed hype-man Ninja Ninja, which is either a great joke or a stroke of genius, probably both. Pure revenge-movie energy poured into anime form.

Michiko Malandro

Anime: Michiko & Hatchin

Michiko breaks out of prison in the first episode and never really slows down after that. Motorcycle, short fuse, incredible fashion sense, and a stubborn streak a mile wide, she blasts across a sun-baked, Latin-inspired world chasing a man from her past with a reluctant kid in tow. She is not always likable, which is the whole point, and she is impossible to ignore. Nobody in anime carries themselves quite the way she does.

Killer Bee

Anime: Naruto Shippuden

Bee fights with seven swords at once, mentors Naruto through the toughest training in the series, and insists on rapping through most of it whether anyone asked or not. His bars are famously terrible, and we love him more for it. Under the goofball routine sits one of the strongest and most stable characters in the whole franchise, a guy who made peace with the monster sealed inside him and came out the other side laughing. Bee rules, no notes.

Canary

Anime: Hunter x Hunter

Canary gets maybe fifteen minutes early in Hunter x Hunter and makes every second land. A teenage apprentice butler for a family of professional killers, she plants herself at the Zoldyck gate and beats back a whole mob solo, all to do a job most people would have walked away from. Her loyalty to Killua quietly wrecks you once you understand what that household is actually like. Give her a spin-off, cowards.

Yasuke

Anime: Yasuke

Yasuke is the rare anime hero ripped straight out of a history book. The real Yasuke was an African man who served the warlord Oda Nobunaga in the 1500s, and the Netflix series reimagines him as a burnt-out ronin dragged back into a war he thought he had left behind. As an African anime character built on an actual historical figure, he has no real competition, and a Flying Lotus soundtrack gives the whole thing a hazy, melancholy pulse. Worth it for the mood alone.

Carole Stanley

Anime: Carole & Tuesday

Carole is scraping by on a colonized Mars, busking on keys and sax for spare change until she runs into Tuesday and the two decide to actually chase music. She is warm and quietly exhausted in a way that feels real, the kind of lead who makes a low-stakes story hit harder than it has any right to. If you have ever worked a dead-end shift while refusing to give up on the one thing you care about, she gets it.

Dutch

Anime: Black Lagoon

Dutch runs the Lagoon Company, piloting a boat full of gunrunners through the nastiest port in Southeast Asia without ever raising his voice. He is one of the coolest black anime characters around for a simple reason: nothing gets to him. Bullets, betrayal, a crew of certified lunatics, he handles all of it like he is deciding what to order for lunch. Every friend group needs a Dutch, and most of them are not lucky enough to have one.

Ogun Montgomery

Anime: Fire Force

Ogun throws fire and forges weapons, and his reunion with Shinra is one of the warmest stretches in Fire Force. Series creator Atsushi Ohkubo has said he built characters like Ogun because he wanted more Black heroes in his work, and it shows in how much life the guy gets to have. A genuinely good dude who also happens to be a monster in a fight. He deserved more screen time, and we will say that to anyone who listens.

Kilik Rung

Anime: Soul Eater

Kilik is Ohkubo doing the same thing a few years earlier over in Soul Eater. He fights by channeling his partners, the Pot of Fire and Pot of Thunder, basically turning his own body into a weapon, and he looks fantastic pulling it off. He is one of those cool black anime characters who never needs to be the main event to steal a scene. Underrated then, underrated now.

Mohammed Avdol

Anime: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure

Avdol is the steady hand of the Stardust Crusaders, the Egyptian fortune-teller whose Stand, Magician's Red, is basically a flamethrower with an attitude. He plays the wise older-brother type who always seems to have the plan, right up until the series decides to break your heart with him. Calm, loyal, and criminally dependable in a cast full of hotheads. Respect the man.

Onyankopon

Anime: Attack on Titan

Onyankopon shows up in Attack on Titan's back half and immediately becomes the guy keeping everyone alive, the engineer and pilot who gets the Survey Corps airborne right when the story needs a miracle. He is named after an Akan sky god, a small touch that tells you somebody cared. Level-headed and decent in a show that is allergic to both, he is a small mercy every time he walks on.

Agil

Anime: Sword Art Online

Agil is the axe-swinging shopkeeper who has Kirito's back inside the death game and runs a bar once everyone makes it out. He is the dependable big-brother figure every long series needs, proof that you do not have to be the chosen one to be the most-liked person in the room. Reliable to a fault and endlessly patient with a much younger crowd. The kind of friend you actually want in your corner.

Musa Kamara

Anime: Run with the Wind

Musa is the odd one out on this list, and we mean that as a compliment. No powers, no Stands, just a kind-hearted international student and long-distance runner in a grounded drama about a college relay team. His arc is all about finding where he belongs, and it creeps up on you until you are somehow shouting at a screen during a track race. Sports anime works, and Musa is a big reason this one lands so hard.

Semiu Grier

Anime: Gachiakuta

Semiu is the newest face here and already one we are attached to. She works as a Cleaner in Gachiakuta, the 2025 breakout from Studio Bones, and she gets one of the show's sharpest introductions. Fun bit of trivia: creator Kei Urana came up as an assistant to Atsushi Ohkubo, the same guy who made Kilik and Ogun, so the whole tradition of great characters runs straight through her. Confident, quick, and instantly magnetic. Keep an eye on this one.

Why the roster keeps getting deeper

The old guard used to carry all the weight, a short list of legends you could rattle off in one breath. Now Yoruichi and Afro share the screen with new favorites turning up every year, and Gachiakuta alone dropped a few more onto the pile. The top black anime characters are not a fixed hall of fame anymore, they are a growing crew, and some of the best black anime characters are probably still a season or two out.

Keeping up with the newest black anime characters is half the fun, and it is what we do all week. Come hang out with us at Kaminari, where our anime newsletters cover the characters, shows, and moments worth your time, and we will make sure you meet the next Semiu before your group chat beats you to it.

FAQs

Who is the most popular black anime character?

Yoruichi Shihouin from Bleach tends to top fan polls, with Afro Samurai and Killer Bee right behind her. It shifts by generation, though, and Gachiakuta's Semiu is climbing fast with newer fans.

Are there black anime main characters?

Plenty of them. Afro, Michiko, Yasuke, and Carole all headline their own shows, and series like Cannon Busters and Michiko & Hatchin are built around them rather than tucking them into the background.

Is Yoruichi black?

Yoruichi is a dark-skinned character the community has claimed and celebrated for years. Bleach never spells out real-world nationality, but her design and her huge following make her a lock for any list like this one.

Which anime has the most black characters?

Cannon Busters and Michiko & Hatchin lead the way with diverse casts, and Gachiakuta joined them in 2025 with Semiu, Jabber, and Corvus. Fire Force and Soul Eater are stacked too, thanks to creator Atsushi Ohkubo.

Who was the first black anime character?

The honest answer is that it is hard to pin down, since it depends on how you define both anime and the character, with candidates going back decades. Rather than crown a single first, it is fair to say the early ones were rare and scattered, which is part of why the current run of new faces feels so good.

Title: 16 Timeless Female Anime Characters Fans Keep Falling in Love With
Summary: Explore 16 female anime characters spanning decades and genres, modern best girls beside classic icons. ✨
Meta Title: Female Anime Characters: 16 Icons Fans Adore
Meta Description: Discover the female anime characters fans keep rewatching, best girls both modern and classic. Join Kaminari for more anime lists.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
The best female anime characters are the ones who run the whole show, sometimes literally. Mikasa, Yor, Maomao, and Frieren are the names fans reach for first, and the roster behind them runs deep through every genre anime has to offer. Some are unstoppable in a fight. Others land with a single quiet line, no punches required.

What ties this group together is presence, not a look or a trope. These are characters written with real interiority, the kind who carry a series on personality alone and stay with you for years. A few have been icons since the nineties. A couple showed up last season and already feel permanent, which tells you how strong the writing has gotten.

These sixteen female anime characters blend modern favorites with the legends who paved the way, and every one earns her spot on how much fans genuinely love her. Expect strong opinions and at least one pick guaranteed to start a fight. Fair warning: we play favorites.

Top 16 female anime characters

It runs deeper than the usual top 10 female anime characters roundups, and it spans decades of shows across just about every genre. The most popular female anime characters sit right next to a few cult favorites here, and these are the popular female characters anime fans actually rewatch for, in no particular order.

Maomao

Anime: The Apothecary Diaries

Maomao is the reigning best girl of modern anime, and she earned it by caring more about poison than palace politics. Sold into the imperial court as a lowly maid, she cracks deadly mysteries with an apothecary's brain and a total refusal to be impressed by handsome nobles. She would rather test a new toxin on her own arm than flirt with anyone, and that single-minded weirdness is the whole appeal. Proof that the most magnetic thing a character can have is a sharp mind.

Frieren

Anime: Frieren: Beyond Journey's End

Frieren is an elf mage who outlives the hero party she once traveled with, and her story becomes a gentle quest to truly know the people she loves while she still can. She is quiet, a little detached, and completely disarming once the series shows you the warmth underneath. Watching her discover that ten years with a human meant more than a century on her own is one of the most moving things anime has done recently. She is peak fiction, and we will not be taking questions.

Mikasa Ackerman

Anime: Attack on Titan

Mikasa is arguably the most capable soldier in Attack on Titan, and she spends the whole series proving it while carrying a quiet, complicated love for Eren. She is calm where everyone else panics, decisive when the world is literally ending, and terrifyingly good with the maneuver gear. Her strength never cancels out her tenderness, which is exactly what makes her land so hard by the finale. Few characters this powerful get written with this much heart.

Yor Forger

Anime: Spy x Family

Yor is a deadly assassin moonlighting as a wife and mother, and the joke that never gets old is how bad she is at the domestic half. She can clear a room of henchmen without blinking, then panic completely over cooking dinner. Underneath the comedy she is genuinely tender, a woman who took on a fake family and quietly decided to love it for real. The Forgers work because she means it.

Nezuko Kamado

Anime: Demon Slayer

Nezuko gets turned into a demon in the very first episode and spends the series refusing to act like one, protecting her brother Tanjiro with a ferocity that somehow keeps her human. She barely speaks, since there is usually a bamboo muzzle in the way, and still communicates more than most characters manage with full dialogue. Fierce, loyal, and weirdly adorable for something that punches demons into next week. Everyone wants a sibling who has their back like she does.

Kurisu Makise

Anime: Steins;Gate

Kurisu is the genius neuroscientist who keeps Steins;Gate grounded while everyone around her spirals through time travel. She is sharp-tongued, secretly a huge softie, and mortified that she posts on science forums at two in the morning. Her back-and-forth with Okabe is some of the best-written banter in anime, the kind that turns into something real without ever getting saccharine. Brilliant people written as actual people are rare, and she is the gold standard.

Rem

Anime: Re:Zero

Rem is the blue-haired maid whose devotion to Subaru became one of the most talked-about arcs in modern anime. What makes her land is not the loyalty itself but the road to it, the way she moves from suspicion to a love she chooses with her eyes wide open. Her big speech pulling Subaru out of his lowest point is a certified anime moment. She believes in someone before he believes in himself, and that wrecks people every time.

Makima

Anime: Chainsaw Man

Makima is the rare character who is magnetic precisely because you should not trust her for a second. Calm, poised, and utterly in control, she pulls the strings of Chainsaw Man from behind a soft voice and a warmth that never quite reaches the intent underneath. She is a masterclass in quiet menace, the kind of antagonist who makes you understand exactly how everyone gets pulled into her orbit. Villains this compelling do not come around often.

Violet Evergarden

Anime: Violet Evergarden

Violet starts as a former child soldier who does not understand her own emotions and slowly learns to, one letter at a time, working as a ghostwriter for other people's feelings. Her arc is about someone taught only how to destroy figuring out how to connect, and the series lets it unfold at a devastatingly patient pace. Gorgeous to watch and quietly gutting to sit through. If a character has ever made you cry over the words “I love you,” it was probably her.

Motoko Kusanagi

Anime: Ghost in the Shell

Major Motoko Kusanagi is the cybernetic icon a huge chunk of modern sci-fi quietly borrowed from. She leads Section 9 through cases that keep asking what is left of a person once the body is fully artificial, and she carries that existential weight without ever slowing the action down. Cool, philosophical, and always three steps ahead. Decades on, nobody has done cyberpunk quite like the Major.

Faye Valentine

Anime: Cowboy Bebop

Faye is a con artist, a gambler, and a woman with no memory of who she used to be, drifting through Cowboy Bebop in search of a past worth returning to. She acts out for attention and pushes people away, and the series slowly peels back the loneliness under all of it. Prickly, flawed, and completely human, she is one of the most quietly tragic characters in a show full of them. Bebop would not be Bebop without her.

Revy

Anime: Black Lagoon

Revy is the trigger-happy heart of Black Lagoon, a dual-wielding gunfighter who solves most problems with an absurd amount of ammunition. She is loud, mean, and clearly running from something she will never talk about, which makes the rare cracks in her armor land like gut punches. Nobody has more fun in a firefight, and nobody needs the chaos more. She is a walking bad decision, and we love her for it.

Nico Robin

Anime: One Piece

Robin is the archaeologist of the Straw Hats, the only person alive who can read the history the world wants erased, which turned most of her life into a lonely fugitive nightmare. When she finally lets herself be saved, screaming that she wants to live, it is one of One Piece's most cathartic moments. Calm, deeply intelligent, and quietly kind once she trusts you. She waited her whole life for a crew that would fight for her, and the payoff is worth every tear.

Erza Scarlet

Anime: Fairy Tail

Erza swaps armor and weapons mid-battle faster than most fighters can throw a single punch, and she runs Fairy Tail's guild with a reputation that terrifies her own friends. Under the discipline is a survivor of real trauma who pours all of it into protecting the people she calls family. Terrifying, dependable, and secretly a giant softie about cake and knights. You would follow her into any fight, mostly because saying no seems unwise.

Homura Akemi

Anime: Puella Magi Madoka Magica

Homura looks like a cold, aloof transfer student, and the reveal of what she actually is recontextualizes all of Madoka Magica in one gut-punch. She has looped through the same tragedy more times than she can count, all to save a single friend, and every reset chips a little more warmth away. Watching devotion curdle into obsession is bleak, brilliant character writing. She gave up everything, over and over, for someone who barely remembers, and it never stops hurting.

Asuka Langley Soryu

Anime: Neon Genesis Evangelion

Asuka is loud, competitive, and desperate to be seen as the best, and Evangelion spends its runtime slowly revealing the wounded kid underneath all that bravado. She is not always easy to like, which is the point, a painfully real portrait of someone using confidence as armor over deep hurt. Few characters have been picked apart by fans as endlessly as she has. Messy, human, and unforgettable, she is a big reason the show still gets argued about today.

Honorable mentions

A few more just missed the cut, and every one is worth a shout. Bulma basically runs the science of Dragon Ball and kept Goku alive long enough to matter. Tsunade is a legendary healer, a reckless gambler, and one of the most commanding leaders in Naruto. C.C. brings mystery and dry humor to every Code Geass scene she touches. Nami is the sharp, brave navigator who holds the Straw Hats together, and Power is Chainsaw Man's gloriously selfish blood fiend who becomes weirdly lovable anyway. Lucy carries the aching heart of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners, a netrunner chasing a quiet dream of the Moon in a city built to grind it out of her. Marin Kitagawa rounds it out with the open, infectious enthusiasm that made My Dress-Up Darling such a hit.

Loved for more than a design

The through-line here is simple: the most iconic female anime characters last because they are written like people, not decorations. Maomao out-thinks a palace, Frieren learns to treasure the people around her, Revy shoots straight through her own grief, and each one earns the love on personality first. The best female anime characters have always worked this way, and the roster only gets deeper from here.

Keeping up with the next great one is half the fun, and it is what we do all week. Come hang out with us at Kaminari, where our anime newsletters cover the characters, shows, and moments worth your time, and we will make sure the next Maomao lands on your radar before everyone else's.

FAQs

Who is the most popular female anime character right now?

Maomao from The Apothecary Diaries has swept recent fan polls and awards, with Mikasa Ackerman and Yor Forger close behind. Popularity moves fast, though, and Frieren has a serious claim of her own.

Who are the best-written female anime characters?

Kurisu Makise, Maomao, Violet Evergarden, and Homura Akemi get named constantly for depth and development. The best female anime characters tend to be the ones whose personalities drive the story rather than just decorate it.

Are there anime with strong female leads?

Plenty, and more every year. The Apothecary Diaries, Frieren, Violet Evergarden, and Attack on Titan all put complex women at or near the center of the story.

Who is the most iconic classic female anime character?

Motoko Kusanagi, Faye Valentine, and Bulma are the usual answers, characters who shaped how anime wrote women long before the current wave arrived.

Frieren or Maomao for best girl?

It comes down to taste. Frieren is the meditative, melancholy pick, while Maomao is the sharp, funny, poison-obsessed one. Both make the same case, that brains and heart age better than any trope.

Title: Top 19 Popular Anime Characters Even Non-Fans Know by Name
Summary: Cover 19 popular anime characters spanning four decades, global mascots beside modern breakout icons. 🌟
Meta Title: Popular Anime Characters: 19 Faces Everyone Knows
Meta Description: Meet the popular anime characters the whole world knows, global icons and modern breakouts alike. Come hang out with Kaminari for more.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
The popular anime characters everyone can name are the ones whose faces you would recognize even if you had never watched a single episode. Goku, Pikachu, Naruto, and Luffy crossed over from anime into plain old pop culture years ago, and the roster behind them is stacked with legends and modern juggernauts. Some built their fame over hundreds of episodes. Others became icons almost overnight.

What makes this group special is reach. These are the most recognizable anime characters on the planet, the ones printed on lunchboxes, turned into memes, and reliably ranking among the most searched anime characters online. A few have been famous since the eighties. A couple blew up in the last two years and already feel permanent.

Our lineup of popular anime characters mixes the global icons everyone knows with the fan favorites who rule the community, spanning shonen, space westerns, and everything between. Expect the obvious picks done right, plus a few you will want to argue about. Fair warning: we play favorites, and the comment section is welcome to disagree.

Top 19 popular anime characters

It goes well past the usual top 10 most popular anime characters lists and spans four decades of shows. The most popular anime characters of all time sit next to a few modern breakouts here, and the full list of popular anime characters below covers the icons and the fan favorites alike. These are the top popular anime characters that fans and newcomers both keep landing on, in no particular order.

Goku

Anime: Dragon Ball

Goku is the closest thing anime has to a universal mascot, a spiky-haired martial artist who has been powering up since the eighties and shows no sign of stopping. He is a lovable idiot with a bottomless appetite for food and fighting, the guy who turned “going Super Saiyan” into a phrase even your non-anime friends understand. Dragon Ball built the template nearly every shonen hero still follows. If anime has a single face, it is his.

Pikachu

Anime: Pokémon

Pikachu might be the single most recognizable cartoon character on earth, anime or otherwise. The electric mouse has been Ash's partner since the Pokemon anime began, and that cheerful “pika-pika” has moved more merchandise than most studios see in a lifetime. His fame long ago outgrew the show and the games that spawned him. Even people who have never watched an episode know exactly who he is.

Naruto Uzumaki

Anime: Naruto

The loudmouth orphan who became Hokage, Naruto Uzumaki talked and fought his way up from village reject, and a whole generation grew up doing his arms-back ninja run to school. His story of earning respect the hard way hit a nerve worldwide and turned Naruto into one of the defining anime of its era. That orange jumpsuit is readable across any crowd. He basically raised half the fandom.

Monkey D. Luffy

Anime: One Piece

Rubber-limbed and permanently grinning, Monkey D. Luffy chases the greatest treasure in the world as captain of the Straw Hats. One Piece is the best-selling manga of all time, and Luffy's mix of goofiness and terrifying resolve is a huge part of why. He collects friends like treasure and throws down like the world depends on it, usually because it does. Two decades in, he is only getting bigger.

Sailor Moon

Anime: Sailor Moon

Usagi Tsukino, better known as Sailor Moon, is the crybaby heroine who defined the magical girl genre for the entire world. Her transformation sequence and that “in the name of the Moon” line are burned into pop culture, and she opened the door for countless fans, especially girls, to fall for anime in the first place. Clumsy, kind, and braver than she thinks, she is a nineties icon who never went out of style.

Totoro

Anime: My Neighbor Totoro

The giant, gentle forest spirit who became the face of Studio Ghibli itself, Totoro grins out from the studio's logo before most of its films even start. My Neighbor Totoro turned a quiet story about two sisters and a magical creature into one of the most beloved animated films ever made, and that rain-soaked bus stop scene is pure movie magic. He barely does anything and somehow means everything. Decades on, he is comfort in character form, recognized even by people who have never watched another anime.

Satoru Gojo

Anime: Jujutsu Kaisen

Gojo is the strongest sorcerer alive, and he knows it, strolling through Jujutsu Kaisen with a blindfold, a smirk, and enough charisma to carry the whole franchise. Fans lost their minds over him instantly, and for good reason, since he is powerful, funny, and just tragic enough under the swagger to hurt. He became a merchandise machine almost overnight. Few modern characters have taken over a fandom this fast.

Tanjiro Kamado

Anime: Demon Slayer

Kindhearted to a fault, Tanjiro Kamado hunts demons to cure his sister while somehow keeping his empathy for the monsters he fights. Demon Slayer exploded into a global phenomenon on the strength of his sincerity and some of the best-animated fights ever put to screen. That checkered green haori is now instant shorthand for modern anime. He carries the entire series on pure heart.

Levi Ackerman

Anime: Attack on Titan

Levi is humanity's strongest soldier, a compact, deadly captain who spins through the air cutting down Titans with a scowl and zero wasted motion. He barely says more than he has to, and fans adore him for it, voting him to the top of popularity polls year after year. His clean-freak habits somehow make him more beloved, not less. Cool under pressure has rarely looked this good.

Vegeta

Anime: Dragon Ball

Vegeta is the proud Saiyan prince who spent years chasing Goku and became one of anime's most beloved rivals in the process. His arc from arrogant villain to grudging hero to devoted family man is one of the genre's great redemption stories. That scowl and those crossed arms are as iconic as anything in Dragon Ball. Nobody stays mad at Vegeta, least of all his own fans.

Light Yagami

Anime: Death Note

Give a bored genius a notebook that kills anyone whose name is written in it, and you get Light Yagami, who promptly decides he should be god of a cleaner world. Death Note turned his cat-and-mouse game with the detective L into one of anime's tensest thrillers, and his slow slide from idealist to monster is riveting. Writing in a notebook has never felt more menacing. He is the villain everyone secretly roots for, right up until they cannot.

Saitama

Anime: One Punch Man

Saitama is the bald, blank-faced hero who ends any fight with a single punch, which is exactly his problem, because nothing is a challenge anymore. One Punch Man flipped the superhero genre on its head with him, pairing incredible action with the most relatable existential boredom in anime. That plain yellow suit and dead-eyed stare are meme royalty. He is a parody who became a legend in his own right.

Edward Elric

Anime: Fullmetal Alchemist

Pint-sized and permanently furious about it, Edward Elric lost an arm, a leg, and his brother's body to a forbidden experiment, then spends the series trying to set it all right. Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood routinely tops best-anime lists, and Ed's blend of brilliance, temper, and heart is a big reason. Just do not call him short. He proved a shonen hero could carry real philosophical weight and still be a blast.

Lelouch vi Britannia

Anime: Code Geass

Lelouch is the exiled prince who gains the power to command anyone to do anything, then wages a chess match of a rebellion against an empire. Code Geass made him one of anime's most magnetic masterminds, equal parts brilliant strategist and theatrical drama queen. Every plan is a gambit and every episode a twist. His finale is still one of the most debated and beloved endings the medium has produced.

Spike Spiegel

Anime: Cowboy Bebop

Spike is the effortlessly cool bounty hunter drifting through space with a jazz soundtrack and a past he cannot outrun. Cowboy Bebop is many people's gateway into anime, and Spike's laid-back swagger, martial arts, and quiet melancholy are why it endures. He made looking bored while dodging bullets an art form. Decades later, he is still the coolest guy in any room he floats into.

Ichigo Kurosaki

Anime: Bleach

Orange hair, a giant cleaver of a sword, and a stubborn streak a mile wide, Ichigo Kurosaki becomes a Soul Reaper to protect the living and the dead. Bleach runs on his refusal to let anyone he cares about get hurt, plus some of the sharpest character designs and fights around. That massive blade is unmistakable in any silhouette. He is peak 2000s shonen, and the fandom never really left.

Denji

Anime: Chainsaw Man

Denji is the broke, feral teenager who fuses with his chainsaw dog to become a devil hunter, and wants nothing more than a normal life and a decent meal. Chainsaw Man turned his crude, tragic, weirdly sweet story into one of the biggest hits of recent years. He is a hero driven by the simplest wants imaginable, which somehow makes him hit harder. Anime rarely gets this messy and this lovable at the same time.

Anya Forger

Anime: Spy x Family

Anya is the telepathic little girl stuck between a spy dad and an assassin mom, with none of them aware of what the others really are. Her scheming faces and that “waku waku” delight turned her into one of the most memed characters in years, plastered across the internet within weeks of her debut. She is chaos in a tiny package. Try watching a single episode without wanting to keep her safe.

Gon Freecss

Anime: Hunter x Hunter

Bright and relentless, Gon Freecss is searching for the father who left him, and he anchors one of the most acclaimed shonen ever made. Hunter x Hunter uses his cheerful determination as a lens on some genuinely dark places, which makes his rare moments of fury absolutely chilling. Sweet as he is, you do not want to make him truly angry. He is proof a hero can be pure of heart and still terrifying. Also, fun fact: the creators of Sailor Moon and Hunter X Hunter are married!

Honorable mentions

Narrowing anime down to nineteen faces still means leaving out some heavy hitters. Roronoa Zoro nearly made it on sword skills and directional incompetence alone. Mikasa Ackerman and Kakashi Hatake are perennial poll-toppers who could headline their own lists. Yuji Itadori and Nezuko Kamado carry two of the biggest modern hits, while Eren Yeager might be the most argued-about protagonist of the decade. Sasuke Uchiha and Killua Zoldyck could fill another list this size on their own.

Why these faces define anime

The through-line is bigger than any single show: the popular anime characters that last catch on by giving people something to hold onto, a hero to grow up with, a villain to obsess over, a design that turns into a meme overnight. Goku, Pikachu, and Sailor Moon opened the door, and Gojo, Denji, and Anya prove the next wave is just as strong. The best popular anime characters do not just top polls, they stick around for decades.

Keeping track of who breaks out next is half the fun, and it is what we do all week. Come hang out with us at Kaminari, where our anime newsletters cover the characters, shows, and moments worth your time, and we will make sure the next Gojo lands on your radar before everyone else's.

FAQs

Who is the most popular anime character of all time?

Goku is the usual answer, and it is hard to argue, since he has been the face of anime worldwide for nearly forty years. Naruto and Luffy round out the all-time top three for most fans.
