A swordsman with a giant black blade and an uncontrollable inner demon makes his way through an elite military society divided into specialized squads led by eccentric, god-tier captains, which is Asta's black anti-magic sword, the devil sealed inside him, and the Magic Knight squads under their larger-than-life captains almost point for point. The ranked hierarchy, the squad structure, and the escalating sword battles all give it a strong Black Clover flavor. Ichigo is more naturally gifted than Asta, which keeps it just below the premise twins, but the black-sword-and-squads build is a strong match.

4. My Hero Academia

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Izuku Midoriya is born without a superpower in a world where almost everyone has one, until the greatest hero alive sees his heart and passes him a legacy. He enrolls at an elite hero academy, trains relentlessly, and sets his sights on becoming the number one hero. His class becomes a found family, and his explosive childhood rival pushes him at every turn. It is bright, earnest, and emotionally charged.

The modern shonen sibling: a powerless protagonist in a superhuman society builds himself up to inherit a rare ability, takes entrance exams, and climbs the hero ranks toward the top. Swap magic for superpowers and this is Black Clover's build down to the studs, a found-family class standing in for the Black Bulls, a fierce childhood rival in Bakugo echoing Yuno, and the hero rankings mirroring the Magic Knight stars. It runs more school-focused than Asta's story, but the never-back-down heart is cut from the exact same cloth. Our My Hero Academia filler list keeps your watch clean.

5. Fairy Tail

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Natsu and the rowdy wizards of the Fairy Tail guild take jobs, blow up half the scenery, and treat each other like family across a sprawling magic world. Lucy, a celestial wizard, joins them and finds the home she was missing. The guild faces bigger and bigger threats while leaning hard on the bonds between its members. It runs long, loud, and unapologetically sentimental.

Fairy Tail is the closest match for the Black Bulls. A rowdy, destructive guild of outcast magic users treats one another as family, throws down in elemental clashes, and tangles with demon curses, which is Asta's squad to a tee. The bond-powered magic and the friendship-fuels-strength engine are exactly what the Black Bulls run on, and the guild's found-family heart is the same one that makes Asta's crew so easy to love. It lacks the powerless-underdog hook and the strict climb-to-a-title ladder, so it sits below the premise twins, but for the guild spirit, it is the closest there is. Our Fairy Tail filler list helps you skip the slow patches.

6. Mashle: Magic and Muscles

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Mash Burnedead is born with no magic in a society where magic is everything and the powerless are discarded. To protect his quiet life, he bluffs his way into an elite magic academy, aiming to earn the title of Divine Visionary, solving every obstacle with absurd physical strength instead of spells. The tone is deadpan and frequently hilarious. It plays like a magic-school shonen crossed with a bodybuilding gag.

Mashle is the parody sibling. An innocent, magicless, bowl-cut boy physically suplexes and out-muscles complex spells in an elitist magical society, grinding up a ranked magic academy toward its top title by outworking the prodigies who were handed everything. Mash swinging muscle where everyone else casts is Asta swinging a sword in the same spot, right down to the rival classmates and the climb. It plays the premise for laughs rather than drama, which keeps it just under the top twins, but for the magicless-underdog-in-a-magic-world build, it is as direct as it gets.

7. The Seven Deadly Sins

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Prime Video

Synopsis: In a European-flavored medieval kingdom, a disgraced band of legendary knights, the Seven Deadly Sins, are hunted as traitors until a princess seeks them out to save the land from the corrupt Holy Knights who truly seized power. Their leader, Meliodas, hides enormous strength behind a goofy grin. The series mixes raucous comedy with escalating magical warfare. It became one of the most popular fantasy shonen of its era.

The build connection is the European medieval kingdom setting and the corrupt Holy Knight squads, which rhyme with Black Clover's Clover Kingdom and its orders of Magic Knights, right down to the organizational intrigue. Meliodas's “Full Counter,” reflecting and canceling out magic spells with physical force, even echoes Asta's anti-magic sword nullifying what everyone else relies on, and the guild-like band of outcast fighters gives it real Black Bulls energy. Its leads are not powerless underdogs, which keeps it mid-list, but the medieval-knights-and-counter-magic build is a strong match. One note: it streams on Netflix, so availability depends on your region.

8. Radiant

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Seth is a young sorcerer in a world that fears and hunts magic users, blamed for the monsters called Nemesis that fall from the sky. Determined to find their source and prove sorcerers are not the enemy, he sets out on a journey full of prejudice and danger. He is brash, optimistic, and endlessly stubborn. It is a European-made take on the shonen formula with a bright, bouncy style.

The connection is the hated-outcast magic-user grinding forward against a world that rejects him, which is Asta's treatment by the Clover Kingdom turned into a whole premise. Seth is an energetic, horned sorcerer outcast with an inner dark power, fighting to prove his worth against constant discrimination, and there is a magic system to master and a monster-hunting purpose on top of it. It lacks the ranked-guild ladder and the central rival, so it sits mid-list, but the underdog-magic-user-proves-himself spirit is a strong match.

9. Chivalry of a Failed Knight

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll, Prime Video

Synopsis: Ikki Kurogane is written off as a failure, an “F-Rank” knight with almost no magical output in an academy that trains students to materialize weapons from their souls. Dismissed by nearly everyone, he wins through relentless training, technique, and a sheer refusal to lose, catching the eye of a prodigy classmate. It blends magic-academy action with a central romance. It is a slick, confident underdog story.

The build link is the “F-Rank failure” formula that Black Clover runs on: an underdog with negligible magical output who methodically dismantles noble mage prodigies through sword technique and sheer body conditioning rather than raw power. Ikki outworking those handed everything, in a ranked magic academy that counts him out, is Asta's exact journey, down to proving the rankings wrong one duel at a time. It is more of a focused academy duel-drama with a romance than a sprawling guild epic, which keeps it mid-list, but the F-rank-underdog-outworks-the-elites build is a genuine match.

10. Blue Exorcist

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Rin Okumura learns he is the son of Satan, born with blue flames and a demonic heritage he never asked for. Rather than embrace it, he enrolls at a school for exorcists, training to hunt demons and one day take down his own father, a flaming blade in hand. He is hot-headed and reckless, hated and feared for what he was born as. The tone balances real darkness with warmth and humor.

The connection is the Satan-blooded outcast at a ranked academy: a boy harboring forbidden blue flames trains at an exorcist school alongside his prodigy younger brother and a squad of cadets, climbing toward the top rank of Paladin, which rhymes with Asta being written off by the Clover Kingdom and clawing up the Magic Knight ladder. The magic-school structure, the prodigy-sibling tension, and the blade at the center give it a strong Black Clover flavor. Rin is powerful rather than powerless, so it lands mid-list, but the ranked-academy-plus-outcast setup fits. Our Blue Exorcist filler list shows what to skip.

11. Magi: The Labyrinth of Magic

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Aladdin, Alibaba, and a handful of chosen few explore deadly magical dungeons, bind powerful djinn, and get swept into the rise and fall of kingdoms. The world runs on a rich, rule-heavy magic system of magoi and metal vessels. Politics and destiny weave through the action as alliances form and empires clash. Its best arcs hit genuinely hard.

The connection is the high-fantasy scope and the rich, rule-driven magic: royal court intrigue, djinn equips that work like a deep spell-and-vessel system, and a sharp divide between commoners and nobility that recalls Black Clover's peasant-born Asta pushing into a noble's world. There are chosen heroes climbing toward greatness and kingdom-sized stakes to match. It lacks the powerless-underdog hook and the magic-knight ladder, so it sits at the lower end, but for the rich-magic-world adventure, it delivers.

A few anime similar to Black Clover that watch differently

Search around for anime similar to Black Clover and plenty of huge shonen come up that share the energy or a power system but not the actual build, the powerless underdog climbing a ranked magic order. They are fantastic, and we would happily point you to them. We just want the match to feel honest.

Jujutsu Kaisen and Demon Slayer both give you ranked fighters, explosive battles, and a hero growing stronger, so they feel adjacent, yet neither is built on a magicless outsider grinding up a magic-knight ladder driven by a rival. Gurren Lagann, meanwhile, bottles Asta's pure never-give-up spirit better than almost anything, just without the magic world or the organization around it. Every one of these is worth your time. Just go in knowing they scratch the shonen itch or the underdog spirit, not Black Clover's specific underdog-climbs-the-ranks build.

Keep the magic going as Asta returns

The best part of being a Black Clover fan right now is that the wait is basically over. Chase the premise twins with Wistoria or Mashle, the ranked climb with Naruto or Bleach, the magic worldbuilding with Magi, and the guild heart with Fairy Tail or The Seven Deadly Sins, and you will have a full queue ready while the new season finds its footing. The whole point of a good set of anime like Black Clover is to keep that never-quit feeling alive between episodes.

While you line it all up, come hang out with us at Kaminari, where our weekly newsletter rounds up the shows worth your time, the news that actually matters, and takes written for people who love this stuff as much as you do. We will keep you posted on every twist of Asta's return, so you never miss a beat of the new season.

FAQs

Is there an anime exactly like Black Clover?

Not a perfect twin, but a few come remarkably close. Wistoria: Wand and Sword and Mashle: Magic and Muscles both run on Asta's exact premise, a powerless underdog refusing to quit in a world built on magic. For the rivalry, the sealed demon, and the climb to the top, Naruto is the clearest ancestor.

What to watch after Black Clover

If you want the smoothest transition, begin at the top of this list: Wistoria: Wand and Sword, Naruto, Bleach, My Hero Academia, or Fairy Tail. Each one carries over the underdog grit, the ranked climb, or the magic that made Black Clover so easy to root for.

When does the new Black Clover season come out?

The anime returns in October 2026 on Crunchyroll, more than five years after the original run ended in 2021. It picks up the story from where the Sword of the Wizard King movie left off, heading into the series' final saga.

What are the best anime like Black Clover for the magic system?

For rich, rule-driven magic, Magi: The Labyrinth of Magic is the strongest pick, with Fairy Tail close behind for its guild-and-spell worldbuilding and Radiant for fans who loved watching a hated underdog master his power.

Where can you watch anime like Black Clover?

Most of these stream on Crunchyroll, including Black Clover itself and Bleach, though The Seven Deadly Sins is on Prime Video. Availability shifts by region and over time, so confirm what is on your service before you settle in for a binge.

Title: 11 Heartfelt Anime Like Frieren to Cure Your Post-Series Void
Summary: Pull together 11 anime like Frieren with the same quiet melancholy, slow fantasy journeys, and reflections on time. 🍃
Meta Title: Anime Like Frieren: 11 Heartfelt Picks to Watch
Meta Description: Fall for the anime like Frieren that sit with you, gentle fantasy, bittersweet journeys, the ache of passing time. Come hang out with Kaminari.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Still sitting with the ache Frieren left behind? Plenty of anime like Frieren can meet you there: the slow, unhurried pace, the quiet beauty of small moments, the long shadow of time and everyone we outlive, and a fantasy world you just want to wander. None of them are Frieren exactly, because almost nothing is, but the closest ones reach for the same feeling.

The timing helps, too. Season 2 arrived on Crunchyroll in January 2026, picking up Frieren, Fern, and Stark's journey and leaning deeper into the memory, mortality, and connection that made the first season a phenomenon. So these picks are less about filling a void and more about holding onto that specific, bittersweet mood a little longer.

We ranked these from closest match to loosest, judged on one thing: how much each shares Frieren's actual build, a slow, contemplative fantasy journey about time, memory, and the people we lose, carried by atmosphere and quiet emotion rather than spectacle. There is a quick table up top, plus honest notes at the end.

11 anime like Frieren at a glance

If you just want the fast read, here is the whole roster. The Similarity column is our call on how close each one gets to Frieren itself, not how good the show is on its own.

TitleSimilarityWhy it shares the buildWatch on
Mushishi5/5A wandering healer and quiet, melancholy vignettesCrunchyroll, Prime Video
To Your Eternity5/5An immortal processing loss across the agesCrunchyroll
The Ancient Magus' Bride4/5A mentor, a student, and gentle, mystical magicCrunchyroll
Spice and Wolf4/5A long-lived being who outlives everyone she meetsCrunchyroll
Girls' Last Tour4/5A slow, peaceful journey through a world that endedPrime Video
Natsume's Book of Friends4/5Soft, bittersweet encounters about letting goCrunchyroll
Somali and the Forest Spirit3/5A dying guardian and the child in their careCrunchyroll
Kino's Journey3/5A quiet traveler and reflective, standalone stopsCrunchyroll

Wandering Witch: The Journey of Elaina3/5A solitary witch drifting through vignettesCrunchyroll
Flying Witch3/5Gentle, everyday magic and small, calm momentsCrunchyroll

Streaming rights shift by region, so these are a starting point. Check what is available where you are before you commit.

The anime most like Frieren, ranked

Here are the anime like Frieren that genuinely share its build, ranked from the closest match to the loosest. The Similarity Rating is our read on how near each one gets to Frieren specifically, not how good the show is overall, and we kept the stars to whole numbers. The build we are measuring against is simple: a slow, contemplative journey carried by atmosphere and quiet emotion, usually about time, memory, and the people we outlive.

1. Mushishi

Similarity Rating: 5/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 5/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll, Prime Video

Synopsis: Ginko is a traveling Mushi master, wandering a timeless, nature-steeped Japan to study and help people troubled by Mushi, strange primordial life-forms that exist between the living and the spiritual. Each episode is a self-contained story about someone whose life has brushed up against these quiet, often melancholy phenomena. There is no grand villain and no overarching war, just people, nature, and the mysteries in between. It is hushed, gorgeous, and deeply contemplative.

For the actual feeling of watching Frieren, nothing comes closer. It shares the unhurried episodic rhythm, the wandering healer moving from one small human story to the next, and the gentle melancholy that lingers after each one. The fantasy here is quiet and grounded rather than flashy, exactly like Frieren's, and its themes of time, memory, and coexistence echo Frieren's reflections on a long life. If you loved the show's stillness, start here.

2. To Your Eternity

Similarity Rating: 5/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: A mysterious immortal being is sent to Earth with no self and no memory, able to take the shape of anything it has lost. Named Fushi, it slowly learns what it means to be alive by living alongside people, loving them, and watching them die as the centuries pass. Each arc introduces a new place, a new era, and a new set of people to lose. It is beautiful and frequently devastating.

On premise, this is the closest match to Frieren there is: an immortal protagonist processing mortality, memory, and grief across a span of time no human could live. Fushi outliving everyone it loves is Frieren outliving her party, the same ache from the same impossible vantage point. It runs more overtly tragic and plot-driven than Frieren's gentle melancholy, so brace yourself, but the emotional core is identical.

3. The Ancient Magus' Bride

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Chise Hatori, a girl who has only ever been unwanted, is bought at auction by Elias, a towering, bone-headed magus who declares she will be his apprentice and, one day, his bride. In his cottage on the edge of an old, folklore-rich England, she begins to learn magic and, slowly, to heal. The world is full of fae, dragons, and quiet wonder. It is a gentle, atmospheric fantasy about being seen.

The build overlaps on several fronts: a slow, mood-soaked magical world, a mentor-and-student bond at the center, and an organic, mystical approach to magic that rewards curiosity rather than spectacle, much like Frieren teaching Fern. Atsumi Tanezaki even voices both Chise and Frieren, and the two shows share a wavelength, the quiet, bittersweet, healing kind of fantasy. It is more about emotional recovery than mortality, which is the one place it drifts.

4. Spice and Wolf

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Kraft Lawrence, a traveling merchant, picks up Holo, a centuries-old wolf deity who takes the form of a sharp-tongued young woman longing to return to her northern home. Together they travel the roads, working through markets, schemes, and their own growing bond. The series runs on dialogue, economics, and the slow warmth between two very different travelers. It is talky, clever, and quietly romantic.

The Frieren connection is Holo herself: a near-immortal being who has watched generations of humans live and die, carrying the loneliness of a lifespan that outlasts everyone she meets. That is Frieren's exact burden, explored through a slow, dialogue-driven road trip rather than a quest. The measured pace, the bittersweet awareness of time, and the tender odd-couple traveling pair all land for Frieren fans, even with the lighter, warmer tone.

5. Girls' Last Tour

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Prime Video

Synopsis: Chito and Yuuri are the last two people wandering the upper levels of a vast, dead city, puttering along in a little motorized vehicle through a world that has already ended. They search for food and fuel, talk about nothing and everything, and find small pockets of beauty in the ruins. There is no rescue and no grand goal, only the quiet act of continuing. It is spare, melancholy, and strangely peaceful.

What it shares is the mood and the pacing: a slow, contemplative journey through an atmospheric world, where the point is not the destination but the small, human moments along the way. Like Frieren, it sits with loss and impermanence without melodrama, finding gentle warmth in a world shadowed by endings. If what you loved about Frieren was the quiet philosophizing between stops, this is a kindred spirit.

6. Natsume's Book of Friends

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 5/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Takashi Natsume can see the spirits, or youkai, that everyone else ignores, a gift that left him lonely and distrusted as a child. Inheriting a book that binds many of their names, he sets about returning those names, and with them their freedom, aided by a grumpy spirit bodyguard. Each episode is a gentle, often bittersweet encounter with a different spirit and its story. It is warm, quiet, and quietly healing.

The overlap with Frieren is the tone and the structure: a soft-spoken, episodic drift through encounters that are small in scale but heavy with feeling, usually about connection, loneliness, and letting go. Natsume moving among the long-lived youkai, who remember people long dead, mirrors Frieren's place among humans whose lives flicker past. For the gentle melancholy and the kindness at Frieren's heart, few shows match it.

7. Somali and the Forest Spirit

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: In a world where humans have been nearly wiped out, a golem who guards a forest finds a lost human child named Somali and sets out to reunite her with others of her kind. The catch is that the golem is slowly running down, with only a short while left to live. Their journey takes them across a strange, beautiful fantasy world full of non-human peoples. It is tender and bittersweet from the first episode.

What lines up is the traveling pair and the shadow of mortality: a long-lived, non-human guardian and the fragile human in their care, making a journey they both know cannot last forever. That ticking clock and the quiet parent-child warmth echo Frieren's reflections on time and the people we cannot keep. It is gentler and more episodic than plot-heavy, which is exactly the Frieren register, even if it is softer around the edges.

8. Kino's Journey

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Kino, a young traveler, rides a talking motorcycle named Hermes from country to country, staying just three days in each before moving on. Every land has its own strange customs, philosophy, or quiet cruelty, observed rather than judged. Kino rarely intervenes, choosing instead to watch, learn, and move along. It is a contemplative, episodic travelogue with a melancholy streak.

The build match is the reflective, episodic journey itself: a quiet traveler passing through a series of self-contained stories, each one a small meditation on people and how they live. Like Frieren, it values observation and stillness over action, and it leaves you turning its quieter moments over long after. It is more philosophical and less warm than Frieren, so it sits mid-list, but the wandering, thoughtful spirit is a close relative.

9. A Place Further Than the Universe

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 5/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Four high school girls, each carrying something unspoken, band together on an improbable quest to reach Antarctica. One of them is chasing the memory of a mother who went there and never came back. What begins as a lark becomes a genuine expedition, and a story about grief, friendship, and finally moving forward. It is funny, heartfelt, and quietly devastating.

Here is the one pick on the list that is not fantasy, included because it nails Frieren's emotional build so precisely: a meaningful journey that becomes a way of processing loss, memory, and the people who shaped us. The arc of grieving someone who is gone, of retracing their steps to understand them, is the exact emotional engine of Frieren's travels. If you came for the feelings rather than the magic, this will wreck you in the best way.

10. Wandering Witch: The Journey of Elaina

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Elaina, a gifted young witch, sets out to see the world the way her favorite storybook heroine once did, drifting from town to town with no particular destination. Some stops are whimsical, some are dark, and a few are quietly haunting. She observes more than she fixes, keeping a traveler's distance. It is a pretty, episodic road story with an uneven but memorable emotional range.

The build overlap is the episodic travelogue and the wandering-mage framing: a solitary magic user drifting through self-contained vignettes, some gentle, some bittersweet, in a lovely fantasy world. It leans lighter and less thematically focused than Frieren, and the tone swings more, but when it lands a melancholy story it reaches for the same quiet ache. Think of it as the breezier cousin of Frieren's travels.

11. Flying Witch

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Makoto, a young witch in training, moves in with relatives in rural northern Japan to continue her studies, bringing a little everyday magic into their ordinary lives. Nothing dramatic happens, and that is the point, as she gardens, meets gentle spirits, and drinks tea while the seasons turn. The magic is woven quietly into the slow rhythm of country life. It is one of the most soothing shows around.

The connection is the gentle, slow-life side of Frieren, the quiet appreciation of small, ordinary moments made a little magical. It has none of the mortality or the grand history, so it sits at the loosest end of this list, but for the comfy, unhurried, everyday-fantasy feeling that makes Frieren such a balm after a long day, it is a lovely match. Put it on when you want calm more than catharsis.

A couple of close matches to know about

Two of the shows nearest to Frieren's heart, Violet Evergarden and Delicious in Dungeon, stream on Netflix, where availability swings hard by region, so we kept them off the main list rather than send you somewhere you might not be able to follow. Both are worth seeking out if you have it, Violet Evergarden for the same ache about memory and connection, and Delicious in Dungeon for a warm, worldbuilding-rich party journey, though it trades Frieren's quiet melancholy for food-fueled comedy.

One more comes up constantly: Mushoku Tensei: Jobless Reincarnation. It shares Frieren's love of a deep, lived-in fantasy world and the feeling of growing alongside a character across a lifetime, but it is a louder, more fan-service-heavy isekai, so the real overlap is the worldbuilding, not the gentle, reflective tone.

Sit with the feeling a little longer

Frieren is a hard act to follow, because so much of its magic lives in the silence between moments. Start at the top with Mushishi or To Your Eternity for the purest version of that feeling, lean into the long-lived loneliness of Spice and Wolf, or let the gentle melancholy of Girls' Last Tour and Natsume's Book of Friends carry you, and you will have a quiet, lovely queue to sit with while Season 2 plays out. The whole point of a good list of anime like Frieren is to hold onto that bittersweet stillness a little longer.

While you line it all up, come hang out with us at Kaminari, where our weekly newsletter rounds up the shows worth your time, the news that actually matters, and takes written for people who love this stuff as much as you do. We will keep you posted as Frieren's journey continues, so you never miss a step.

FAQs

Is there an anime exactly like Frieren?

Not really, and that is part of why it stands out. The closest in feeling is Mushishi, which shares the quiet, episodic, wandering structure, while To Your Eternity comes closest on premise, with an immortal lead processing the same loss and passage of time that Frieren does.

What to watch after Frieren

If you want the smoothest landing, start at the top of this list: Mushishi, To Your Eternity, The Ancient Magus' Bride, or Spice and Wolf. Each one carries over the slow pace, the atmospheric fantasy, or the ache about time and memory that made Frieren so special.

When does Frieren Season 2 come out?

Season 2 premiered on January 16, 2026 on Crunchyroll, with Studio Madhouse returning. It continues Frieren, Fern, and Stark's journey and leans further into the show's themes of time, memory, and connection.

What anime has the same feeling as Frieren?

For the quiet, bittersweet mood specifically, Mushishi, Girls' Last Tour, and Natsume's Book of Friends are the closest. If it is the emotional-journey feeling you are after, A Place Further Than the Universe captures the grief-and-growth side of Frieren beautifully.

Where can you watch anime like Frieren?

Every pick on this list streams on Crunchyroll, including Frieren: Beyond Journey's End itself. Streaming rights shift by region and over time, so a couple of the closest matches sit on other services, and it is worth double-checking what is available where you are before you settle in.

Synopsis: Hajime Nagumo is pulled into a fantasy world with his whole class, except he draws a weak crafting skill and is mocked for it, then is betrayed and left to die at the bottom of a monster-infested dungeon. Instead of dying, he claws back up through the depths, devouring monsters and remaking himself into something ruthless and overpowered. He emerges cold, scarred, and far stronger than the classmates who abandoned him. The tone is dark, and the payback is the point.

Arifureta is about as pure as the genre gets. A protagonist is wronged in the cruelest way, left for dead, and uses a second chance at power to climb out and face the people who betrayed him on his own terms. Hajime's transformation from bullied nobody to merciless powerhouse is the exact arc the genre is built on, and the early dungeon descent is some of the most satisfying bottom-to-top payoff around. If you want the betrayal and the comeback at full strength, start here.

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Naofumi is summoned to another world as one of four legendary heroes, handed a shield, and almost immediately framed for a crime he did not commit by a princess who betrayed him. Branded a criminal and stripped of everything, he turns bitter and trusts no one, leveling up the hard way to prove the kingdom wrong. His slow rise from the most hated man around to the one everyone needs is the heart of the show. It is a betrayal story first and a fantasy adventure second.

It is the flagship of the betrayed-hero subgenre for good reason. The false accusation, the public disgrace, and the cold determination to climb back and expose the people who wronged him are the genre's blueprint. Naofumi's vindication, especially the moment the truth finally comes out, delivers the payoff of a straight revenge tale with the edges filed just enough to keep him sympathetic. For the betrayal and the comeback with real heart, nothing beats it.

Furious at the entity who put her there, she sets out to climb the military ranks and secure a safe, comfortable life, waging brutal magical warfare in open defiance of her maker. She is ruthless, brilliant, and utterly unsentimental. The result is a sharp, dark military fantasy.

The revenge here is aimed upward, at the god who reincarnated her against her will, and Tanya's whole campaign is a defiant rejection of the one who wronged her. The reincarnation-into-a-new-life framework and the ruthless, calculated climb to power are squarely in the genre's territory, even if the target is divine rather than human. He is laid-back but quietly unstoppable, and he has no interest in bowing to the deity who discarded him. It balances comedy, worldbuilding, and the occasional brutal fight.

The setup is a classic betrayal wound: betrayed and thrown away the moment he arrives, Makoto responds by thriving in open defiance of the goddess who rejected him. His rise is less about bloody payback and more about outgrowing and outshining the ones who wrote him off, which is its own kind of satisfying vengeance. Told partly as a survival diary, it tracks his steady rise from prey to predator. It is a grim, grind-heavy monster fantasy.

The build fits neatly: a protagonist killed through betrayal, reborn at rock bottom, who turns a second life into a relentless climb to power. Gobrou starting as the weakest thing in a world that eats its weak and becoming one of its apex forces is the bottom-to-top revenge-fantasy engine in monster form. Finding himself fully in the game world with god-tier power, he sets out to understand it and, slowly, to dominate it. He schemes, bluffs, and erases anyone who stands in his way without hesitation. The series is honest about how unsettling a protagonist like that really is.

Overlord is less about revenge and more about pure domination, but it delivers the same crush-your-enemies satisfaction that draws people to the genre: an isekai protagonist with overwhelming power, systematically outmaneuvering and destroying everyone who opposes him. Reborn as Lugh, the son of an assassin noble house, he trains his lethal craft from childhood and builds toward his impossible target. The series is slick, cold, and methodical. It plays its fantasy-assassin premise straight and stylish.

The revenge thread is quieter here, but it opens on exactly the right note: a master betrayed and discarded by the people he served, handed a second life to do things his way. Lugh's calculated, ruthless competence and his reincarnation into a world where he answers to no one carry the genre's cold-payback energy, even as the plot shifts toward his new mission. For the reincarnated-killer power fantasy, it is a sharp pick.

The joke is that the conspiracy he made up is completely real, and he is secretly the strongest person alive without realizing how serious any of it is. His followers take his improvised nonsense as gospel. It is a comedy that keeps paying off its own absurd premise.

There is no betrayal to avenge here, so the revenge angle is loose, but the core thrill overlaps hard: a reincarnated protagonist with overwhelming hidden power dismantling his enemies utterly, usually when they least expect it. The moments where Cid drops the act and effortlessly erases a room deliver the same untouchable-power payoff the genre runs on. Re:Zero is a second-chance isekai more than a revenge one, but the do-over engine is the same one that powers the genre: a protagonist handed repeated chances to go back and overturn a terrible outcome. Subaru's resets are aimed at saving people rather than punishing them, so the vengeance is faint, but the suffering-and-redo structure and the hard-won payoffs will land for anyone who loves watching someone claw back from the bottom. He throws himself into battle with an almost gleeful intensity, assembling a party of strong companions and tearing through increasingly dangerous foes. The series is a fast, combat-forward power fantasy. It knows exactly what it is and leans into it.

The revenge drive is thin, but Black Summoner nails the other half of the genre's appeal: a reincarnated protagonist who answers every threat with overwhelming, ruthless force and never loses. The reborn-with-power framework and the relentless, one-sided victories give it the same crush-everything satisfaction, even without a betrayal to settle. It is a popcorn pick for when you want the power trip without the heavy backstory.

11. I'm the Villainess, So I'm Taming the Final Boss

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Aileen wakes up remembering a past life and realizing she has been reborn as the villainess of an otome game, doomed to a terrible ending once the heroine arrives. Refusing to accept her scripted fate, she uses her knowledge of what is coming to outmaneuver everyone, starting by winning over the game's demon-lord final boss. The result is a sharp, funny reverse-engineering of her own downfall. It is romance and scheming in equal measure.

It comes from the villainess side of the second-chance isekai boom, where the appeal is a protagonist reborn with foreknowledge, rewriting a bad ending and turning the tables on everyone who would have ruined her. Aileen's scheming, her refusal to be a victim of the plot, and her calculated climb echo the revenge fantasy from a lighter, wittier angle. It swaps bloody payback for social chess, but the beat-the-ones-who-wronged-you spine is the same.

A couple of isekai that get recommended but skip the revenge

Search around and a few beloved isekai come up that share the second-chance setup but not the drive to get even. They are worth your time. We just want the match to feel honest.

Banished from the Hero's Party opens on a betrayal, with the lead kicked out of the group he helped carry, but the response is a cozy slow life in the countryside rather than any kind of payback, so the vengeance never comes. That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Slime gives you the rock-bottom-to-overpowered climb in full, yet its hero is a benevolent nation-builder with no one to avenge. Both are excellent. Just go in knowing they deliver the isekai rise without the revenge that defines the list above.

Pick your flavor of payback

There are more ways to enjoy a comeback than you might expect. For the purest betrayal-and-vengeance arc, go with Arifureta or The Rising of the Shield Hero, take the colder, sharper route with The Saga of Tanya the Evil, or lean into the untouchable power trip with Overlord and The Eminence in Shadow. Whatever mood you are in, a good revenge isekai turns getting even into the most satisfying part of the ride.

1. The Eminence in Shadow

Synopsis: Cid Kagenou reincarnates into a fantasy world chasing one fantasy of his own: to be the mastermind who secretly controls everything from the shadows. He invents a fake evil organization to roleplay against and builds a secret order called Shadow Garden, only for the world-ending conspiracy he made up to turn out completely real. He is also, without quite realizing it, the strongest being alive. His devoted followers treat his improvised nonsense as the words of a genius.

This is the undisputed number-one match for the “Sasuga, Ainz-sama!” engine. An overpowered protagonist acts like an ominous dark mastermind who stumbles into actual conspiracies, surrounded by fanatically loyal, god-tier subordinates in Shadow Garden who interpret his every casual offhand remark as a ten-thousand-year divine master plan. Cid and Ainz are two sides of the same coin, the secretly all-powerful leader bluffing through a performance his underlings take as gospel. Synopsis: A ruthless salaryman is killed and reincarnated, by a god he refuses to acknowledge, as a small girl named Tanya in a war-torn, early-twentieth-century-style world. Coldly determined to secure a safe, comfortable life, she climbs the military ranks and wages brutal magical warfare without a shred of sentiment. She is brilliant, merciless, and utterly pragmatic. The result is a sharp, dark military fantasy.

Tanya is the closest match for Overlord's ruthless, cynical salaryman psyche. An amoral corporate bureaucrat reincarnates into a world at war and uses cold optimization, modern military doctrine, and overpowering magic to butcher her enemies, while military command continuously misinterprets her ruthless efficiency and promotes her into greater geopolitical chaos. That gap between her self-serving intent and how her superiors read it is the same loyal-misreading engine that drives Ainz's story. It swaps the fantasy kingdom for a military campaign, so there is no Nazarick to command, but the merciless-overpowered-lead energy is a direct hit.

3. That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Slime

Synopsis: A middle-aged man is stabbed and reincarnated as a slime in a fantasy world, with a skill set that lets him absorb abilities and a calm voice guiding his growth. As Rimuru Tempest, he evolves from the weakest monster imaginable into one of the most powerful beings alive, gathering devoted followers at every step. Rather than conquer for its own sake, he sets out to build a nation where monsters can live safely. It is cozy, funny, and quietly epic.

Slime is the direct sibling for monster nation-building and subordinate hierarchy. A former salaryman reincarnates as a non-human creature, unites wild monster tribes, names them to evolve them into loyal floor-boss-tier lieutenants, and founds a sovereign state, which is Ainz's Sorcerer Kingdom with the lights on. It only ranks behind Tanya because Rimuru is ultimately benevolent and diplomatic rather than coldly self-interested, so the dark edge is softer. Cast out and shunned by humans, he falls in with the demi-humans and monsters nobody else wants, and discovers his otherworld origin makes him absurdly overpowered. He builds a hidden home and a trading company while two devoted, monstrous companions fight over him. It is a warm, funny, slightly melancholy power fantasy.

Tsukimichi is a direct counterpart to Nazarick's monstrous isolation. Shunned by the goddess and rejected by humans, Makoto is forced to align with demi-humans and monsters, and he builds a hidden pocket dimension called the Demiplane populated by loyal orcs, lizardmen, and ancient dragons. His two closest retainers, Tomoe and Mio, rival Albedo and Shalltear in sheer possessive adoration, and he runs a covert merchant alter ego on the side, much like Ainz operating under an assumed name. The tone is gentler and the hero kinder than Ainz, but the overpowered-outcast-and-his-devoted-monster-household build is a close fit.

Synopsis: Thousands of players wake up trapped inside the MMO Elder Tale, unable to log out, and must build a functioning society out of the chaos. The hero is Shiroe, a brilliant strategist who wins through planning, politics, and a deep command of the game's systems rather than brute force. He works to establish order and institutions among the stranded players. It is the thinking person's trapped-in-a-game story.

Log Horizon is the masterclass in MMO mechanics turned reality and guild logistics. It lacks the dark villainy, but Shiroe, nicknamed the Villain in Glasses, uses complex MMO raid mechanics, cooldown timers, spell combinations, and economic subversion to establish order and govern an entire player society, which captures Ainz's deep technical knowledge of the game underpinning his world. Watching Shiroe scheme three moves ahead and found a functioning city-state rhymes directly with Overlord's strategic side. It is heroic and talky rather than villainous, so it ranks mid-list, but the game-world statecraft is a strong match.

The catch is that his every ruthless, self-serving act somehow lands as noble, and his subjects adore him as a benevolent hero. The more he tries to be cruel, the more beloved he becomes. It is a sharp, funny space-opera spin on the villain fantasy.

This one directly shares Overlord's comedy of administrative misunderstandings. A reincarnated noble resolves to become a tyrannical, corrupt despot who exploits his subjects, but his self-serving schemes accidentally result in beloved economic reforms, military triumphs, and subordinates worshiping him as an infallible, saintly ruler. The gap between how Liam sees himself and how his adoring followers interpret him is the exact comedic engine that powers Ainz's story, where fearsome intent and loyal misreading keep colliding. It is one of the closest picks here on the aspiring-overlord concept, just routed through a sci-fi empire.

He pulls his goblin kin up with him, forging them into a disciplined, terrifying fighting force. It is a brutal, amoral survival climb.

Re:Monster is a brutal, amoral monster-evolution story that shares Overlord's non-human, no-conventional-morality streak. The protagonist reincarnates as a lowly goblin with a ruthless survivalist mindset, devouring beasts and enemies to acquire their abilities and evolving himself and his goblin clan into an organized, terrifying monstrous army that butchers foes without hesitation. The monster-side perspective and the cold, pragmatic empire-building echo Ainz marshaling Nazarick's horrors toward his own ends. What follows is a razor-sharp battle of wits with the whole world as the board. It is one of anime's definitive psychological thrillers.

If your favorite part of Overlord is the cold, masked anti-hero playing four-dimensional chess against entire nations with zero moral hesitation, Death Note delivers that purely. Light Yagami operates with the same calculated, amoral superiority as Ainz Ooal Gown outmaneuvering political rivals, always several moves ahead and utterly convinced of his right to rule. How Not to Summon a Demon Lord is a direct match for the social anxiety behind the terrifying persona. An introverted gamer is summoned into his MMORPG world with his max-level avatar and endgame gear, and he is forced to constantly roleplay as an arrogant, menacing demon lord to hide his intense panic and total lack of real-world confidence. That is Ainz's exact routine, the private scrambling under the fearsome mask, down to the game-system logic running the world and settling every fight. Demon Lord, Retry! is squarely Overlord-shaped. An adult game developer is transported into his game as his endgame character, the Demon Lord Kunai Hakuto, and he explores the fantasy world, manages loyal subordinates, and relies on administrator-style game mechanics to effortlessly overpower native fantasy mages. Kunai's final-boss strength and the way the world builds him up into a looming legend echo Ainz's accidental infamy almost beat for beat. A few overpowered isekai that skip the overlord part

Cautious Hero and Wise Man's Grandchild both give you a wildly overpowered lead who steamrolls every threat, but they are heroic and good-natured, with no dark ambition or kingdom to command. Just go in knowing they deliver the overpowered part without the scheming overlord and his loyal legion.

The first season is a tight, nerve-shredding battle of plans and counter-plans. It comes from the same magazine that ran Death Note.

Often called Death Note's spiritual successor, it runs on the exact same engine: a battle of wits between brilliant minds where every move is a gambit and one slip means death. The planning, the bluffing, the constant recalculating as the opponent adapts all echo Light and L, just with children against an adult jailer. The first season especially is as tense and cerebral as anything in the genre, which is why it lands so high for Death Note fans.

5. Terror in Resonance

Synopsis: Two mysterious teenagers calling themselves Sphinx set off a bomb in Tokyo and begin taunting the authorities with cryptic riddles, daring them to keep up. A disgraced detective is the only one who starts to see the pattern behind their attacks. As the game escalates, the tragic reason behind it slowly surfaces. It is a stylish, melancholy thriller with a haunting score.

The build match is the cat-and-mouse itself: brilliant young masterminds running rings around the authorities with elaborate, carefully planned moves, pursued by one sharp investigator who can actually challenge them. The riddle-by-riddle duel and the morally complicated motives rhyme with Death Note's L-versus-Light chess match. It is shorter and more somber, trading Death Note's scope for a tight, emotional story, but the tension is cut from the same cloth.

Behind the bland exterior is a mind that quietly orchestrates events from the shadows, several steps ahead of everyone. As the school's games grow more cutthroat, his real talents slowly surface. It is a cold, calculating drama of social strategy.

The connection is the hidden-genius manipulator: a protagonist who looks unremarkable while secretly pulling strings, outthinking rivals through layered plans and psychological reads, much like Light operating behind his honor-student mask. The school's high-stakes mind games and Ayanokoji's unreadable, morally-grey nature give it a strong Death Note flavor. There is no supernatural power and the stakes are social rather than life-and-death, which keeps it a step below the top.

Alongside his brothers, he engineers elaborate crimes against the cruel and powerful of Victorian England, styling himself the villain the world needs. Eventually a certain famous detective is drawn into his orbit. The series plays out as a run of intricate, morally tangled schemes.

The Death Note parallel is strong: a charismatic mastermind who appoints himself judge of a corrupt society and executes elaborate, meticulously planned crimes to reshape it, convinced his ends justify his means. Moriarty is essentially Light in Victorian dress, and his eventual duel with Sherlock is a pure battle of equal intellects. The period setting and the inverted detective story give it its own identity, but the genius-antihero build is unmistakable.

The tension is relentless and the stakes are life-altering.

The build link is the pure battle of wits under pressure: elaborate games where victory comes down to out-thinking, out-reading, and out-bluffing the opponent, with everything on the line. Kaiji sweating through a deathtrap of a gamble delivers the same white-knuckle, who-is-ten-steps-ahead tension that makes Death Note's confrontations so gripping. The last one standing becomes a god. His only real ally is Yuno, a classmate whose devotion to him is as terrifying as it is useful. It is a chaotic, bloody thriller built on paranoia and mind games.

The overlap is the deadly game of foresight and counter-strategy: competitors using special powers and careful planning to predict and outmaneuver one another, with godhood as the prize and death as the penalty. The constant guessing of who knows what, and who is setting whom up, echoes Death Note's information warfare. The connection is the genius protagonist locked in a high-stakes mental battle against forces he can barely see, forced to out-think an impossible situation with careful planning and nerve. Okabe's desperate, calculated attempts to stay one move ahead of catastrophe carry the same cerebral tension that powers Death Note, even without a direct rival. It is science-fiction rather than supernatural crime, and the duel is against fate more than a person, which places it mid-list, but the brains-over-brawn thrills are there.

It is dark, stylish, and quietly devastating.

The Death Note link is thematic rather than structural: both sit with hard questions about judgment, justice, and what people deserve, watching a cold arbiter weigh lives with chilling detachment. Decim passing sentence on souls echoes Light appointing himself judge of the world, and the series shares Death Note's talent for making you squirm over your own moral instincts. There is no cat-and-mouse here, so it ranks lower, but the dark exploration of judgment is a strong match.

A couple that get recommended but watch differently

Search around for anime similar to Death Note and a few titles come up that share a connection but not the build. They are worth your time. We just want the match to feel honest.

Bakuman comes from the exact same creators as Death Note, so it is a natural recommendation, but it is a warm, grounded drama about two friends chasing a manga career, with none of the thriller tension or moral darkness. Re:Zero is often called psychologically intense, and it is, yet it is a fantasy time-loop about trauma and endurance rather than a calculated battle of wits. Both are excellent. Just go in knowing they scratch a different itch than Light and L's chess match does.

Outthink the wait for the next masterpiece

Nearly two decades on, Death Note is still the gold standard, and nothing has fully replicated its blend of mind games and moral dread. The good news is that plenty of shows capture a piece of it beautifully. Start at the top with Code Geass and Monster for the closest battles of wits, bring the philosophy with Psycho-Pass, or sweat through the pure tension of The Promised Neverland. The whole point of a good list of anime like Death Note is to keep that cerebral, edge-of-your-seat feeling going long after Light and L take their final bow.

Title: 11 Brutal Anime Like Attack on Titan Where Humanity Fights for Survival
Summary: Stack up 11 anime like Attack on Titan, brutal survival wars heavy with stakes and tragedy, Vinland Saga and Kabaneri up top. 🧱

Meta Description: Brace for the anime like Attack on Titan that match the dread, dark survival wars heavy with tragedy. Swing by Kaminari for weekly recs.
Author: devin-morris
Content:
Still haunted by the walls, the Titans, and everything that came after? Plenty of anime like Attack on Titan deliver the same gut-punch: a dark, brutal fight for survival against an overwhelming threat, where nobody is safe, the stakes keep climbing, and the truth is always worse than it looks. The best of them pair breathtaking action with real tragedy and the kind of moral weight that lingers for days. No show replaces Titan, but the closest ones get dangerously near.

There is no new season to wait on, because Attack on Titan finished its ten-year run in 2023, and the recent compilation film The Last Attack gave the finale a proper theatrical sendoff. That makes it a complete, towering legend, and it leaves a very specific void that only a certain kind of dark, epic anime can fill.

We ranked these from closest match to loosest, judged on one thing: how much each shares Attack on Titan's actual build, a dark, brutal survival war against an overwhelming threat, with high stakes, major deaths, a deepening mystery, and a slow descent into morally-grey tragedy. There is a quick table up top, plus honest notes at the end.

If you just want the fast read, here is the whole roster. The Similarity column is our call on how close each one gets to Attack on Titan itself, not how good the show is on its own.

The anime most like Attack on Titan, ranked

Here are the anime like Attack on Titan that genuinely share its build, ranked from the closest match to the loosest. The Similarity Rating is our read on how near each one gets to Attack on Titan specifically, not how good the show is overall, and we kept the stars to whole numbers. The build we are measuring against is simple: a dark, brutal survival war against an overwhelming threat, heavy with stakes, death, and tragedy.

1. Kabaneri of the Iron Fortress

Similarity Rating: 5/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Prime Video

Synopsis: In a steam-powered, isolationist Japan, humanity huddles inside fortified stations while the Kabane, armored undead monsters, overrun the land. Ikoma, a young engineer, survives a Kabane attack half-transformed and becomes a Kabaneri, strong enough to fight back without fully turning. He joins survivors fleeing aboard an armored train, battling to reach safety. The action is fast, stylish, and desperate.

Of everything here, this is the direct studio sibling. It was produced by Wit Studio and directed by Tetsuro Araki, the exact team behind Attack on Titan's first three seasons, and it shares Hiroyuki Sawano's booming score. It is set in an isolated civilization where humanity lives barricaded inside fortified stations, using high-speed steam gear and armored trains to fight off relentless swarms of cannibalistic, infected monsters, with a hero who straddles the line between human and the thing everyone fears. It is shorter and less thematically deep, but on look, sound, and premise it is practically a twin.

2. 86 (Eighty-Six)

Similarity Rating: 5/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: A nation claims to wage a bloodless, drone-only war, but the truth is that a persecuted underclass, the Eighty-Six, are forced to pilot the machines and die unrecorded. Shin leads one such doomed unit, while a privileged commander named Lena fights to see them as human. The war grinds on with a staggering cost no one in power will acknowledge. It is a heavy, beautifully made military tragedy.

86 is the closest thematic and military twin. The Republic of San Magnolia maintains the illusion of peace and zero casualties behind massive protective walls by dehumanizing an entire minority class, the 86, mirroring Titan's Eldians, and forcing them into lethal front-line mech warfare against the Legion. It shares Hiroyuki Sawano's soundtrack, the systemic state propaganda, and the heavy survivor's guilt of disposable soldiers, which pulls straight from Titan's later-season reckoning with discrimination and the cycle of hatred. It trades Titans for mecha, but the tragedy and the moral complexity are pure Attack on Titan.

3. Claymore

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Prime Video

Synopsis: In a world preyed on by shape-shifting man-eaters called Yoma, an organization fields half-Yoma women, the Claymores, who wield massive swords to hunt the monsters down. Clare is one of them, driven by a vengeance rooted in a childhood the Yoma destroyed. The deeper she goes, the more she risks losing herself to the monster in her own blood. It is grim, bloody, and quietly tragic.

Claymore is the dark-fantasy prototype. Silver-eyed warriors hunt flesh-eating monsters disguised among human settlements, using swords and monstrous flesh grafted into their own bodies to fight back, which mirrors Attack on Titan's core rule, becoming a monster to kill the monsters, almost exactly. It even delivers the same kind of shocking mid-series revelation: that their isolated landmass is merely a controlled petri-dish experiment for a global war overseas, which is Paradis Island's reveal in a different coat. It is older and smaller in scope, but the monster-hunting grimness and the grander hidden truth fit squarely.

4. The Promised Neverland

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll, Disney+

Synopsis: Three gifted children at a seemingly idyllic orphanage live behind high walls under the care of a mother they adore, until they discover the horrifying truth: they are livestock, raised as food for the demons beyond the gate. With the clock ticking, they begin a tense, high-stakes game of wits to escape before they are shipped out. The first season is a masterclass in dread. It is a nerve-shredding survival thriller.

The Promised Neverland captures the terrifying claustrophobia of Attack on Titan's first season. Children live in idyllic peace behind high boundary walls under the illusion of safety, only to discover the horrifying truth: they are livestock being raised as meat for grotesque demon overlords, which mirrors the early Survey Corps dread and the humans-as-cattle horror that defines Titan's opening. It plays out as a high-IQ, suspenseful survival game to escape containment, trading Titan's military scale for intimate cat-and-mouse tension. There is no war or army, which keeps it mid-list, but the walled-in-and-farmed horror is a superb match.

5. Seraph of the End

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: A virus wipes out most of humanity and leaves the survivors enslaved as livestock by vampires who rule the ruins. Yuichiro escapes and joins a military order dedicated to exterminating the vampires and avenging the family he lost. Armed with cursed weapons, he and his squad wage a brutal war against beings far stronger than themselves. It is dark, tragic, and revenge-fueled.

Produced by Wit Studio with music co-composed by Hiroyuki Sawano, Seraph of the End sets a humanity devastated by a catastrophic event and herded into walled livestock cities by an aristocratic vampire regime. An enraged, vengeance-driven orphan in Yuichiro, who heavily mirrors early Eren, escapes, joins an elite military extermination unit, and wields demonic cursed weapons to fight back. The besieged-humanity premise, the walled cities, and the rage that powers the hero map closely onto Eren and the Survey Corps. It is more conventional shonen than Titan's grim realism, but the bones are a clear fit.

6. Neon Genesis Evangelion

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 5/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Prime Video

Synopsis: In a post-apocalyptic future, a traumatized teenager named Shinji is summoned by his cold father to pilot a towering bio-mechanical giant, the Evangelion, and defend a fortress city from monstrous beings called Angels. As the battles escalate, so does the psychological toll and the sinister truth behind the organization he serves. It is as much a study of depression and identity as a mecha war. It is one of the most influential anime ever made.

Evangelion is the structural ancestor to the Titan Shifter. A traumatized teenager is drafted by an authoritarian military organization in NERV to pilot a bio-mechanical giant, which is secretly a restrained organic beast made from the enemy's own flesh, to protect humanity from city-leveling monstrosities while unraveling apocalyptic global conspiracies. Swap the Eva units for the Titans and NERV for the walls, and the DNA is unmistakable, right down to the psychological damage and the world-ending secrets. The pace is older and far more introspective, but the bio-mechanical-giant-against-monsters build is a strong match. One note: it streams on Netflix, so availability depends on your region.

7. Vinland Saga

Similarity Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 5/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll, Prime Video

Synopsis: Thorfinn grows up in the brutal world of Viking raiders, witnessing his father killed by a cunning mercenary named Askeladd and devoting his childhood to revenge. He joins Askeladd's band, fighting in savage wars across medieval Europe while waiting for his chance to strike. The first season is a bloody revenge epic; the second becomes a profound meditation on violence and what comes after it. It is historical, grounded, and utterly uncompromising.

Vinland Saga was initially produced by Wit Studio before transitioning to MAPPA, mirroring Attack on Titan's exact production journey, and it reflects Eren's descent into vengeance just as closely. Thorfinn is a boy consumed by hatred who sells his soul to violence, and the series explores the devastating cycle of war, the human cost of conflict, and the elusive, philosophical meaning of true freedom, all of it the same ground Titan walks in its back half. There are no monsters here, but the epic scope, the moral weight, and the willingness to put its hero through hell feel exactly like Eren's arc.

8. Berserk

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Guts is a lone mercenary with a monstrous sword and a body covered in scars, hunting the demonic Apostles and the man who betrayed him. His story reaches back to a brotherhood of warriors and a horror that shattered it, leaving him marked for a lifetime of slaughter. The world is medieval, merciless, and crawling with nightmares. It is one of the darkest, most influential dark-fantasy tales ever told.

Berserk is the atmospheric foundation. It captures the reality of battlefield attrition, mercenary brotherhood, and human fragility against incomprehensible horrors, the same bleak textures Titan runs on. Most pointedly, Griffith's willingness to sacrifice his comrades for an imperial dream directly parallels Eren's final ideological gambit, the friend who becomes the greatest betrayal. It leans fully into dark fantasy rather than Titan's grounded sci-fi mystery, which keeps it mid-list, but the uncompromising tone and the betrayal at its heart are a direct line.

9. Tokyo Ghoul

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Synopsis: Ken Kaneki is an ordinary college student until a date with the wrong person leaves him half-turned into a ghoul, one of the flesh-eating creatures that secretly live among humans. Caught between two worlds, he has to survive a brutal hidden war while slowly losing his grip on who he is. The series is a dark, violent descent into identity and horror. Kaneki's transformation is one of anime's most harrowing.

Tokyo Ghoul focuses on the internal horror of being forced into a predatory species. Kaneki is an ordinary youth turned half-ghoul who wrestles with the moral agony of feeding on flesh while hunted by CCG investigators, and the series explores the tragedy that both sides are trapped in an inescapable cycle of slaughter, which is Titan's cruelest theme in miniature. The body horror, the human-turned-monster blurring that echoes Eren's own line, and the moral murk all land for Titan fans. It is more introspective and less epic, but the grim tone is a close cousin. Our Tokyo Ghoul filler list sorts out the rough patches.

10. Parasyte: The Maxim

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 4/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: Shinichi is a normal high schooler until an alien parasite tries to burrow into his brain and ends up stuck in his right hand instead. As more parasites quietly infest humanity, devouring people and wearing their faces, Shinichi and his strange new companion are caught in a war for survival. The series asks hard questions about what makes a monster, and what makes a human. It is tense, gory, and surprisingly thoughtful.

Parasyte is a grounded, psychological exploration of predatory creatures that butcher humans from within civilian society. Shinichi's hand is fused with a parasite, forcing him to adapt, lose his sentimentality, and evolve into an emotionless combatant to survive against cannibalistic horrors, which rhymes with the way Titan hardens its survivors into something colder. The visceral body horror, the heavy death toll, and the hard questions about humanity and violence echo Titan's darker instincts. It is smaller in scale, with no walls or armies, but the dread and the moral weight are a strong match.

11. Made in Abyss

Similarity Rating: 3/5 ⭐⭐⭐

Anime Overall Rating: 5/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Watch on: Prime Video

Synopsis: Riko lives on the edge of the Abyss, a vast, mysterious pit filled with ancient relics and horrors, where her mother vanished years ago. When she finds a robot boy at the bottom of a dig, the two begin a descent into the Abyss to find her, unaware of just how cruel it will become. The deeper they go, the more beautiful and the more brutal the world turns. Its adorable art style hides some of anime's most devastating gut-punches.

Made in Abyss shares Attack on Titan's environmental dread, its visceral body horror, and its sense of human vulnerability against an unforgiving, monstrous world. A journey into a beautiful place that grows steadily more horrifying, built on mystery and the willingness to inflict real suffering, echoes Titan's own dark surprises. It sits at the bottom because it trades the military geopolitical war for a downward survival expedition, but the beauty-meets-horror tone is a strong match.

A few that get recommended but watch differently

Search around for anime similar to Attack on Titan and a few big names come up that share a surface element but not the grim, tragic build. They are worth your time. We just want the match to feel honest.

Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood has the war, the conspiracy, and the gut-punches, but its heart is ultimately warm and hopeful in a way Titan refuses to be, so the tone lands softer. Jujutsu Kaisen and Chainsaw Man both deliver dark, bloody monster-hunting with real casualties, yet they run on modern shonen energy rather than Titan's bleak, world-spanning tragedy. All three are excellent. Just go in knowing they trade some of Titan's despair for a lighter touch.

Fill the void a finished masterpiece leaves

Attack on Titan ended its ten-year run in 2023, and The Last Attack gave the finale a theatrical sendoff, which means there is no new season coming and a very particular hole to fill. The good news is that plenty of shows capture a piece of what made it unmissable. Start at the top with Kabaneri of the Iron Fortress and 86 for the closest matches, feel the walled-in dread of The Promised Neverland, or sink into the revenge-and-war weight of Vinland Saga. The whole point of a good list of anime like Attack on Titan is to keep that dark, breathtaking intensity alive now that the walls have come down for good.

While you line it all up, come hang out with us at Kaminari, where our weekly newsletter rounds up the shows worth your time, the news that actually matters, and takes written for people who love this stuff as much as you do. We will keep flagging the best dark, epic anime as they land, so you never miss the next obsession.

FAQs

Is there an anime exactly like Attack on Titan?

Not a perfect twin, but two come very close. Kabaneri of the Iron Fortress is the direct studio sibling, made by Titan's own Wit Studio and director, with humanity walled in against man-eating monsters, while 86 matches the military tragedy and the systemic discrimination of Titan's later seasons almost note for note. Each nails a core piece of what made Titan great.

What is the best anime like Attack on Titan?

For the closest overall experience, Kabaneri of the Iron Fortress and 86 lead the pack, one for the premise and production, the other for the war tragedy and political weight. If you want the walled-in survival horror specifically, The Promised Neverland is the one to beat, with Vinland Saga close behind for the revenge and the moral descent.

What anime has monsters like Attack on Titan?

The strongest picks are Kabaneri of the Iron Fortress for its armored undead, Parasyte for its people-eating aliens, Claymore for its shape-shifting Yoma, and Tokyo Ghoul for its flesh-eating ghouls. Each centers humanity's survival against monstrous predators.

Is there an anime as dark as Attack on Titan?

Yes. Berserk, Vinland Saga, Tokyo Ghoul, and Made in Abyss all match or even outdo Titan's darkness, whether through grimdark brutality, unflinching war, body horror, or beauty that masks devastating cruelty.

The city-leveling clashes and the monster-of-the-week rhythm scratch the same giant-monster-spectacle itch Kaiju No. 8 runs on. It is a solo tokusatsu hero rather than a defense force, and a strange mystery pulls the story somewhere weirder, which keeps it mid-list, but the kaiju spectacle is a direct hit.

As more parasites quietly infest humanity, devouring people and wearing their faces, Shinichi and his strange new companion are caught in a war for survival. The series asks hard questions about what makes a monster, and what makes a human. It is tense, gory, and surprisingly thoughtful.

Parasyte digs into the tension of an alien creature taking over a human body, which puts its hero in a bind close to Kafka's. Shinichi ends up fused with a parasite and has to throw himself into high-speed, close-quarters brawls against the cannibalistic infiltrators hiding in plain sight, all while keeping his own transformation secret from his family and the police. The monsters-among-us threat and the body-horror change echo the kaiju-within hook at the heart of Kaiju No. 8. There is no defense force or big spectacle here, so it sits lower, but the human-and-monster-in-one-body pressure is a strong partial match.

The squad becomes a tight-knit family, and the mythology runs deeper than it first appears. The action is flashy and stylish.

Fire Force runs on specialized municipal defense brigades, the Special Fire Force, who scramble to urban disaster zones the moment the alarms sound to put down Infernals, the people who spontaneously combust into rampaging demons. That alarm-to-deployment rhythm, the ranked companies, and the found-family squad all feel a lot like Kafka's unit. The difference is that Fire Force leans harder into shonen tournament beats and flashy fantasy fire powers, and its hero is not a monster himself. Still, the brigade-versus-urban-monsters build is a solid match.

It is one of the most influential anime ever made.

So much of the modern kaiju-defense playbook traces back to Evangelion, now overseen by Studio Khara. The emergency siren alarms, the tactical command rooms coordinating a response, the artillery bombardments that bounce uselessly off giant invaders, and the biological war machines grown from the enemy's own DNA all show up here first, and Kaiju No. 8 clearly inherited that vocabulary. The difference is tone: Evangelion is a bleak psychological study rather than an underdog crowd-pleaser, so the heart is heavier and stranger. A couple that get recommended but watch differently

Godzilla Singular Point delivers plenty of kaiju, yet it is a slow, cerebral sci-fi puzzle about the science behind the monsters rather than a spectacle-driven shonen. Both are excellent in their own right. Just go in knowing they trade Kaiju No. 8's crew camaraderie and underdog heart for something more solitary or more heady.

Still sitting with Thorfinn's long road from vengeance toward peace? Plenty of anime like Vinland Saga deliver the same weight: grounded, brutally realistic stories with no fantasy and no easy heroes, carried by deep character study, grey morality, and a hard, honest look at violence and what it costs. Nothing fully replicates it, because its blend is genuinely rare, but the closest ones hit the same nerve.

The timing makes a watchlist worth it, too. Season 2 wrapped in 2023, and while a third season is widely expected to adapt Thorfinn's voyage east, no release date has been confirmed. So there is a real wait ahead, and these picks are built to fill it with the same grounded intensity.

Synopsis: During Prohibition-era America, Angelo Lagusa watches his entire family murdered by the mafia, then vanishes. Years later, a letter draws him back under a false name, and he worms his way into the very family that destroyed his, plotting an intricate revenge from the inside over the course of ninety-one days. Every bond he forms is a weapon and a wound. It is a tight, grounded crime tragedy with no wasted motion.

For Vinland Saga's revenge core, this is the closest match on the list. It is a completely grounded, fantasy-free story about a man who loses his family to violence and devotes himself to vengeance, only to be hollowed out by what it costs him, which is Thorfinn's early arc in a different century. The mature tone, the moral greyness, the real historical backdrop, and the hard look at where revenge actually leads make it feel like a cousin cut from the same cloth.

Standing between them and the treasure are escaped convicts, rogue soldiers, and a one-eyed warlord, each as dangerous as the last. The violence is brutal and the history is meticulously researched. It balances all of that with hunting, cooking, and genuine warmth.

The build match is the grounded historical seinen with real brutality and real heart: a story rooted in actual history, carried by damaged, morally complicated people, that never flinches from violence but refuses to be only about it. Like Vinland Saga, it treats its period and its cultures with care, and it finds humanity in the bloodshed. It is more of an adventure with an ensemble than a single-character study, which is the main difference, but the grounded, brutal, humane build is a direct hit.

3. Kingdom

Watch on: Crunchyroll

Synopsis: In the Warring States era of ancient China, a war orphan named Xin dreams of becoming a Great General of the Heavens, rising from the lowest rung through sheer will and skill on the battlefield. His path tangles with a young king determined to unify the land, and together they wade through massive, brutal campaigns. The war is depicted on an enormous scale, with real strategy and real cost. It is a sprawling historical epic.

The connection is the grounded historical war epic built on an underdog's growth: a fantasy-free story of ambition, loyalty, and survival across sweeping campaigns, where battles are won with tactics and paid for in blood. Xin's climb and the political weight around him echo the scope and the realism of Vinland Saga's wars. It is more rousing and heroic than Vinland's somber meditation on violence, which keeps it a step below, but the historical-war-epic build is a strong fit.

Haunted by the blood on his hands, he protects the people he meets while his violent past keeps catching up with him. The recent remake brings his story to modern animation. The darker prequel, Trust and Betrayal, is a brutal, grounded tragedy in its own right.

The build link is the arc at the heart of Vinland Saga: a man forged by violence who renounces killing and spends his life trying to atone. Kenshin's vow never to take another life is the same turn Thorfinn makes, the warrior deciding that true strength means refusing to use it, in a grounded historical setting. The main series runs lighter and more action-driven than Vinland, but the atonement-from-a-life-of-violence core is a near-perfect thematic match.

Johan is one of anime's greatest villains.

The connection is the grounded, mature seinen that treats its characters and its moral questions with total seriousness: no fantasy, no spectacle, just real people wrestling with guilt, violence, and what a person owes the world. Like Vinland Saga, it is a prestige character study that asks whether a good person can stay good in a brutal world. It is a modern thriller rather than a historical war epic, but the grounded depth and the moral gravity are squarely Vinland territory.

Synopsis: Guts is a lone mercenary with a monstrous sword and a body covered in scars, hunting the demonic forces and the friend who betrayed him. His story reaches back to a brotherhood of warriors and a horror that shattered it, setting him on a lifetime of vengeance. The medieval world is merciless and the violence is relentless. It is one of the most influential dark tales ever told.

The build match is the brutal medieval saga of violence, betrayal, and a warrior consumed by revenge, carried by one of the genre's deepest character studies. Guts and Thorfinn are kindred spirits, men defined by a loss that sent them down a path of blood, and the Golden Age arc in particular shares Vinland's grounded, war-torn weight. The one real caveat is the supernatural, since Berserk is dark fantasy with demons and curses where Vinland Saga stays strictly grounded, so the realism is where they part ways.

Its politics are as sharp as its gunfights.

The build connection is the grounded, fantasy-free world of violence and the characters trying to find meaning inside it: no magic, no chosen ones, just mercenaries, dealers, and the real cost of the trade. Jonah's hatred of the very violence he is surrounded by echoes Vinland Saga's central question about whether peace is possible in a brutal world. It is slicker and more modern than Vinland, but the grounded, morally grey, character-driven build fits.
